Taking HRT in perimenopause may ward off cardiovascular disease

New Scientist September 24, 2026

Taking hormone replacement therapy during the perimenopause or early menopause may reduce the risk of heart attacks and stroke. A study of nearly 2800 women over 20 years suggests that starting HRT around this time lowers the risk of serious cardiovascular events. However, much more research is required to understand how the treatment may have this effect and the optimal time to take it.

“I want to emphasise: our study does not support using menopausal [hormonal] therapy to prevent cardiovascular disease,” says Samar El Khoudary at Virginia Commonwealth University.

Everything is perimenopause now – but what if it’s not?

A recent study in Spain suggests that nearly 80 per cent of women experience vasomotor symptoms – hot flushes and night sweats – around the menopause. However, other research from this year suggests this varies substantially around the world. These symptoms can be treated via HRT, which is available in different formulations, such as tablets, patches, gels and sprays. These replace oestrogen and progesterone, hormones that fall as the menopause approaches.

Advertisement

The controversy around HRT started in 2002, when a large trial linked it to an increased risk of breast cancer, heart attacks and stroke. The method of this trial, and subsequent ones, has since been called into question. Newer research has also put the results into context by comparing them with other lifestyle choices, such as alcohol intake. In 2021, a study found that HRT doesn’t increase the risk of early death.

What’s more, earlier studies generally looked at women around the age of 60. This is despite menopause usually occurring between the ages of 45 and 55, and some people taking HRT during the perimenopause.

Free newsletter

Now, El Khoudary and her colleagues have looked at 2737 participants in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation, which was made up of women in the US aged 42 to 52 at enrollment. All these women experienced hot flushes and night sweats, but only 755 took some form of HRT over the 20-year study period.

During this time, 224 fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events occurred. The researchers estimated that the women who started HRT 10 years or less after the onset of vasomotor symptoms were 27 per cent less likely to experience these events than those who didn’t take HRT. The effect was much less clear among women who initiated the treatment more than 10 years after their onset, says El Khoudary. The timing seems to be “very critical”, she says.

As to why HRT may have this effect, El Khoudary says the “underlying mechanisms are complex and multifactorial”.

Oestrogen is involved in regulating cholesterol and blood sugar levels, and contributes to blood vessel flexibility. Previous research suggests that HRT dose and formulation – which may vary depending on the person’s age – affect artery structure, which may impact heart health. The perimenopause is also increasingly being recognised as a period of distinct vascular changes.

The brain undergoes a full renovation during menopause. Although these changes are profound, we’re learning that the long-term impact needn’t be all bad

The researchers also found that HRT’s seemingly protective effect was most pronounced among the Black participants, who may be more likely to experience vasomotor symptoms. Further research is needed to uncover why the results vary among women of different races, says El Khoudary.

For now, people shouldn’t start HRT to prevent cardiovascular events. Another recent study suggests that oral HRT is linked to a 0.09 per cent higher risk of venous thromboembolism (the formation of blood clots in the veins), a 0.06 per cent higher risk for ischaemic stroke (when a blood clot or other blockage cuts off blood supply to the brain) and a 0.03 per cent higher risk of a heart attack per year.

“The most important thing to understand about observational studies is that they cannot establish causality,” says Tara Iyer at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. El Khoudary now wants to see randomised, placebo-controlled trials testing the cardiovascular effects of HRT during the perimenopause and early menopause.

JAMA Internal Medicine DOI: 10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.2922

Blood test could gauge if a baby has a dangerous infection in 15 minutes

New Scientist September 26, 2026

A blood test could determine whether a feverish baby has a bacterial or viral infection in 15 to 20 minutes. This would help doctors gauge whether the infection is serious or may pass without treatment, which could prevent unnecessary use of antibiotics.

When babies are brought into hospital with fever, they “are considered high-risk until proven otherwise”, says Tommaso Bellini at the Giannina Gaslini Institute in Genoa, Italy.

Severe meningitis outbreak caused by bacteria that took genes from microbiome

A fever can be the result of several things, including infection by viruses or bacteria. These different types of pathogens require different medications. Furthermore, most common viruses are fairly benign, while bacterial infections are generally more dangerous, says Bellini.

Advertisement

Existing tests to gauge infection type take at least a few hours, so babies with fever are often given antibiotics against bacteria as a precautionary measure. But only about 15 per cent of them actually have a serious bacterial infection, says Bellini. This unnecessary use of antibiotics helps drive the spread of bacterial resistance.

To develop a test that determines infection type, Bellini and his colleagues followed 85 babies, all younger than 90 days old, who were brought into emergency rooms with fever after previously having no serious health concerns. The team took blood samples and tested for two proteins: CD64 and CD169.

Previous studies have shown that these proteins become more common in certain blood cells when the body responds to infections. CD64 is made at higher levels in response to bacteria and is found on the surface of white blood cells called neutrophils. CD169 rises in response to viruses and appears on the outer membranes of monocytes, another type of white blood cell.

Free newsletter

By comparing the levels of both proteins in neutrophils and monocytes, the test correctly identified all 15 cases of bacterial infection, 44 incidences of viral infection and 26 cases of no infection. Bellini presented the results at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris, France.

The results came through in 15 to 20 minutes in a lab, says Bellini, who is trying to develop a version that can be used as quickly in hospitals.

This builds on several years of research to develop a CD64/CD169 test. Fabrice Malergue at Beckman Coulter Life Sciences in Marseille, France, has spent much of the past decade working on it. In 2021, his team found that CD64 and CD169 levels reliably distinguish between bacterial and viral infections among adults in an emergency room.

Heartland virus and Bourbon virus, which are transmitted by lone star ticks, have killed at least seven people in the US

Other groups have since replicated that finding, found ways to perform the test more quickly and easily, and demonstrated that it works in children. Performing the test on babies in a hospital setting is a significant advance, says Malergue. It was crucial to investigate the test in this age group because their immune systems are still developing, which meant “some people had doubts about the capacity of these [CD64 and CD169] markers to arise”, he says.

Malergue says one of his collaborators used the test in Martinique during an outbreak of dengue fever, which is caused by a virus and is usually mild. The collaborator found that some people actually had a bacterial infection called leptospirosis, which is life-threatening without antibiotics.

Bellini now hopes to assess the test in a trial of 300 to 500 infants at multiple hospitals. Meanwhile, Malergue and his colleagues have developed a benchtop machine that can quickly analyse finger-prick blood samples to determine whether an infection is viral or bacterial, which is approved for research use.

Virtual green spaces and classical music reduce blood pressure in hospital

New Scientist September 25, 2026

Gazing at a flowing river while listening to classical music could lower the blood pressure of people in the emergency room. Luckily, as these landscapes and live orchestras are hard to come by in hospitals, virtual reality and playlists do the job.

Dangerously high blood pressure, known as hypertensive urgency, is common among people in intensive-care settings. Medication can prevent it from causing damage to the eyes, heart and brain. However, relaxation approaches, such as looking at aquarium scenes and listening to classical music, have also shown promise.

What is the best workout to lower your blood pressure?

Now, Safa Dönmez at the University of Health Sciences in Ankara, Turkey, and his colleagues have combined these two approaches to relaxation. The team recruited 130 adults who arrived in an emergency department with hypertensive urgency. These patients are often anxious, which can make their bodies release stress hormones that tighten blood vessels and further hike up blood pressure, says Dönmez.

Advertisement

The researchers gave all the participants standard medication to reduce blood pressure. Half also viewed a scene of the Columbia River in Canada flowing through a forest via a VR headset while listening to a soothing playlist of classical music from the likes of Debussy, Bach and Mozart. “Overall, the aim was to create a calm, natural and relaxing environment,” says Dönmez.

Free newsletter

Before treatment, the participants’ arterial pressure was about 130 to 138 mmHg, on average. Fifteen minutes after the intervention, it had dropped by about 12mmHG among those who only took medication, compared with about 16 mmHg for those also having the VR and music experience. The results were presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris, France.

Verónica Saldaña-Ortiz at the European University in Madrid, Spain, says that seeing such results so quickly is clinically significant. “In an emergency department, even a relatively simple non-pharmacological intervention that helps patients feel calmer during the initial phase of care could be clinically valuable,” she says.

After 30 minutes, the difference had shrunk, and by 60 minutes, the blood pressure readings of the two groups were about the same.

The intervention’s initial positive effect on blood pressure may be related to its impact on anxiety, says Dönmez. Anxiety fell by a greater amount in the VR/music group, according to ratings using a questionnaire called the State Anxiety Inventory.

“The results are consistent with a growing body of work that shows that even virtual nature can help reduce stress, including reductions in blood pressure, in stressful situations,” says Mathew White at the University of Exeter, UK. “Extending this approach to an emergency room setting seems like a wonderful idea, and hopefully results can be replicated and more widely implemented if confirmed.”

The VR and classical music were delivered together, so we cannot determine whether the benefit came from the music, the virtual environment or both, says Saldaña-Ortiz. Dönmez says the team is planning to do larger studies with longer follow-up periods to disentangle this and see whether patients choosing their own music makes a difference.

Is China catching up to the US and SpaceX on reusable rockets?

New Scientist September 25, 2026

Last month, LandSpace – China’s commercial SpaceX rival – launched a Zhuque-3 rocket and landed its booster stage safely back on Earth. The mission was a first for China, but the country has yet to actually use a booster more than once – something that SpaceX has routinely done hundreds of times. Can China catch up in the reusable rocket race?

China’s 15th Five-Year Plan sets out the country’s ambitions to become a “space power” by 2030, including developing reusable rockets that will be crucial to its goals to put Chinese astronauts on the moon and build a Starlink alternative.

Zeno Leoni at King’s College London says space is of growing importance for militaries and economies, and a stormy geopolitical climate means that nations need their own ability to cheaply and quickly put things into orbit or risk being shut out by others.

Advertisement

SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight

“If you look at previous speeches from [Chinese President] Xi Jinping, there is the idea that if you are the leading technological power, then you also are the leading geopolitical superpower,” says Leoni. The country has an ambitious list of areas it wants to master by the centenary of its founding in 2049 including AI, quantum, fusion and space, and while Leoni says it will overtake the US in some of these, it can’t hope to master them all.

Kevin Sagis at the University of Texas at Austin says the benefits of reusable rockets are simple: they’re cheap. “The cost of the Saturn V rocket in the Apollo days – that we threw away after every launch – was about a billion dollars. The SLS is about $5 billion. It’s just not sustainable,” he says.

Sagis sees strong parallels between the unfolding reusable rocket space race, and the cold war space race between the Soviet Union and the US. China has many of the same advantages now that the Soviet Union had then: a one-party government that can coral huge resources and single-mindedly chase a target unswayed by election cycles and changing leaders, a strong motivation for success and loose regulation.

See Helen Sharman at New Scientist Live 2026

SpaceX is often said to be taking a new, extremely capitalist approach – testing fast, failing often and rapidly reiterating – that’s more like Silicon Valley than traditional aerospace. But Sagis says that while this is an advantage, it’s also a return to the bold Apollo days at NASA. “It’s sort of come full circle,” he says. And he believes that it’s an approach that is paying off for SpaceX.

“What they’re aspiring to do is something audacious. Their talent and their expertise is exceptional. If you look at their track record, every mission is better than the previous one. I’d be shocked if we don’t look back at this and assess it as a success,” says Sagis.

But Sagis also sees risks in the US system. He warns that it will be important to learn from the cold war race and not lose interest or pull funding and scrap plans if the US lags behind at one point. Instead, the focus should be on the long-term benefits of advanced space travel. Russia put the first satellite into orbit, then the first animal, man and woman, says Sagis – but the US still put the first man on the moon.

“It’s the hare and the tortoise,” says Sagis.

SpaceX rocket crashes into moon at 8700 kilometres per hour

China also has an advantage shared by the Soviet Union in that it is more tolerant of risk. An expensive failure or the injury or death of an astronaut could put an end to space ambitions, but Sagis sees that as less likely to occur in China, where politicians are less concerned with public perception and winning elections. “Space isn’t risk-free, right? If you wanna do something audacious, you have to accept some risk,” says Sagis.

As far as today’s technology goes, China is 10 years behind, says Chris Ellis at the University of Nottingham in the UK. But he also points out that the race isn’t one linear problem solved from start to finish, but a cluster of hundreds of small challenges – and that China may be ahead in some. For instance, China’s Zhuque-2 became the first methane-fuelled rocket to reach orbit in 2023, a feat yet to be matched by SpaceX.

Both countries have other projects on the go; the US has Blue Origin and China has Galactic Energy’s Pallas-1, which flew for the first time this month – albeit with no attempt at recovery. The founder of Chinese space firm Deep Blue Aerospace has gone on record to say that China can catch up with SpaceX by 2030.

SpaceX’s secretive plans to deliver cargo to Earth from space

The Zhuque-3 is LandSpace’s latest design, which first flew only last year. It’s just 66 metres tall, making it more like SpaceX’s 70-metre-tall Falcon-9. Landspace doesn’t yet have a rocket along the lines of SpaceX’s vast 124-metre Starship, so it still has plenty of catching up to do. But Zhuque-3 will allow the country to rapidly and cheaply launch satellites for a competing Starlink internet constellation.

China’s state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation also has the Long March 9 rocket still under development. It will feature a reusable first stage, and there are long-term plans to make the second stage reusable too. Some variants of another rocket under development, Long March 10, will also be partially reusable, and a test earlier this year recovered the first stage of a Long March 10 at sea.

Ellis says that China may not be as open about its progress as SpaceX is being, perhaps distorting public perception of its capabilities. Chinese companies and SpaceX will be scouring footage of each others’ launches for clues and information, he adds, and they may all choose to make deliberately vague disclosures.

There are now over 10,000 satellites in orbit, more than at any point in history, and this growing number is starting to reveal how solar storms could disrupt internet mega constellations like SpaceX’s Starlink

“They also don’t want to be sharing what they’ve lost. So I think China might have lost some more [rockets in testing] and they won’t publish it because that’s not what they want the world to see,” says Ellis.

Because of the direct applications to national security, space research is constrained by export controls and a certain amount of state secrecy. Ellis says that his own research is no different and that it has to pass both internal and government vetting before publication. He believes that, in a perfect world where countries could work together on designs, we’d likely already have bases on the moon.

“A lot of researchers working at universities are very keen to collaborate with other people, but when you’ve got big money and geopolitics involved, you don’t have that luxury,” he says.

Anthropic’s discovery will, at best, be just another gene-editing tool

New Scientist September 25, 2026

The pioneers of the CRISPR gene-editing tool won a Nobel prize in 2020, and for good reason. The breakthrough has revolutionised biology, and is also transforming medicine and farming. Now, AI company Anthropic has announced that it has discovered an enzyme system with properties “reminiscent of CRISPR”. In fact, though, the two discoveries aren’t remotely comparable.

On 23 September, Anthropic said it has turned its attention to biology and that its large language model, called Claude, has discovered “a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats”.

How CRISPR therapy could cure everything from cancer to infertility

What Anthropic did was ask Claude to search through a large DNA database for “interesting new” proteins of a kind called a reverse transcriptase. These are enzymes that can make a DNA copy of an RNA sequence. Normally, DNA is transcribed into RNA, hence the reverse part.

Advertisement

Why is Anthropic interested in reverse transcriptases? Because if the aim is to genetically engineer anything from bacteria to people, being able to add specific DNA sequences to specific sites in a genome is really useful. There are already ways of doing this, but they all have limitations.

Claude agents found around 200,000 sequences in the database that probably code for reverse transcriptases. While analysing one family of reverse transcriptases, which are found in bacteria-infecting viruses, one agent detected a series of repeated sequences next to the sequence for the reverse transcriptase.

“I can see by eye a tandem repeat array… that’s a CRISPR-like… repeat array?!” the agent outputted.

What you need to know here is that CRISPR stands for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. In other words, an area of DNA where there are lots of short repeated sequences separated by non-repeating DNA.

Free newsletter

Such repeats were first spotted in E. coli in 1987 by researchers in Japan and later dubbed CRISPR by Francisco Mojica at the University of Alicante in Spain. In 2005, Mojica reported that the pieces of non-repeating DNA match bits of viral DNA.

He correctly deduced this must be some kind of bacterial immune system, but it took years of research by many different teams to uncover how it works, with a protein called CRISPR-Cas9 playing a key role. The real breakthrough came in 2012 when Jennifer Doudna at the University of California, Berkeley, and her colleagues worked out how to create pieces of RNA that can hook up with the CRISPR-Cas9 protein and guide it to destroy specific sequences. This was the start of CRISPR gene editing, which has revolutionised biology.

So it is really intriguing that Claude has found a similar set of repeats in bacteria-infecting viruses. It was already known that some viruses have CRISPR systems, but this is something different that is worth studying further.

Bacteria-killing phage viruses souped up with DNA-destroying CRISPR appear to have helped clear up a very serious infection caused by antibiotic-resistant E. coli

In terms of significance, however, Claude’s work is comparable to the 1987 discovery in E. coli, not the 2012 breakthrough that won a Nobel prize. And with regard to AI contributions to biology, Claude’s work isn’t even close to being in the same league as DeepMind’s AlphaFold system for predicting protein structure, which is proving to be truly transformative.

Will Claude’s discovery lead to powerful new gene-editing tools? The context here is that we have discovered many CRISPR variants, along with a few other natural systems – most notably bridge recombinases – that could be useful for gene editing.

What’s more, proteins such as CRISPR-Cas9 have now been extensively altered and evolved in the lab to make them better for gene editing. For instance, base editors – which are already saving lives – are CRISPR proteins engineered to change a single letter at a time without cutting DNA strands, as the original Cas9 protein does.

When standard leukaemia treatments failed, 13-year-old Alyssa Tapley was told she had only weeks left – but then she was offered an experimental procedure

Then there are prime editors, which consist of a reverse transcriptase fused with part of the Cas9 protein, that can add short sequences of DNA to genomes. In other words, we have already adapted reverse transcriptases for RNA-targeted gene editing.

It is impressive that Claude has identified what the Anthropic team is calling array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ART. And it is possible, if unlikely, that this viral system works in a unique way that allows us to do things that cannot be done with existing genetic tools. But there is a lot more work to be done to find this out, and at best the outcome will be one more gene-editing tool in a rapidly expanding set.

See Turi King at New Scientist Live 2026

Mathematician discovers rare eight-faced shape

New Scientist September 25, 2026

A scientist has discovered a strange new eight-faced shape in which every face touches every other face, using a set of simple integer coordinates.

Mathematicians can define abstract patterns, describing which vertices, edges and faces should connect. But working out whether those rules can actually be turned into an object in three-dimensional space, without parts intersecting where they shouldn’t, can be extremely difficult.

Ruslan Mizhaev, an independent researcher and design engineer, has produced a geometric realisation of a genus-3 polyhedron – essentially a surface with three holes – made from eight flat, nine-sided faces. It has 24 vertices and 36 edges, with three faces meeting at every vertex.

Advertisement

Why physicists think geometry is the path to a theory of everything

“There are eight flat, polygonal faces, and each is a neighbour of all seven others along an edge,” says Mizhaev. “Together, they form a closed surface with three handles.”

In topology – the study of a shape’s properties that can’t be changed by stretching, twisting or squeezing the shape – a handle is essentially a hole or tunnel through a surface. A doughnut, for example, has one handle.

That makes the object reminiscent of a tetrahedron and the better-known Szilassi polyhedron, which also have faces that are all neighbours. However, in Mizhaev’s design, some pairs of faces share two edges, rather than exactly one.

See Jim Al-Khalili at New Scientist Live 2026

Mizhaev says he stumbled across the property, rather than setting out to find it, while experimenting with polyhedral surfaces in computer-aided design (CAD) software. The underlying structure isn’t entirely new – it is something Mizhaev first described it in 2020.

But the new work gives all 24 vertices integer coordinates, alongside equations that allow other mathematicians to check the shape, ensuring that the faces are flat, the surface closes properly and no parts accidentally intersect (which can be a common issue in shapes like this).

The discovery is an interesting one, but should be seen as a piece of a larger puzzle, rather than an entirely new innovation, says Lars Schewe at the University of Edinburgh, UK. “It’s more a small piece that we didn’t have before,” says Schewe. The result doesn’t overturn existing conjectures, he says, but “constructing these has always been a difficult task”.

Physicists have created a 3D shape called the cosmohedron, which can be used to reconstruct the quantum wavefunction of the universe – and potentially do away with the idea of space-time as the underlying fabric of the universe

The reason it is so difficult to construct such shapes is that there is no reliable way to do so. One brute-force approach involves writing down a huge set of equations specifying where every vertex can sit and how all the faces must fit together, says Schewe – but that approach can rapidly become practically impossible to solve.

Researchers instead often depend on computer searches, geometric intuition or even physical models. Mizhaev used ChatGPT to help with some verification calculations and to write Python scripts for the new version of his shape. But he says the original shape was developed in 2020, before he began using ChatGPT.

For Schewe, the gap between describing which parts of a shape can connect and actually building it is what makes these problems interesting. “I can tell you these are the rules,” he says. “But when I try to build it and I try to draw it, I can’t do it.”

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.17700

The first season of Heroes is almost perfect – here’s why

New Scientist September 25, 2026

You rarely appreciate the significance of a moment while you are still living through it. But that is exactly what happened to me, 20 years ago this month, when a show called Heroes first aired.

As you may have gathered from the title, it followed ordinary people whose genes have blessed (or cursed) them with extraordinary abilities, from time travel to telepathy. Made in the wake of the Human Genome Project, it was an elaborately plotted mystery, blending comic book aesthetics with a glancing interest in evolution. And for the past two decades, it has had the dubious honour of becoming a byword for failure: after a stellar first season, Heroes limped its way through three more outings of questionable quality.

The minute I saw Heroes, I knew I was changed. It was the first TV series to set a fire in my head, at age 10. If I wasn’t watching it, I was talking about it; if I wasn’t talking about it, I was thinking about it. Chances are I was probably dreaming about it, too. But the extent of my obsession, combined with that notorious drop-off in quality, has stopped me from rewatching it or its spin-off, Heroes Reborn, in the years since.

Advertisement

The 4 best science-fiction shows of 2026 so far

That changed last month with the sad news that Hayden Panettiere, who played the show’s most iconic character, Claire Bennet, had died. Since then, I have been revisiting that almost-perfect first season – and you should do the same.

Even before its narrative spiralled out of control, Heroes had a sprawling ensemble of leads. Claire, a 16-year-old cheerleader living in Texas, was the most consequential. Her body rapidly regenerates its cells when injured, making her practically indestructible – and attracting the attention of Sylar, a superpowered serial killer. Meanwhile, geneticist Mohinder Suresh seeks to complete his late father’s work by contacting similarly gifted individuals, such as Peter Petrelli, a hospice nurse who dreams of flying, and Isaac Mendez, who can paint the future when under the influence of heroin.

Heroes, like Isaac, had a knack for striking images. Its first season is full of them: a cracked pair of horn-rimmed glasses; an office worker from Tokyo teleporting to Times Square in New York; a nuclear blast that Claire, somehow, can help prevent. “Save the cheerleader, save the world,” time traveller Hiro Nakamura tells Peter. This uncanny ability to distil essence and theme into potent symbols or phrases was the series’ own superpower. Not to mention the music: a whirling updraft of drones and chimes, featuring ethereal vocals from L. Shankar, it became a landmark score in television history.

Fabulous time travel novel is part-thriller and part-romance

It’s easy to dismiss Heroes as a Lost-alike: it was perhaps the best in a flurry of shows trying to emulate that legendary series, right down to its characteristic blend of science fiction and mysticism. But like Lost, Heroes explains a lot about what high-concept TV has become today – and has admirable qualities that its successors are thoroughly lacking.

It is a wholly original idea from creator Tim Kring, albeit one inflected with the tropes of classic comic books. It is also stuffed with action – certain plotlines, like psychic cop Matt Parkman’s collaboration with the FBI in the hunt for Sylar, could have been a show all on their own. And it proves that a show that captures true brilliance, however infrequently, will always be worth watching.

So I implore you to watch (or rewatch) the first season of Heroes. You may be averse to starting a series known to nosedive, but, as I have explained to many sceptical friends over the years, it is worth the hurt. And upon rewatching with an adult’s eyes, I have appreciated just how special Panettiere was as Claire. Her performance deserves to be remembered as one of the best of the 2000s.

Taranaki solar-powered piggery tackles rising costs and welfare reforms

New Zealand Herald September 27, 2026

Karl Stanley in the farrowing shed at Stanley Bros. Photo / RNZ, Sally Round

By Sally Round of RNZ

Taranaki pig farmer Karl Stanley hopes a multimillion-dollar extension to his piggery, powered by solar energy, will help future-proof the business amid changing welfare regulations, increasing costs and consumer demands.

The new 75m x 16m shed, which will house up to 1000 grower pigs and allow reconfiguration of the rest of Stanley Bros’ 5000-pig operation near Ōpunake, is well underway.

With automatically controlled temperature, lighting and ventilation systems, it’s impressed Stanley. “It’s going to be a cracker of a shed when it’s done,” he told RNZ’s Country Life.

“We’ve got a long road ahead of us, but we’re up for the challenge.”

Stanley, who originally started out in viticulture and winemaking, came back to the family farm 12 years ago.

His grandfather and great-uncle bought the original farm, a rehab block, and farmed both dairy cows and pigs.

That was continued by Stanley’s father and his brother.

Six years ago, the family decided to expand the pig operation and move into cropping “because we thought that we could make better utilisation of our fertiliser that the pigs were creating for us”.

The 133ha farm now grows silage, hay and maize for neighbouring livestock farmers, “and we do it on 100% natural fertiliser”.

The “farrowing [birthing] to finish” operation runs 500 sows and delivers 240 to 260 grown-on pigs weekly to the domestic market, Stanley said.

Stanley Bros is among the 52% of New Zealand’s commercial pig farms that keep pigs fully indoors.

Stanley’s grandfather used to keep his sows outside, but the family learnt Taranaki’s volcanic soils were not suitable.

“Pigs can tend to turn the place over in the mud pretty quick.”

Going indoors was also a way of staying viable “when you’re competing with the foreign pork coming in”.

Three years ago, a $1 million upgrade to the four farrowing units saw larger pens and nesting areas alongside the farrowing crates, which restrict the sow’s movement.

“We’ve always had this mentality on the farm that we’d always be hoping to be two or three steps ahead.”

The welfare code is tightening to reduce the time sows spend in the metal crates (from a maximum of 33 days to seven).

Moveable rails will be mandated and minimum space for grower pigs increased by 13.3%.

These changes must happen by the end of 2035.

Debate continues over whether farrowing crates should still be allowed at all, after animal welfare advocates won a High Court case in 2020 banning them outright, as in a handful of European countries.

That ruling was superseded by an easing of regulations brought in by the coalition Government in 2025, with a 10-year transition period.

Stanley said his new shed will lower stocking density throughout the farm and should be up and running by Christmas.

“Our changes will be certainly towards making sure that we’re well and truly ahead of the new regulations.

“Being steps ahead gives you flexibility and also better efficiencies, but also just being a few steps ahead means that you can really get yourself scope.”

Stanley took Country Life on a tour of the piggery and farrowing area, where newborn piglets scurried between a nesting box under a heat lamp to suckle on their mum, who is restricted to lying – enclosed by the rails – for two and a half weeks, able to sit up but not move around.

“It’s 100% protection of the piglet. A sow can be a little bit clumsy at times and lay-ons are certainly a concern,” he said.

“When the new system gets put in place with the temporary confinement, she’ll be confined for the first three days after farrowing and then she will be able to hop out and rotate around and do her thing.”

He hopes the current 9% piglet mortality rate will not climb further under the new system, which will see a refit to allow the rails to be pushed back.

“It’s going to find that balance between the welfare and protection of the piglets and also the welfare of the sow.

“Probably the hardest part is we’re competing with imported product that’s not following the same standards.”

Stanley’s refit comes as the pork industry continues to warn that local producers are struggling against a flood of lower-welfare imports.

He hopes to make changes to the first farrowing unit in the next year to 18 months, then acclimatise staff and fine-tune things “to make sure that the piglet welfare and the sow’s welfare is at the optimum and before we make the changes to the rest of the facility”.

Along from the farrowing area, a nursery houses hordes of tiny piglets in 22C warmth, “running around and being silly buggers like they want to be”, Stanley said.

Welfare regulations require enrichment, which Stanley said would be enhanced in the new development.

“We’ve gone from little ballcock balls that they can push around and play with or else going to the chains, which they quite enjoy ... because they sit there and chew it with their teeth and just something for them to do – a bit of fun.

“We’ll be certainly adding more.”

Stanley said experts from Europe – where some countries’ welfare regulations are tightening too – had advised on the new development.

“They’re 100% to increase the square metreage of the entire farm without really increasing the actual production.

“So this expenditure is not a gain in production, unfortunately, but it’s certainly going to give us a better, how would I say, a better future knowing that we’ve got that scope.”

The adjoining 400-panel solar farm, put in two years ago, produces 200 kilowatts, enough to power the piggery from 9am to 5pm during the summer, with lower production during the winter, Stanley said.

It’s a saving of $75,000 annually and with power at 10% of the farm’s cost, he hopes to invest further in wind turbines and batteries to create more energy.

“It’s a great investment and it’s good for us, lowers our footprint.”

Stanley said the overall investment had been daunting and had caused “a few headaches” but he hoped consumers would back New Zealand pork growers like him.

“We’re doing our part and we just need that support back.”

New Zealand Herald September 27, 2026

Firefighters were called to numerous wind-related incidents in Central Hawke's Bay on Sunday. Photo / NZME

One person has serious injuries after a campervan was blown onto its side while travelling on a Hawke’s Bay state highway.

The incident was one of many reported to emergency services as severe gusts hit the region, in particular through Central Hawke’s Bay, on Sunday afternoon.

A police spokeswoman said emergency services were called to the campervan crash on State Highway 50 near Tikokino Rd about 2.45pm.

The road was blocked in both directions, and the serious crash unit called, as firefighters worked to free two trapped people from the vehicle.

One person in the campervan had a serious injury, while the other had a minor injury, the spokeswoman said.

The pair were taken to hospital, and the road was reopened around 6.30pm.

Email us

Just minutes before the crash, a truck travelling on an exposed stretch of State Highway 2 near Takapau had its trailer blown over.

A Fire and Emergency NZ spokeswoman said the truck stayed upright, but both lanes of the highway through Central Hawke’s Bay were blocked by it.

A police spokeswoman said there were no reports of injuries, but a crane was requested to right the trailer.

Firefighters were also called to at least six other wind-related incidents in Central Hawke’s Bay, including three burnoffs spreading, and several trees down.

In one incident, on Hatuma Rd, a grass fire was sparked when trees brought down power lines.

After power was isolated, firefighters extinguished the small fire.

Later on Sunday night, firefighters were also called to a crash on Waimārama Rd, Waimārama.

One person had moderate injuries after their car rolled about 9.45pm and they were taken to hospital.

A Fire and Emergency NZ spokeswoman said it had been a “very busy day” for volunteers and emergency services.

MetService meterologist Silvia Martino said winds reached significant levels, particularly in Central Hawke’s Bay and Dannevirke.

Between 3pm and 4pm, gusts of 84km/h were recorded at Napier Airport. There was a 117km/h gust on the Takapau Plains station between 1.30pm and 2pm.

In the foothills of the Ruahine Range, there was a 144km/h gust recorded, while in the perennially exposed Cape Turnagain a whopping 174km/h gust was recorded.

Letters: New Zealand could lead the way at the UN General Assembly and declare neutrality

New Zealand Herald September 27, 2026

World leaders have been gathering at the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York. Photo / Getty Images

The benefits to New Zealand of neutrality

When New Zealand gets to speak at the United Nations General Assembly, it would be a great time to set an example to other countries and declare ourselves “neutral”. In 1987, we gained notoriety by becoming “nuclear-free” and many other nations have subsequently followed our example.

Permanent neutrality has already been adopted by Switzerland, Austria, Ireland and others so we wouldn’t be the first. However, it seems a good strategy to me as it would enable us to have excellent trading relationships with both the world superpowers – the United States and China – without appearing to play favourites.

It might also mean that going forward we could prioritise our armed forces’ resources. Maybe the ailing Navy frigates could be better replaced with smaller vessels designed to protect our fisheries.

AI tells me that the three most aggressive countries in the world are Israel, Russia and, top of the list by far, the US.

I would suggest that Israel is too busy with Iran and likewise Russia with Ukraine. The US needs us for our beef and, given that we love Coca-Cola and McDonald’s so much, are highly unlikely to invade us any time soon.

So to summarise, if we were “neutral”, then we could happily get on trading with everyone going forward and save lots of money on frigates.

Glen Stanton, Mairangi Bay.

Blasts from the past

Christopher Luxon seems to be basing his campaign on repeating negativity about Labour’s nine taxes.

I would love to know what those nine taxes are and I wonder if he could list them if asked.

I realise that in campaign mode all sorts of things are claimed and counter-claimed but aren’t we all sick of hearing from Luxon and Willis about what Labour did in office? We know, we lived through that time (or most of us did).

As far as many of us are concerned, Labour did what it had to do in an unprecedented pandemic and, guided by the World Health Organisation, saved many New Zealanders’ lives.

In the process, it inconvenienced a lot of people who can’t forgive that, but it was inevitable at the time. But we know all that and it is very patronising and unnecessary of the coalition to keep harping on about it as if we don’t.

Meanwhile, we can all see what this Government has done as we wait for hours in ED, try to get to see a GP in under three weeks or try to make ends meet in the supermarket.

There is no excuse this time for the appalling rise in the cost of living. But all we hear from National is what Labour did or didn’t do.

Sue Rawson, Pāpāmoa Beach.

How to handle AI

While Professor Alexander Gillespie rightly urges the Government to take a precautionary approach to AI technology (Sept 25), it must be noted that our everyday use of digital devices has thoroughly addicted us to the convenience and speed they offer.

AI and the reckless profusion of data centres are the inevitable progression of our utter dependency on this technology.

Captured governments and regulators are now woven into the powerful profit-driven technocracy, effectively disabled from managing risk and exercising precaution. They just roll over and play ball with the big guys.

Where was the Precautionary Principle when the massive 5G rollout of 2019-2020 proceeded without safety testing for effects on humans and the environment?

Over 200 international scientists called for a 5G moratorium and were ignored. Caution was tossed to the winds of hype and profit.

If the AI horse has bolted onto the fast track, it is people, not governments, who must rein in the excesses through our daily choices.

Reduce the digitalisation of our interactions and the densification of our living spaces.

Michael Fleck, Waiheke Island.

Protecting our parks

Your editorial “Global acclaim is great, but can Kiwis still afford their own backyard?” (Sept 24) rightly argues that the New Zealand we sell to the world must remain within reach of those who live here.

In Auckland, regional parks have long done that job: ratepayer-funded coast, farmland and bush, with low-cost campsites and baches close to the city; there is no $5000-a-night lodge required.

The question is whether that network will keep pace with Auckland’s growth. If Aucklanders in 30 years are to have somewhere affordable to holiday, Auckland Council needs to plan for it now by reviewing its Open Space Strategy to expand regional parks, not just maintain them. Future generations need to secure the land while it is still available.

Luella Bartlett, chair of Friends of Regional Parks Auckland.

Ministry delays rules on too-hot homes

New Zealand Herald September 27, 2026

Jared Laidlaw says the aluminium front door behind him can get so hot to the touch in summer that it burns. Photo / RNZ, Kate Newton

By Kate Newton of RNZ

Advocates for people living in overheating new builds are dismayed that officials will not consider comprehensive changes to fix the issue until 2031.

Residents of the glut of townhouses and apartments built in the last few years have repeatedly raised concerns about dangerous heat in their homes during summer, because of common design flaws.

The Building Research Association and Green Building Council are among organisations advocating for changes to the Building Code, which currently does not include any controls on overheating or maximum internal temperatures.

However, Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment officials have confirmed the issue would not be part of a regular code review in 2028, and instead would be considered during the subsequent review in 2031.

“We’re really shocked to hear that we’re facing a significant delay in dealing with this,” Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles said.

“That’s hugely alarming when you talk to these families and they’re in sweltering conditions.”

Jared Laidlaw and his family moved into their two-storey Auckland townhouse at the end of 2021 and discovered almost immediately that the upstairs overheated.

The house was west-facing, with a floor-to-ceiling window in the master bedroom, minimal ventilation, no eaves and no external window shading.

“You just have five or six hours straight of sun smashing that side of the house,” he said.

Temperatures upstairs typically got to 35C during the day and were still in the high 20s late in the evening, he said.

Some parts of the house were not just uncomfortable but dangerous – like the aluminium front door, which reached 60 or 70 degrees on a summer day and radiated heat back into the house.

“You can’t touch the door – it burns your hand.”

When his young sons were born, he and his wife were hyper-vigilant about monitoring the temperature.

“We used to have thermometers and stuff because ... it’s not safe for babies.”

In the time they had lived in the house, they had tried ceiling fans and a noisy portable air-conditioning unit, and finally paid $2500 for ducted air-conditioning.

He and his next-door neighbour ordered a roll of foil-covered bubble wrap from Temu, which they used to make huge shades that could be attached by Velcro to the internal window frames.

“That has made the biggest difference, aside from the AC,” he said.

“This will stay up weeks or months at a time ... We can’t enjoy the view because it’s 35C in here during the day.”

The features that contributed to overheating at Laidlaw’s house were typical of many new-build townhouses and apartments, Andrew Eagles said.

“You’ve often got windows going floor to ceiling ... you’ve got no eaves and no shading allowance,” he said.

“You’re then getting the full effect of the sun during the day and smaller rooms, so the combination of all of that is you just get this massive heat build-up.”

His organisation and the Building Research Association both supported an interim fix to a schedule in the Building Code that would require modelling at the design stage to check if a dwelling would overheat.

The software capable of doing that modelling was already used by hundreds of firms around the country, he said.

“I [would] need to put into a calculator the size of the home, the orientation, the size of the windows, and then it comes back and says, oh look – you are going to overheat this proportion of that time.”

The design would then have to be tweaked until it was under the modelling limits, Eagles said.

“The steps people are likely going to take is reduce the amount of glazing – that will save them money – or put some shading on or put some eaves on or slightly change the orientation, those sorts of things.”

Branz senior building physicist Stephen McNeil said without regulation, people in Laidlaw’s predicament would suffer even more as average temperatures increased.

“It’s also those extremes ... and we have other concerns with the increasing humidity in the air as well.”

In a written response, MBIE manager for building performance and engineering Dave Gittings said overheating was a complex issue without a single fix.

“We need to make sure any changes work together as a package and don’t create unintended consequences elsewhere in the building system. That includes considering an approach where designers would need to demonstrate through modelling that their designs will not exceed a maximum indoor temperature.”

The 2031 review was appropriate timing because of the considerable technical and policy work involved, he said.

“Overheating is influenced by a broad range of interconnected factors, including solar gain, shading, the heat absorption of building materials, ventilation, airtightness and building orientation. It takes time to consider any consequences, develop options for change and thoroughly consult on any changes to ensure we’ve considered every angle before implementing them.”

The ministry would provide informal guidance to designers and home owners in the meantime.

Introducing a requirement such as the one proposed by the Green Building Council would involve “more than simply setting a temperature limit”, Gittings said.

There would also need to be appropriate capability among those doing the modelling, which would require industry acceptance with any changes, with clear expectations for building consent authorities about the evidence they should receive, what they needed to check and when specialist review may be required.

But Stephen McNeil said changes could be staged.

“Rather than one big hit where you deliver this perfect regulatory thing that solves every problem, you’ve got to take the industry on a journey and give them time to build into it,” he said.

“Simple measures now will save us a lot of pain down the track because we could capture the riskiest buildings quite early in the piece.”

Andrew Eagles said in this case, “perfect is the enemy of good”.

“We should just get the bloody hell on with it.

“We’ve already got people writing to us horrified that they’re spending tens of thousands of dollars and that their kids are in rooms that are far, far too hot.”

Jared Laidlaw agreed five years was too long to wait.

“I’d anticipate a lot of houses in between now and then are going to be townhouses, so you’re going to only exacerbate the situation,” he said.

“It’d be a great time to be an HVAC business.”

Smart glasses privacy: Meta’s New Zealand release raises consent questions – Editorial

New Zealand Herald September 27, 2026

Mark Zuckerberg wears a pair of Meta Ray-Ban Display AI glasses. Photo / Getty Images

It’s becoming increasingly difficult to know when we are being watched.

Closed-circuit television cameras are constantly tracking us, as we walk about our towns and cities, driving in our cars and we ourselves surveil people entering our homes with technology like doorbell and security cameras.

Society has largely accepted a degree of surveillance in exchange for greater security.

However, the recent news that Meta is releasing smart glasses in New Zealand is a wake-up call for those expecting privacy in public spaces.

The line-up, for sale at retailers plus through Meta’s local AI glasses website, includes the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer (Gen3), which will sell from $809 and the Oakley Meta Vanguard, priced from $989.

Some models of the glasses feature cameras in their frames that let the wearer capture high-resolution photos and video. A white LED light appears when they are recording. Pictures can be captured hands-free with voice commands or via a button.

While Meta has previewed audio-only models with no camera, an apparent acknowledgment of privacy concerns, camera-equipped versions remain available and are likely to attract the greatest scrutiny.

The challenge is not simply whether people are being recorded, but whether they know they are being recorded.

Consent becomes difficult when the camera is sitting on someone’s face rather than being held in their hand.

There are complicated privacy implications.

The technology may be sharp, but the lines become blurred when privacy legislation takes time to catch up.

Like the proverbial frog in the pot of cold water on a stove, we accepted CCTV in public spaces, we accepted smartphones with cameras.

Now we are being asked to accept internet-connected cameras attached to people’s faces without the privacy legislation to back it up.

Australia is poised to ban the glasses in government offices and service centres and may consider banning imports. It is leaving state-run schools and hospitals to implement their own policies.

It should raise questions when governments themselves are examining whether smart glasses belong in offices, schools and other public institutions.

While it is not argued that the devices come with genuine benefits, including accessibility for blind and low-vision users, the convenience of hands-free communication, instant access to information and navigation, the challenge becomes: how do we enjoy their value without sacrificing privacy?

Smart glasses are not controversial because they contain cameras.

Smartphones contain cameras too.

They are controversial because they make surveillance effortless, discreet and increasingly normal.

The technology may be clever, but society has not yet decided whether it wants to live in a world where anyone, anywhere, could be recording at any time.

Before smart glasses become commonplace, that is a conversation worth having.

International students spend more in Bay of Plenty than in other regions, survey shows

Small class sizes, “beautiful landscapes” and the “best” weather in New Zealand are some of the drawcards attracting international students to the Bay of Plenty.

They’re also spending up large.

An Education New Zealand survey found each international student spends about $60,895 annually (excluding tuition fees) in the Bay of Plenty.

This was the highest estimated annual expenditure per student of any region.

“That’s a big amount of money. That’s all flowing into your local hospo and retail and landlords,” Education New Zealand chief executive David Downs said.

In Auckland, international students were spending about $48,272 annually, while the national average was $45,776, the 2024 survey found.

The Government this month announced New Zealand’s international education export earnings had surged to nearly $5 billion, surpassing 2019 pre-Covid levels.

Government data showed 92,580 international student enrolments in 2025 – up from 69,140 in 2023 but down from 115,705 in 2019.

Downs said international students wanted to study in New Zealand for a quality education, safety, connection to the outdoors, experiences and job opportunities.

“If you translate that down to this region, you’ve got that, it’s perfect,” he told the Rotorua Daily Post.

Many were interested in the “New Zealand lifestyle”.

A region with mountain biking, lakes and the “great outdoors” was “the perfect little microcosm of the New Zealand proposition”.

Post-study, international students were also “a great source of talent”, particularly if they began working in industries where skilled workers were needed.

Nationally, about 40% of international students came from China. Many also came from Southeast Asia and India, Downs said.

Originally from Korea, Sung Ae Kim said she and her son, Ari, moved to Tauranga in January 2024 for Ari to learn English.

Her husband stayed in Korea to work but visits frequently.

Ari studied at Mount Maunganui Intermediate for two years. He is now a Year 9 student at Mount Maunganui College.

Kim said most Tauranga primary and intermediate schools allowed one Korean student per class. This is something she wanted for Ari so he could immerse himself in English.

She also chose Tauranga for its warm weather and “beautiful landscapes”.

They initially planned to come for two years. They extended for one more year before deciding to stay until Ari finished college.

“He loves it here ... ”

She said Ari loved playing field hockey, golf, soccer, tennis and swimming.

Hyun Taek Yang, director of the education agency for international students Tauranga Korean Times, said most Korean secondary school students who lived with a homestay spent about $50,000 to $60,000 annually.

The spend for one primary or intermediate student living with a parent in Tauranga was $120,000 per year.

Taek Yang organised a delegation of representatives from 29 Tauranga primary, intermediate and secondary schools to attend the COEX Convention and Exhibition Centre in Seoul this month, which he said was a success.

He expected about 100 international students and one of their parents to arrive in Tauranga in January to study for one to two years.

Taek Yang said smaller class sizes, local hospitality and Tauranga having the “best” weather in New Zealand were drawcards for Korean families.

Toi Ohomai head of international Peter Richardson said about 1000 international students were studying at the institution this year, compared with 1950 in 2019.

Changing demand from international markets, high visa decline rates and the loss of post-study work rights for diploma-level programmes meant it was “taking time to reach pre-Covid numbers”.

However, demand for Toi Ohomai programmes had more than doubled this year compared with last.

Richardson said contributing factors to international students’ higher spend in the region could include high rental costs and lack of public transport options.

University of Waikato deputy vice-chancellor Professor Alister Jones said 83 international students were enrolled at its Tauranga campus – a 261% increase since opening in 2019.

“Demand for international enrolments at our campus is strong and has increased significantly for 2027.”

The university was developing postgraduate programmes “with a strong appeal to international markets” to support growth, Jones said.

These would begin rolling out in 2027 with the launch of its new Master of Construction Management, he said.

Rotorua English Language Academy director Chris Leckie said the school typically taught students aged 15 and older, with the average age in their early 20s.

Many were working holiday visa holders, on a gap year, travelling or needed to improve their English for their job, Leckie said.

“We’ve always emphasised that one of our students is worth a significant amount to the city ... I’ve got about 40 homestay families on my books, and some of them have students all the time.”

They spent money at restaurants, and their parents often visited too, she said.

However, Leckie said the school’s recovery from Covid-19 had been slow, “and we’re still waiting for growth”.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said the city had welcomed many international students and appreciated their value and contributions.

“They bring a great diversity to our communities through their cultures, skills and ideas.”

Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale said international students made a “significant contribution” to Tauranga’s economy, supported local jobs, strengthened the future workforce and enhanced the city’s reputation as “a great place to live, learn, work, and invest”.

International students also brought different perspectives and experiences that enriched schools and communities and helped connect Tauranga with the world.

“Just as importantly, they become part of our community while they’re here, building friendships and sharing their cultures. That’s something that benefits all of us.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Election 2026: What stood out at National, Labour’s campaign launches

New Zealand Herald September 27, 2026

National and Labour officially kicked off their election campaigns in Auckland on Sunday afternoon, providing an insight into the parties’ priorities ahead of the November 7 vote.

At the International Convention Centre (ICC) in Auckland central, Christopher Luxon and his National crew, including former Prime Minister Sir John Key, pushed the message of “no new taxes” and argued Labour was lean on ideas to take New Zealand forward.

Further south at the Due Drop Event Centre in Manukau, Chris Hipkins unveiled a Labour policy to wipe 10% of student loan debt and attacked National for what he said were lies about his party’s tax intentions.

The Herald’s Jamie Ensor and Adam Pearse report from the respective events.

No one will have left the ICC on Sunday afternoon unaware of what National’s primary message is this election.

“No new taxes” was emblazoned on a large screen overhanging campaign chair Simeon Brown as he spoke, was recited ad nauseam by supporters in the crowd before, during, and after the event, and could be found littered throughout the speeches of key party figures.

Christopher Luxon was even introduced as “Mr No New Taxes”.

The “no new taxes” line feels like a much-needed rallying cry for National.

Until the succinct, easily rememberable promise was unveiled late last month, the party was lacking a central unifying narrative at a time when it felt like there was more momentum behind attempts to roll its leader than towards victory.

Now there’s a clear message to fall back on, something volunteers and candidates can deploy if they are ever in a tricky situation while campaigning (members of its youth wing couldn’t stop shouting it at a market walkabout on Saturday).

But while the party may be on message and there certainly weren’t any new taxes on show at the party’s campaign launch, there also wasn’t much new of anything else.

Even Sir John Key’s seemingly heartfelt justification of why he was backing Luxon felt like a reheat of his previous defences of the man cast as his political prodigy, but who has never reached near his level of popularity.

Like at its campaign launch three years ago, National rolled out a new pledge card, a handy-dandy pamphlet of 10 core commitments.

There were mentions of some specific policies – like compulsory KiwiSaver and an extension to paid parental leave – but otherwise it felt like someone had copy and pasted the 2023 pledges, and just changed them up a tad.

Delivering economic growth, tougher consequences for criminals, better infrastructure, better school results – sound familiar?

There is merit in message repetition. We have to remember not everyone is a political journalist listening to every speech and press conference. Some people will only hear one or two comments from a party a week, and politicians want them to be the core ones.

But the recycling of the pledge card, a lack of new policy, and the barrage of “no new taxes” did give a sense of irony to Luxon’s speech, which in part leaned on the argument that Labour was offering little to the electorate other than slogans.

“Chris Hipkins says he’s still warming up. Well, I’ve got one simple message. You ‘better start now’,” Luxon said.

“Because this country needs more than a slogan, it needs a plan. And Labour doesn’t have one. I could give you chapter and verse on Labour’s scandalous lack of policy, just a matter of weeks out from election day. But I’ll cut to the chase. You can’t afford a Labour Government.“

Meanwhile, down the road in South Auckland, Labour was announcing a new policy.

National was right that earlier this year Labour had offered up comparatively little in terms of policy, with the Nats releasing a substantial number.

It’s an understandable bugbear of Luxon’s that National released a large batch in Opposition throughout both 2022 and 2023, while Labour has this term skated around offering little but rhetorical opposition to anything the Government does.

Labour eventually released a handful of policies late last year before another long break until after this year’s Budget.

“If I had dribbled up as little policy as they had, you guys would have crucified us,” Luxon told reporters.

National had a “plan, not just a slogan”, he said, before then rattling off National’s slogan to “fix the basics, build the future”.

But regardless of the delay or how Luxon feels about the policies, Labour is now showing up.

On the matter of showing up, National will get some flak for not filling the auditorium at the ICC.

Organisers reckon about 1000 people were there – that’s probably a fair count – but the party probably wants to book somewhere it can pack out, or risk rows of empty seats being shown on the television.

The crowd seemed to eat up what National was handing out, but there wasn’t the bombastic style of the 2023 launch, which included candidates entering the room like boxers as their names were blasted from the speakers.

The lesser energy may be a symptom of National now being the party of Government as opposed to the fighters in Opposition.

Luxon, possibly aware of the optics of not filling the room, highlighted in his speech “this incredible, vast, venue”. The word “vast” wasn’t in the written speech given to media ahead of time.

If National was looking for anyone to fill the seats, others at the ICC on Sunday may not have been in the usual attire for a political convention.

A couple of storeys below National’s launch was an anime and manga convention. Cosplayers wandered the halls, some with cartoon-style swords or firearms. One was realistic enough for police officers to check it over before they entered the centre.

Asked if he was going to take a look, Luxon said he needed to “keep moving”.

“But I do like the odd bit of anime,” he said.

At least we found out something new.

In equal measure, no one will have left Manukau’s Due Drop Event Centre on Sunday afternoon unaware of what Labour’s primary message is this election.

The first words out of Hipkins’ mouth after greeting the more than 600 people crammed into a tiered theatre-like room were to declare, “This election is about the cost of living”. He finished his speech with the same statement.

That, complemented by a healthy dose of Luxon-bashing, was the central message an impassioned and at times combative Labour leader sought to convey.

While Labour events may not have the glitz of a slick National Party production, culture is where the party thrives.

Beginning with a jovial introduction from candidate Kingi Kiriona, who seemed quite happy under a spotlight, a quite stunning performance from the Pasifika Youth Choir followed, bringing the crowd and Labour MPs to their feet. Notable exceptions included Willie Jackson and Phil Twyford, who seemed comfortable bopping along seated. An enigmatic MC, with flair to rival most of Labour’s own caucus, finished setting up a hard act for Hipkins to follow.

However, helped by a feverish crowd, Hipkins managed to match the energy. He was able to elicit a much better call-and-response than National campaign chair Simeon Brown, whose “No new taxes” appeal was echoed with more of a robotic drone from a crowd clearly weary of the repetition.

While Hipkins faced criticism for a more introverted campaigning style to Luxon in 2023, he can turn up the dial for these kinds of set-pieces, to the point it borders on combative.

In his dismissal of National’s tax attack campaign as “bull****”, Hipkins was all too happy to repeat to reporters after his speech.

In his lambasting of Luxon, Hipkins got plenty of mileage out of the National leader’s “cry me a river” comment; a line Luxon used towards Hipkins in the House this month which the Labour leader brands as the Prime Minister’s message to struggling Kiwis.

Despite talk of a positive campaign, Labour had hired a truck with the quote plastered on its side and had intended the truck to circle National’s campaign bus (unfortunately for Labour, National delayed the release of its bus). Hipkins’ response? Labour can walk and chew gum at the same time.

Together with a fiery address declaring Luxon unfit to be Prime Minister and for him to “do his bloody job”, one could be forgiven for thinking a combination of some shadow-boxing and an electric cattle prod might have convinced him to up the ante amid questions about his campaigning.

But when asked about the contrast, Hipkins returned to his favourite word of the day, “You’re just listening to National Party spin bull***”, having earlier said it was an indictment on the media if Aucklanders were still unaware of his transport fare cap policy.

Labour’s policy of wiping 10% of student loan debt certainly met the brief for Hipkins’ cost of living focus, which remains the most important issue for voters.

The expected attack from National’s Brown came swiftly, claiming it only adds to Labour’s “hidden bill” of spending promises, which voters will soon get clarity on following Tuesday’s pre-election fiscal update.

The way Hipkins is going, it’s only a matter of time before that bill gets its own bull**** condemnation.

New Zealand gets another taste of winter on Monday as cold southwesterlies bring showers to western areas and snow in Fiordland.

Eastern areas will enjoy a brighter start to the working week, before showers ease across both islands on Tuesday.

“It will be a tale of two halves,” MetService meteorologist Oscar Shiviti said.

A front was moving north over the central North Island on Sunday, with cold southwesterlies following in its wake, Shiviti said.

All South Island state highways reopened on Sunday after snow shut Lewis Pass and trapped vehicles near Lake Pūkaki.

MetService lifted all South Island weather warnings, but urged motorists to watch for frost overnight and on Monday morning.

Southwesterlies are set to bring showers to western New Zealand on Monday, especially the South Island’s west and south coasts.

Snow could dust Fiordland down to about 600-700m during the morning.

Shiviti said the snow should be the last of the season.

Showers in the west of the North Island could become heavier during the afternoon and continue into the evening, Shiviti said.

The eastern North Island “looks the place to be” on Monday, with generally fine weather while showers linger in the west, Shiviti said.

Christchurch residents will wake to patches of frost on Monday before cloud moves in, bringing the chance of an afternoon shower.

Aucklanders will want to keep a raincoat handy for the start of the working week, with partly cloudy skies and a few showers forecast on Monday.

The showers will be lighter in the morning, while southwesterly winds will strengthen during the afternoon.

Wellington has a brighter Monday ahead, with mainly fine weather and only the chance of an afternoon shower.

Northwesterlies will blow through the capital before turning southwesterly at night.

Waikato’s Sunday rain was forecast to ease to isolated showers in the evening, with northwesterlies turning southwesterly after a period of strong late-afternoon winds.

Taranaki will have to wait until Tuesday for its brighter spell, with fine weather apart from isolated showers.

Tuesday will bring fine weather to Wellington, with westerlies turning northeasterly in the evening, Shiviti said.

Across the wider North Island, scattered showers will affect western areas on Tuesday before clearing in the evening. Mainly fine weather will prevail elsewhere, he said.

The South Island’s south and west will also see showers, but these will ease and become isolated later in the day, Shiviti said.

“The rest of the island can expect mainly fine weather.”

Tom Eley is a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. Before he joined the Hamilton-based team, he worked for the Weekend Sun and Sunlive. He previously worked as a journalist at Black Press Media in Canada and won a fellowship with the Vancouver Sun.

Brisbane’s smallest suburb packs a pocket-sized punch. I was lucky to buy while it was still affordable

Sydney Morning Herald September 28, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Between Countess Street, Hale Street, Musgrave Road and Milton Road sits Brisbane’s smallest suburb. There are only 41 streets, roads and lanes in Petrie Terrace, but it packs a pocket-sized punch – for its history, its people, and its perfect evening light.

Most people know Petrie Terrace for Suncorp Stadium, just over the Hale Street border, and the infamous Caxton Street, Brisbane’s NRL hub. But any day there isn’t a game on – midweek, or a Sunday afternoon without a footy jersey in sight – is the Petrie Terrace I know and love. When the stadium is quiet and empty, the streets are strangely peaceful. It’s a place to belong.

I first came to know Petrie Terrace in the early 2000s, when I left my hometown, the mountain village of Mount Glorious, to move “downtown”. I was a twenty-something bartender who wanted cheap rent and easy access to the Valley nightlife.

For a few years, I lived on Sheriff Street, pulling coffees in the CBD’s Elizabeth Arcade by morning and pulling beers at O’Leary’s on Caxton Street by night, with a bit of sunbaking at Ithaca Pool in between.

Eventually I left, travelled across Australia and abroad for 20 years, not really belonging anywhere, and then – like a homing pigeon – I returned to Petrie Terrace when I started looking for schools for my daughter, who was about to start prep. I was trying to replicate my upbringing, but an urban version. The requirement was simple: a small school with a big community. I visited a handful of tiny schools around the city until I found Petrie Terrace State School, with just 240 primary students. It wasn’t quite the 30 I’d grown up with, but close enough.

I moved back first as a renter on Belgrave Street, and later as an owner in the more urban end of the suburb, under the flickering fairy lights of the Barracks and the neon glow of the newly erected digital billboard sitting annoyingly atop the old Casablanca restaurant and bar.

Buying an apartment in Petrie Terrace will likely stand as one of my life’s greatest accomplishments. I somehow secured a tiny piece of Brisbane’s most wonderful suburb before anyone realised how cool it was. And it was on these steep streets that I rediscovered community, and my daughter grew up belonging to a place.

There’s something about knowing people, and being known, that makes me fall in love with this suburb daily. I can’t walk down the street without bumping into someone I know: at the pub, dog walking or, like me, just using the streets for what they were meant for: wandering, meandering, having the kind of meaningless conversations that make life meaningful.

Petrie Terrace has what every town planner hopes to achieve but few manage: genuine “third spaces”, those informal places that aren’t home and aren’t work, but where we find ourselves belonging anyway. Petrie Terrace is full of them, if you know where to look.

A friend of mine, an architect who lives on one of Petrie Terrace’s narrow lanes, has more than once closed her street – no council approval, just a couple of witch’s hats and an idea – to set up a makeshift cinema projected onto a sheet on a garage door, or to gather the neighbourhood kids to make papier-mache baubles at Christmas, or run Halloween in the ’hood. When the neighbours and children spill onto the road, I’m taken back to a time that barely exists for most people in most places any more.

The suburb encompasses the old Victoria Barracks, built by Andrew Petrie – superintendent of works in the Moreton Bay Penal Colony – whose family, Brisbane’s first free settlers, gives the suburb its name. Andrew’s eldest son, John Petrie, became Brisbane’s first mayor, while another son, Thomas Petrie, learnt the Turrbal language and wrote reminiscences of early Queensland. These included the fact that Indigenous clans from across south-east Queensland gathered in Petrie Terrace for events up until the 1840s.

In the 1970s, Petrie Terrace had cheap accommodation that attracted artists, musicians, actors and bohemians. One of those rundown houses was No. 4 on Petrie Terrace (the street), a sharehouse occupied by seminal punk band The Saints. It briefly and thunderously became known as Club 76 after Ed Kuepper suggested painting the name over a boarded-up window and using the house for unlicensed gigs – until the cops shut it down.

Today, the suburb gathers hundreds of thousands of football fans every year to pack the stadium and surrounding streets. But that is not the type of gathering that I, as a local, love about this place. It is the gathering of light as it falls in the afternoon on Princess Row, or the way people gather in Hardgrave Park to let their dogs run amok. It is parents gathering to teach their kids how to ride at Suncorp Stadium, the only flat surface in the suburb.

Contributor

It is gathering at the school gates, waiting for smiling faces alongside people who have become part of the thread of my family’s life. It is gathering with friends on decks and in backyards to chinwag about how wonderful it is that we discovered this place, and each other.

It is gathering on the corner of Petrie Terrace and Caxton Street, chatting with Tory and the Caxton Street Brewing crew in the late afternoon. It is gathering for Mexican family dinners at La Carmela, served by Angel and cooked by Fabian, or gathering with my mates at our late-night rum haunt, Pago Pago, watching streams of jersey-clad football fans navigate the street as we conspire to keep this place ours, against the current of their fandom.

We’re one of Brisbane’s littlest ’burbs, and our neighbours hog the limelight, but we have heritage homes, Paddle Pop skies – and colourful characters too.

Bohemian. Progressive. Hippie. Alternative. The cliches aren’t entirely wrong, but those words flatten a place that flatly refuses to be simple.
