Republic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over Israel

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 21:24:03 GMT

Football and politics are inseparable in the modern world, no matter how many people wish that weren’t true. But whether the beautiful game can ease the ills of our age is another matter. After a week in which the issue of Irish support for the people of Gaza had turned this fixture into a battle of conscience, the outcome of this underwhelming match ultimately felt inconsequential.

In the end the result was indeed a walkover, just not because of a boycott. On Saturday night the question had been whether Heimir Hallgrimsson’s side would take to the field in Hungary at all. If they did, would their heads be in the game? It turned out that a week of internal angst had been enough to produce collective resolve amongst the Irish squad, or at least those selected to play. Strong and assertive from the off, their forwards each scored a goal in the first half to settle the contest, with plenty of symbolic action to assure those back home of their feelings.

“It’s probably been the toughest days of my coaching career,” Hallgrimsson said after the match. “But it’s not about me. It’s about the players and they’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them. They represented themselves on the pitch with dignity but also with the power of proud Irishmen. They’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them and hopefully they will have the support of the Irish people.”

In a way the atmosphere in Debrecen was reminiscent of a match played during Covid. Every word uttered in the ground was audible and the nigh-on empty stands carried their own oppressive weight. As the nominal home side, Israel had been allowed a small delegation of fans, about 150, who were doing their best to be excitable. Meanwhile, two blocks away were the Irish contingent, around a dozen people who had got into the ground despite the FAI’s decision not to bring an away allocation. They were all stood hands in pockets in a stairway.

This odd, almost haunted mood was heightened further by Ireland’s mannered approach to the pre-match rituals. Irish staff faced away from the pitch when their national anthem was played. Ireland’s players, all wearing black armbands, stared at the ground during Israel’s. There was no exchanging of pennants and no shaking of hands, with both squads hurried away from the centre circle into their own huddles.

The game had come close to being abandoned on Saturday, when goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu made himself unavailable for selection, his decision prompting emotional exchanges among players and management. Hallgrimsson therefore picked a team with defender Jimmy Dunne nominally a third goalkeeper and also dropped key forward Finn Azaz to the bench in one of five changes to the team that lost meekly to Kosovo. Azaz’s mother has Israeli citizenship and the Southampton forward was reported to have made an impassioned contribution to Saturday’s discussion. “Today we thought others would fit this game better than him”, Halgrimsson said.

After all the soul-searching, Ireland decided the contest in just 11 first half minutes. Troy Parrott opened the scoring in the 14th minute, turning home a low shot through the body of Daniel Peretz after impressive work on the right by wing-back James Abankwah. Two minutes later and the lead was doubled when, running on the shoulder of the last defender, Adam Idah collected a smart through ball from Jack Moylan and wrapped a calm finish inside Peretz’s left-hand post.

In the 25th minute Moylan got a goal of his own, his fourth in as many caps to continue a stellar start to his international career, driving 25 yards into the box before shooting low into the net. Moylan wheeled away to the corner flag, took off his black armband and kissed it.

USA’s McNulty transcends chaos of Montreal road race to claim ‘miracle’ world title

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 20:59:46 GMT

Arizona rider first US champion since Lance Armstrong

Pre-race favourite Evenpoel fails to add second gold

Brandon McNulty, a UAE Emirates teammate of Tadej Pogacar, succeeded the Slovene as world champion with an unexpected solo win in the men’s UCI road race in Montreal.

In the biggest triumph of his career, the 28-year-old American took his country’s first win in the UCI’s blue riband event since Lance Armstrong’s lone victory in Oslo in 1993.

“I’m really at a loss,” McNulty said. “Until the last hundred metres, I didn’t believe it, I was so tired. I was just dying, but I kept pushing. We have said for weeks now that we had a super strong team. We talked about it, but I knew it would take a miracle. I guess miracles happen.”

McNulty’s 50-second lead at the start of the closing lap of the hilly Montreal circuit was enough to hold on to the finish line, despite a last‑ditch attempt by Tom Pidcock to chase down the American that, at one point, reduced his advantage to only a handful of seconds.

Pidcock was one of the animators of the final hour of racing, which followed the same volatile and unpredictable pattern as the women’s road race on Saturday, which was won by Demi Vollering of the Netherlands. A gruelling race, ridden without the benefit of race radios, was at times chaotic, particularly within the Belgium team’s confused tactics, with the Olympic road race champion, Remco Evenepoel, left once again to ponder what might have been.

With 90 kilometres to go, a select group of a dozen riders, including Pidcock’s British teammate Oscar Onley, went clear on the pivotal climb of the Voie Camillien-Houde. That group reduced to an elite six, including the former world champion Mathieu Van der Poel, and this year’s Paris-Roubaix winner, Wout van Aert.

In the constant ebb and flow, the biggest loser, seemingly hamstrung by team tactics, was Van Aert’s fellow Belgian and pre-race favourite Evenepoel, who was seeking to add the road race title to the time trial gold medal he won seven days ago. With the leading group increasing their lead, Paul Seixas’s France team combined with Isaac del Toro of Mexico to lead a nine-man group in pursuit. But Van der Poel, recently the author of a successful 172km lone break in the Tour of Luxembourg, pressed on with Onley, the Slovene Primoz Roglic and Quinn Simmons of the US.

Renewed accelerations from Van der Poel finally distanced Onley and split the peloton to an even greater extent. In a succession of regroupings the lead changed multiple times, until McNulty finally and definitively seized the initiative with just over 30km to race.

Twenty-four hours after Vollering’s last-gasp win in a brutal women’s road race, McNulty’s victory was equally enthralling. Vollering’s joy at her success was dampened by the UCI’s decision to fine her 1,000 Swiss francs and give her a points deduction and a yellow card for a “non-compliant” racing position. However, the results were not affected by the post-race ruling.

Katarzyna Niewiadoma, second to Vollering in the Tour de France Femmes this year, claimed another silver medal, but the Dutch rider paid tribute to her rival’s efforts. “In the end, your greatest competitors are also your greatest motivation,” Vollering said.

As the week of competition ended, the Spanish media revealed that one of the stars of the championships, the Spanish teenager Benjamín Noval, winner of the world junior road and time trial titles in Montreal, had escaped being sanctioned by the country’s anti-doping body Celad.

El País reported that in 2024 Noval, who will race for Netcompany Ineos in 2027, had been found working with José “Pepe” Martí, banned for 15 years in the aftermath of the Armstrong doping scandal and prohibited from associating with athletes in any sport. Martí, who remains banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency until June, met Noval for physiological testing while under Celad surveillance, but Noval, who was only 15 at the time of the incident, was not subjected to any sanction.

Cincinnati’s unbeaten start ends in Pittsburgh

Drake Maye’s turnover woes continue for Pats

Marcus Mariota threw three touchdown passes, and Kain Medrano returned an interception 50 yards for a touchdown to help the Washington Commanders (1-2) hand Seattle (2-1) their first loss since last November. The Seahawks had won 12 straight, including their postseason run to last season’s Super Bowl title, but Mariota was solid in place of the injured Jayden Daniels, and three crucial turnovers enabled Washington to win their home opener. Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught 10 passes for 128 yards and two touchdowns for the Seahawks, and he even completed a short throw on a trick play in the final quarter.

Aaron Rodgers passed for 292 yards and three touchdowns to outduel Joe Burrow as the Pittsburgh Steelers beat the Cincinnati Bengals. Pittsburgh bounced back from a miserable performance in a loss to New England to blunt some of Cincinnati’s early momentum. Rodgers completed 19 of 34 passes, including a 47-yard catch-and-run to 6ft 7in 265lb tight end Darnell Washington that helped set up Chris Boswell’s go-ahead, 33-yard field goal with 2:18 remaining. Cincinnati had a chance late, but Burrow fumbled after being sacked by Derrick Harmon. Rookie Sebastian Joseph-Day fell on the ball. Both teams are 2-1.

Trevor Lawrence threw three touchdown passes, leading the Jacksonville Jaguars to a statement victory over the visiting New England Patriots. Lawrence connected ⁠with Josh Cameron, Jakobi Meyers and Parker Washington for scores, completing 19 of 29 passes for 182 yards with an interception. New England quarterback Drake Maye continued to struggle with turnovers. He paired two interceptions ⁠with one lost fumble to give him seven turnovers in three games, already approaching the 11 he had in 17 regular-season games last season. Maye was 14-of-25 passing for 199 yards, ⁠while Mack Hollins caught six passes for 87 yards for the Patriots (1-2).

Buffalo improved to 3-0 despite Allen throwing two interceptions and losing a fumble. Cook and tight end Dalton Kincaid also lost fumbles.

Chelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derby

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 20:08:51 GMT

Arsenal’s title chances were dealt a significant blow after a narrow defeat at the hands of Chelsea. Alyssa Thompson’s first-half finish was the difference on a competitive afternoon at Stamford Bridge but one that ultimately left Renée Slegers with more questions than answers about how to save their season.

“Worried? No,” Slegers said. “Confidence is something that fluctuates. They know who they are and they know what they can bring. What’s important is that there’s always phases in the season and there’s different things you need to work on or focus on.

“It’s important that we keep any pressure and any complexity away from the players because we believe in them. It’s just really important that we keep that simplicity and clear minds for the players.”

There is no game quite as eagerly anticipated in the Women’s Super League as the meeting between Chelsea and Arsenal. While other derbies and duels are in their early development, the London derby is the one year after year that brings the pressure, the drama and, of course, the eyeballs. While both sides clearly respect each other off the pitch, there is a distinct sense that once they cross the white line there is true competitive animosity there, one that lifts the levels of everyone in the vicinity.

This edition was no different with expectation and apprehension buzzing around Stamford Bridge before kick-off and no shortage of new narratives. This was the first time Katie McCabe, 11 years a Gunner, would face her old team having moved in the summer. Would she help Chelsea to inflict more pain on Arsenal’s stuttering start, or could Slegers’s side put a pin in the pressure balloon and breathe new life into their search for a first title in eight years?

Both teams came into this encounter having not yet hit form. Arsenal have created opportunities but have looked predictable in their buildup and lacked a finishing touch. In contrast, Chelsea have looked energetic and full of ideas but, excluding their win against Manchester United, have also struggled with ruthlessness in front of goal.

Sonia Bompastor was handed a significant boost before kick-off with the news that both Keira Walsh and Lauren James were available to start. Lexi Potter was given the nod alongside Walsh in midfield, a sign of how much trust the head coach has in the 20-year-old, while Melvine Malard was fit enough to begin up front.

Slegers, meanwhile, rang the changes from Arsenal’s hard-fought victory against HB Køge during the week. Two who remained were Kyra Cooney-Cross and the goalkeeper Anneke Borbe, who kept out Misa Rodríguez.

The visitors came out full of energy and looking to make an early statement. They dominated early on with 44.2% of the action happening in Chelsea’s defensive third in the first quarter and Arsenal looking to reap the rewards of their high press.

Their biggest threat early on came from Lisa Baum. The 19-year-old has been one of the more positive aspects of their season to date and was given space down the right by Chelsea.

For all of their control, however, it was much of the same old story for Slegers’s side, haunted by their inability to take their chances. Of the eight shots they created, they failed to register one on target and hit the woodwork twice through Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey.

With every rattle of a post that reverberated around Stamford Bridge, Arsenal’s early confidence dwindled and Bompastor’s side started to find more joy. In direct contrast to their opponents, the Blues took their chance when it came when Malard pounced on Steph Catley as she played out from the back. Borbe made a good save to deny Walsh initially but the rebound fell perfectly for Thompson to hammer home.

It was the ideal time to score and Chelsea went in ahead at the break with the momentum of the game having shifted significantly. They went on to create big opportunities of their own with Malard dragging a shot narrowly wide on two occasions.

While Arsenal were able to create opportunities, the hosts looked comfortable in the circumstances and defended resolutely to see out the game and take home a valuable three points.

Eva Longoria: Searching for France review – this lovely travel show radiates charm

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 19:00:12 GMT

It’s light stuff with more than a touch of Emily in Paris to it, but the actor’s latest travelogue has enough passion to make it highly endearing TV

‘I’m Eva Longoria and I’m a SERIOUS Francophile!” So begins each instalment of the actor’s Gallic travelogue. France, says Longoria, “is my home away from home”, although she’s usually in the country for work, rather than to experience its abundance of “joie de vivre”. (She does, she notes, have some extracurricular experience with the French, having previously been married to the French-American basketball player Tony Parker for three years.) Now, though, she is on her own adventure, having returned to l’Hexagone for something “deeper”. Cut to a clip of our intrepid guide in a vineyard, getting acquainted with cabernet sauvignon grapes (“That’s my favourite!” she whispers animatedly), before we segue to her floating gracefully past the Eiffel Tower.

Eva Longoria: Searching for France follows the equally alarmist-sounding Eva Longoria: Searching for Spain, and sets up the exciting possibility of an extended Longoria televisual universe, where the Desperate Housewives star makes her way across the entire globe (Eva Longoria: Searching for Equatorial Guinea, anyone?). It’s all been done before on television, of course, but the passion and lightness of touch here make it an endearing proposition.

Take the opening scene, as Longoria orders a baguette in a Parisian bakery, in French, only to be immediately addressed in English – an experience that even the most SERIOUS Francophiles must contend with. She is unfazed, concentrating on the “full sensory experience” of the bread, “from the smell, to the colour, to the crunch, to the warmth, to the taste”. It’s a little bit Stanley Tucci, then (he was the original Searching for … host, with Searching for Italy in 2021). And it’s definitely a little bit Emily in Paris.

There’s a soupçon of French history laced through its eight episodes, though never enough for the programme to feel dry. An extravagant meal with the Michelin-hoarding chef Alain Ducasse and the US-born, Paris-based journalist Lindsey Tramuta leads to a gentle conversation about the origins of haute cuisine in the court of Louis XIV at Versailles. We also learn that the bohemian Belleville neighbourhood has strong working-class roots – stemming from the 1871 Paris Commune revolt. Longoria has lunch with Josephine Baker’s son, Brian, who gives a potted history of her life as an entertainer and resistance spy. But trivia is kept to a minimum: this is Searching for France, after all, not Searching for a PhD in French History. Plus, Longoria’s got important business to attend to, such as eating a delicious-looking take on the croque madame, lovingly crafted by the Filipino-Australian chef Hanz Gueco. (“I thought it was a croque madame because the egg was a boob,” offers Longoria, lowering the tone of Gueco’s establishment.)

A few minutes later, Longoria is threatening to lick her pomme puree off the plate at a fancy restaurant (Eva, non!). It’s a joke, of course, but there is definitely a sense that our permanently blowdried host plays up her fish-out-of-water qualities – and eating rich and saucy meals in white cardigans and dresses is surely asking for trouble. She’s chic, she’s elegant … she’s dangerously close to ruining her outfit with bouillabaisse in Provence. Forget The Traitors: this is truly tense TV.

Really, though, Searching for France is a lovely series, unapologetically frivolous and filled with the finer things in life (Champagne! Caviar! Oysters! A whole pound of butter in the pomme puree, which shocks and excites Longoria in equal measure). It also serves as a PR-friendly showcase for some of the country’s buzziest restaurants, not least Mory Sacko’s MoSuke, where west African and Japanese cuisine are fused daringly. It occasionally decides to warm our hearts, too – see episode two, when Longoria visits a social enterprise-slash-restaurant in Marseille, which employs staff with disabilities and offers three-course meals to customers regardless of their budgets. Like Tucci, Longoria radiates easy charm, and – while she isn’t fluent – makes a big effort to conduct her interviews in French. It’s no easy feat, especially in an increasingly anglophone Paris where French conversation can feel more like ritual humiliation. It isn’t exactly meaty stuff, but maybe it doesn’t have to be? What’s more important anyway: learning about the various violent deaths of French kings and queens, or knowing how to make the perfect niçoise salad? Understanding the finer points of Haussmannian architecture, or finding out where to get a slap-up steak tartare? I know what I’ll find seriously useful on my next trip.

Eva Longoria: Searching for France aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer now

Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care service

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 18:56:22 GMT

PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’

Analysis: can Labour hang on to Burnham bounce?

Andy Burnham will fight the next election with a pledge to finally fix the broken social care system, acknowledging he is willing to expend political capital by asking taxpayers to cover the cost.

As Labour’s party conference began in Liverpool, he pledged to “rip the plaster off” to radically transform care, setting out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everyone in England.

The prime minister said the new NHS-style service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details on how his long-term plan would be paid for, indicating that a tax rise may be on the cards.

He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks over “death taxes” would sink the policy.

Burnham acknowledged there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement, although he rejected suggestions it could cost £18bn a year. “It’s not that high,” he told the BBC.

“Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said. “I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].”

But he said he would take his time to work out how it could be fairly funded. “The challenge in the public finances is real. So it has to be done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse. But I will bring forward proposals.”

Labour’s annual gathering is intended to be an upbeat affair, with the prime minister wanting to restore hope that some of the country’s most intractable political problems can be solved despite severe economic headwinds.

With political courage a theme of the conference, he said in an interview with the Guardian at the weekend: “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”

Burnham acknowledged the public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but he said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems.

A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government with limited room for manoeuvre.

On Sunday, Burnham said he did not want to focus on a “narrative of doom” about the UK’s economy but that he would show in his leader’s speech that he was prepared to take tough decisions.

He acknowledged there was “real concern” in the financial markets about the state of the British economy, pointing to the “febrile” global backdrop. He said he was willing to cut government spending to balance the books, and he believed money could be saved by taking a more “productive” long-term approach to issues such as rough sleeping and youth unemployment.

Amid concerns that the government could be hemmed in at the budget by the parlous state of the public finances, he said the chancellor, John Healey, would be “highly prudent” in running the economy. “I won’t do what the previous Tory government did and take risks with the economy that are actually still hurting us right now,” he said.

Burnham suggested to the Guardian that a significant fiscal buffer would be necessary, with speculation that the Treasury could now consider £15bn acceptable.

“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things,” he said. “But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances.”

Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said the “heavy lifting” on making the case for rejoining the EU needed to be done by the government now, after Burnham signalled that the move could be in the next manifesto.

“The pitch rolling must be done now, explaining to the country the dis-benefits of being outside the European Union and the benefits of being part of this family,” Khan said.

However, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, appeared to criticise Khan – and Burnham – telling Politico that the speculation “frankly cause[s] a lot of uncertainty for business”.

Meanwhile, plans for a third runway at Heathrow are once again up in the air after Burnham refused to say whether he backed the “contested” project, which is delayed by up to four years, saying it was “principally” a matter for London.

Counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military.

The suspected plot appears to have been foiled by chance when a member of the public spotted unusual behaviour late at night in the countryside from a group of men and called 999.

During the major incident the residents of 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were rapidly evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre and a 400m cordon was placed around the white vans as robots from the army’s bomb squad examined them.

Tests were ongoing to find out whether the suspected explosive devices were viable, with bomb robots deployed in the Gloucestershire countryside as investigations continued.

After their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act. The pictures of the men with their shirts off could point to a precautionary measure against the risk of suicide vests or concealed weapons.

At least one van carried the logo of a fuel company and a phone number missing a digit. A real fuel company of the same name firmly rejected any connection to the incident and said: “We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission.” It said it was cooperating with the authorities.

In a statement, counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am today (Sunday 27 September), police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase.

“Armed officers responded and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.”

The arrests come as the war between the US and Iran limps on. In July Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.

Counter-terror police and the security services are searching for the motive. The circumstances of the arrest near the base and prior warnings from Tehran leave an Iranian motive high in the investigators’ and government’s thinking. But sources warn nothing is being ruled out, including a jihadist or other motive, and the UK threat level remains at severe, the second highest, meaning an attack is highly likely.

Whether there was any foreign involvement forms part of the investigation, and Iran’s ministry of intelligence and security has orchestrated attacks overseas before.

Any proven link with Iran would be a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the UK and Tehran. While several recent incidents in the UK have been linked to the Middle-Eastern country, including the antisemitic arson attack on four Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, the alleged plot at RAF Fairford appears to be significantly more serious.

And it raises urgent questions for the UK security services after it appeared the authorities had been unaware of the alleged plot, with police only moving on the three vans after a 999 call from a resident who spotted them as she drove home.

The US president, Donald Trump, claimed to have had the suspects under view for a “long time” and alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” – although the Guardian understands the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the incident.

Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.

In March this year, after then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases, four American bombers landed at RAF Fairford and the US started using British bases for “specific defensive operations”.

There have been protests in recent months over the UK government’s decision to allow the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz.

Even Andy Burnham’s closest allies accept that deposing Keir Starmer to install their man as leader was a huge political gamble. But if the mood at the Labour party conference in Liverpool is anything to go by, it is one that – so far – has paid off.

The contrast with last year, when Starmer retained his grip on the party and Burnham slunk away from Liverpool early, could not be more stark. Their relief at their turn of fortune is tempered only by the fiscal headwinds ahead.

Cabinet ministers recount how at their political meeting two weeks ago, they were shown a series of charts showing the metrics behind the Burnham bounce. One in particular stood out to those in the room.

It was a graph showing whether the public felt the government was heading in the right direction. Until the end of June, it had been on a downward trajectory as public frustration mounted over Starmer’s leadership.

But once Starmer announced his intention to step down and Burnham took over in July, the line suddenly rebounded and, while still in negative territory, has been moving definitively upwards since. “We’ve got a second hearing with the public,” one cabinet minister said. “We can’t squander it.”

This time last year, just 14 months after coming to power, several were privately despairing about Labour’s electoral prospects. But with an energetic new prime minister and after a difficult summer for Nigel Farage, they now believe that a second term is winnable.

It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that speculation about a snap election escalated in the run-up to the conference, to the extent that Burnham felt compelled to “knock that dead” and confirm a 2029 date instead.

Some of the prime minister’s closest advisers wanted him to rule out an early election from the off, pressing him to be explicit. “The polling isn’t good enough. We could end up being the biggest party but we could lose our majority,” one said. Another said: “Elections have to be about a choice, not a referendum on an alternative plan.”

But others inside No 10 felt he should go to the country while the polling was good, Farage was on the back foot, and before Burnham’s big plans for change ran headfirst into fiscal reality. “Right now the public is willing to give us the benefit of the doubt – that won’t last for ever,” one said.

For his part, Burnham claims he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite the severe economic headwinds, by delivering tangible – albeit smaller – improvements in the short term while setting out a longer-term vision to transform things such as social care and youth unemployment at the same time.

“There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them,” he told the Guardian at the weekend. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change.”

The slogan of his first conference as leader has been “hope again” – but with the bleak global economic landscape there is less hope around than there was when he walked into Downing Street two months ago.

The first crucial test for Burnham will be next month’s budget, at which he said the government would be “highly prudent” with the public finances, amid concerns that Labour needs to reassure the markets.

But if the budget is about intent, next summer’s spending review is about proof, and as such, that could prove to be a make-or-break moment for this prime minister. It’s easy to make the promises, but much harder to deliver on them.

With obstacles ahead, the relief felt by Labour MPs and ministers in Liverpool is heavily caveated. One cabinet minister quoted Alastair Campbell’s election mantra as a warning to colleagues who might be getting ahead of themselves: “Lots done, lots to do, lots to lose.”

UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 18:00:11 GMT

Exclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossings

UK politics live – latest updates

Shabana Mahmood will announce a new legal route for refugees that prioritises Afghan women and girls and Palestinians, unfreezing a scheme that will put the most vulnerable refugees on a faster path to permanent status.

The change marks a shift in Mahmood’s approach to asylum seekers after the abrupt closure of the Afghan resettlement scheme last year and changes that will keep refugee status under constant review for two decades.

The home secretary is to say the changes will show there is fairness in the immigration system to support the most vulnerable refugees and that a balanced system will “unlock the inherent generosity of this country”.

However, immigration experts and refugee charities have said the numbers who will be eligible are too small to deter asylum seekers crossing the Channel in small boats.

The reopening of the scheme is likely to attract criticism from the right, especially as women and girls and people with disabilities are the most likely to be dependent on the welfare state.

Reform UK and the Conservatives are also likely to raise questions about security checks – which the Home Office says will be carried out – after the Sunday Times revealed that a former Hamas bodyguard had been granted asylum in the UK and was recently arrested on suspicion of being part of a terrorist plot.

Mahmood will tell the Labour conference on Monday that she will reopen the UK resettlement scheme, which was in effect suspended for two years, though never formally closed.

The home secretary will say that a tougher migration system, combined with a new scheme for the most vulnerable, will be the best way to ensure there is still broad consensus for helping refugees.

“Fairness is what unites us in this country. A fair society is what unlocks the very best of us. Because when people think this country is fair, they are more open and generous to others. When this country feels unfair, people turn inwards. They grow less willing to tolerate difference,” she will say.

“I know the British people have not given up on their belief that we should be compassionate, live up to our international obligations, and save the lives of those fleeing war and persecution. But I also know this process must be capped and controlled, and communities must be ready and able to welcome those who come here.

“This is what we can do and who we can be as we restore control to our borders, bear down on the small boat crossings, and unlock the inherent generosity of this country.”

The Home Office expects about one in four arrivals to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, though numbers will initially be very small and capped each year. Under the scheme, potential refugees will undergo security and criminality checks.

Those who arrive via the scheme will have a far more generous route to permanent settlement – granted indefinite leave to remain, which will give them a five-year path, in contrast to the constant review of status for those who arrive via irregular routes such as small boat crossings.

The home secretary will also formally open another scheme announced earlier this year allowing community sponsors from next month to apply to bring refugees to build a new life in the UK. A sponsored work route for refugees is expected to follow in the spring.

Home Office sources said the plan would be to begin with numbers in the hundreds and grow to the low thousands as levels of illegal migration fall. A cap would be set each year, sources said.

Refugees will be identified by the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) and the International Refugee Assistance Project (Irap).

The scheme had stopped taking any new referrals in December 2024. By that point, it was being used by only a tiny number. It will be reopened immediately, Mahmood will announce, with priority given to people with disabilities and for women and girls deemed to be vulnerable.

Family units will be able to come together under the scheme, though not extended families because of a crackdown on family reunification introduced earlier by the government.

Government statistics show that almost 300 “legacy cases” arrived under the existing UK resettlement scheme over the first half of this year. Officials said they were people who had been referred under the scheme before it was suspended and who had taken time to arrive in the UK.

Mahmood will also confirm two of three other settlement schemes that have previously been announced. Starting in October, charities and nonprofits will be able to apply to become sponsors, allowing communities and universities to host refugees. The first batch of arrivals on that scheme are expected to arrive by autumn next year.

Applications for sponsors for a work sponsorship route, under which companies will host refugees, will open in spring 2027. Sponsors must provide accommodation, integration support and help finding work, with the aim of reducing pressure on local authorities.

Numbers across all of the schemes are likely to be tightly limited, meaning the vast majority of refugees in the UK who arrive via irregular routes will still be subject to new and harsh restrictions on their status.

Mahmood has previously announced that refugees will have their status reviewed every 30 months for up to 20 years, with the possibility of returning them to their home countries should those be deemed safe.

Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the reopened route bore similarities to a scheme that was closed by Labour last year, and that its impact would depend on the numbers allowed to enter the UK.

“It has been framed primarily as a matter of principle – in other words, the UK should be doing its bit, and not as a strategy to reduce unauthorised arrivals.

“That is just as well, because there is no reason to believe that resettlement would have a large impact on unauthorised arrivals,” she said. Allowing in the “most vulnerable” in the resettlement part of the scheme would be a “trade-off” because of rising costs to the state, Sumption said.

“On one hand, there is widespread political support for the idea of prioritising more vulnerable refugees who would not have been able to make it over on a small boat.

“On the other hand, previous data suggests that these more vulnerable refugees, for understandable reasons, struggle more to support themselves in the UK, and fare considerably worse in the labour market, for example, than people who arrive through the asylum system,” she said.

Responding to the announcement, Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “The government deserves credit for creating new safe and legal routes that will help refugees reach the UK without risking their lives. Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people-smugglers’ business model, but they only work if they operate at scale. That means thousands of places, not hundreds.”

Reading Polly Hudson’s account of clearing her mother’s house (My mum has died – and every decision I make about her belongings feels wrong, 20 September) made me think about my experience of doing the same. I sort of enjoyed the task, viewing it as the last thing that I could do for my mother, and seeing myself as a curator in reverse.

I was determined to recycle as much as possible, feeding the good things through to charity shops and going back later to see what had and hadn’t sold. When one charity shop in the Welsh border town where my mother lived didn’t want her manual typewriter, on the grounds that nobody would have use for it, I took it to a charity shop in London, which snapped it up and put it in the window.

I kept a number of things, including some clothes that I wear, a sideboard that had belonged to my grandparents and assorted kitchenware. Some things were offered to family and friends who needed them. Correspondence was kept, including a bundle of letters that I’d sent to my mother when I was at college in the early 1980s. Clearing a house can be a peculiar joy – the marking of a life well lived and lovingly remembered. Dorothy StannardLondon

Polly Hudson’s final paragraph is spot-on. So long as you have the physical space, it’s not a “now or never” thing. I went through my mother’s things in waves. Many items that were impossible to throw out the first time around had became less so when I revisited them a few months or a year later. It was a gradual process that felt reliable.

My sister and I evolved the concept of the “family archive”. So much that we as children were familiar with – such as what our parents looked like on holiday in their 40s – is fascinating to grandchildren who have only known them in old age, and the next generation will perhaps never have seen them at all.

We don’t keep everything. Pictures showing 1960s clothing, some predecimal coins and notes, a photograph of the house that was our family home for 50 years. To coming generations, a paper-based diary will be a real curio. A 50s-era small cardboard suitcase will be a suitable home for the archive. Kersti WagstaffBillingshurst, West Sussex

Polly Hudson has my sympathy. My advice would be to take as much as you can to your own home before deciding. Every item holds memories not only of the person but of them in their home. Take any photos of where the items “lived”. Once removed, it can feel different and decisions may be easier.

I am starting a little bit of “death cleaning” before this has to be dealt with by my daughter. It’s slow, because my thoughts are always about “would she like this, would she be upset by me throwing this out or by keeping it?” I still have some of my parents’ stuff. Anyone interested in my mum’s school reports from the 1930s? Jo BannonLondon

Sadly too late now, but maybe Polly Hudson should have persuaded her mother to downsize before she died. I am filled with guilt at the sheer amount of stuff that my daughter will have to deal with, but at least she won’t have the problem of disposing of the contents of six bedrooms and 18 bookshelves. I now make do with two of each. Margaret Squires St Andrews, Fife

The final whistle for the football booze ban?

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 17:27:04 GMT

The rushed law probably increases pre-match binge drinking, writes Prof Geoff Pearson; plus a letter from a concerned reader who lives near a football ground

The prime minister is right to identify that the existing ban on alcohol consumption at football matches is viewed by fans as discriminatory (Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands, 23 September). However, the need for reform of this legislation goes much further.

The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985 was rushed through parliament, despite reservations at the time from the police and football authorities, and the absence of any evidence that it would reduce football-related disorder. Since then, no studies have indicated that the prohibition has reduced drunkenness or disorder at matches, but research has demonstrated how the ban can increase risks to public order and safety.

Prohibitions on drinking in the stands probably increases pre-match binge drinking, as well as causing crushes at turnstiles and in concourses. And the equally important ban on alcohol consumption on chartered transport to matches pushes visiting fans who want to drink into town centres and on to already crowded scheduled train services.

It is time that this outdated and ill-informed piece of panic law is subjected to evidence-based review. Prof Geoff PearsonUniversity of Manchester Law School

Simultaneously, billionaires suddenly see an opportunity to buy influence in the UK’s democracy – loudly denied – and elsewhere tax exiles such as Jim Ratcliffe seem empowered to rant about Britain’s decline from when it was the greatest empire in the world.

Formerly enslaved people in Guyana embraced collective action

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 17:24:29 GMT

We should learn about emancipated people’s extraordinary capacity for mutual endeavour, writes Prof Kathryn A Monk, in response to an article in the Cotton Capital series

Your report (British corporation continued trafficking of enslaved Africans to Guyana 40 years after abolition, 23 August) tells one important part of Guyana’s post-slavery history. There is another that deserves to be better known.

In 1839, little more than a year after full emancipation in British Guiana, 83 formerly enslaved men and women pooled their savings to buy the 200-hectare (500-acre) Northbrook plantation. They renamed it Victoria. Other purchases by other groups followed, developing into what became known as the communal African village movement.

These were not simply individual acts of property ownership. Many had kept their hard-earned savings buried for safekeeping; the first payment for Northbrook was reportedly carried to Georgetown in coins in a wheelbarrow. Formerly enslaved people went on to buy land collectively, establish villages and devise their own arrangements for managing roads, land and other shared resources. Victoria had established its own code of local government by 1845.

Having worked in Guyana, I have always found this one of the most remarkable parts of its history. At almost the same moment that plantation interests were trying to perpetuate the old system, people emerging from slavery were demonstrating an extraordinary capacity for collective action, self-government and mutual endeavour.

The history of emancipation is not only the history of what was done to formerly enslaved people, but of what they chose to build once they were free. Prof Kathryn A MonkBristol

In the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called 999 and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later.

The resident, who asked not to be named but reportedly is a local farmer, told the Press Association: “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they [the men] were planning. A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the airbase is on high alert. I think it’s absolutely astonishing.”

If there had been no 999 call, it appears the authorities would have been unaware of the vans and the potential threat they posed to nearby RAF Fairford.

People living in the area have been used to disturbance from protesters and a heavy police presence ever since the decision to allow the US air force to use Fairford as a base for attacks on Iran. But in recent weeks they have noticed dramatically increased security measures, with the gates of the base newly barricaded.

“In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy vehicles across all gates,” another resident said. She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously.”

The resident said “great big concrete walls” had also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road.

If local people had questioned the necessity of those steps, they may have been persuaded this weekend. In the early hours of Sunday morning, others in Whelford became aware of suspicious activity as the local WhatsApp group lit up with messages.

One resident of Whelford, named Jason, who declined to give his surname, said they were first alerted that something was happening at about 1.30am when people in the chat group started discussing the vans.

Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said the 999 call had only come after an attempt to contact the airbase itself. “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.”

A photograph published by the Daily Mail showed police arresting five shirtless men at night. Police later confirmed that five men had been taken into custody on suspicion of explosives and terror-related offences.

Residents were then woken at 6am by police banging on their doors and telling them to leave immediately. People from 85 households were taken to a nearby leisure centre.

Tudsbery said: “[The police] were banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown. There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.”

Thirty emergency vehicles were seen in the village, with the army, a bomb squad and counter-terrorism police all investigating at the scene. Explosives experts were seen examining three vans.

The RAF base has come to prominence since March and the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran. From the perimeter of the RAF base it has been possible to see heavy bombs being loaded on to American aircraft.

Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs.

Jason, 50, was evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre at 6am on Sunday with his family and 11-week-old puppy, Poppy, and friends who were visiting from London.

“We went to bed [the previous night],” he said. “It was early the next morning when the doorbell rang. It was the police asking residents to evacuate as there had been a major incident.”

Jason, who works in consulting, said there were about 40 to 50 people in the leisure centre, ranging from toddlers to elderly villagers, as well as a number of dogs. He said they had been given no more details than those that had been released publicly by police.

The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds.

It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives. Those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night.

By Sunday afternoon, the cordon around the village had expanded so no one could get anywhere near it. Access to the village of Whelford remained closed. With RAF Fairford located along one side of the road, a single police vehicle acted as a blockade against further passage into the village.

Tudsbery said he hoped he could get home soon. He had left his cat, Misty, behind.

Team Europe reclaimed their Laver Cup title with a dominant 13-5 victory against Team World on the final day of competition at the O2 Arena.

The contest had been finely poised after two days, with Team Europe holding a narrow 7-5 lead at the start of the day. With each match worth three points on Sunday, Europe needed two wins from the four remaining matches to win. They clinched their victory efficiently.

Jakub Mensik and Flavio Cobolli opened the day with a 7-5, 6-3 win against Alex de Minaur and Taylor Fritz before Alexander Zverev, the recent French and US Open champion, closed out the series with a 7-6 (3), 6-3 win against Learner Tien.

This was a logical result. The world No 2, Alexander Zverev, the No 3, Carlos Alcaraz, and the No 7, Flavio Cobolli, are all ranked more highly than Team World’s highest‑ranked players, De Minaur and Fritz, and there is just much more depth in a continent that has won the past 67 men’s grand slam titles. The last non-European player to win a men’s grand slam title was Argentina’s Juan Martín del Potro at the 2009 US Open.

This appeared to be another successful edition of the event on its return to London four years after Roger Federer retired from tennis here. There were packed crowds throughout the weekend, the matches were competitive even though the extremely slow courts did not always make for quality tennis. The interactions between the Team World captain, Andre Agassi, and his group of players were extremely entertaining.

Agassi closed off his second term with one more memorable moment, using his speech during the trophy ceremony as an opportunity to roast Zverev, essentially portraying him as a petulant whiner: “Congratulations Sascha, crazy year, seeing you win for the first time, I know how important that was for you.

“It was important to me because I could start listening to your press conferences again. You weren’t like, ‘[mimicking crying] why do I always lose? I’m third-best in the world, I suck. But then you win and it’s like: ‘I’m only one slam champion and I gotta do it again.’”

However, the defining and most revealing moment of this year’s event came on Saturday. A few hours after Zverev lost his first singles match against De Minaur from match point up, Alcaraz faced two match points against Fritz deep in their final-set tiebreak.

Nevertheless the sight of Banton, 126 from 105 balls, and Cox, 76 from 52, helping to put 355 for seven on the board, before Sri Lanka were derailed for 132 all out in 29.1 overs, said something about what is coming through. Had Jacob Bethell and Jos Buttler been fit, both would have been running the drinks in all likelihood.

Brook provided a bit of ­inspiration himself, cracking 77 from 66 balls before overseeing Sri Lanka’s disintegration. The call to bat first in a match starting at 10.30am in ­September also went against the norm but ended up securing a 2-1 scoreline – ­England’s sixth bilateral series win in ­limited‑overs cricket this year.

“Having not played too much 50-over cricket, you forget how long you have got to bat,” Banton said. “The tempo, hitting a few ­boundaries but going up and down the gears – there were periods they bowled well and I had to respect that.

“It’s been an ­amazing few hours. I got close the other day [73 at ­Headingley] and got out at an important time. I came here today committed to what I have been doing. To finally get over the line with a hundred is difficult to put into words.”

And at the end of a long season that saw him thrust back into Test captaincy came the dismissal that has haunted his summer, trapped lbw by a medium-pacer in Janith Liyanage.

Banton ransacked 16 fours and five sixes overall, his half-century ­coming off 51 balls and three-figures just 44 more. Nerves were pretty ­nonexistent as the milestone came into view, Banton dancing down to the spinner Dunith Wellalage and ­creaming him through extra cover to trigger a deserved standing ovation.

What happens when Bethell is fit may not just be a question for the Test side and it was not a great day for Ben Duckett to endure a fifth‑ball duck. That said, even in a topsy‑turvy summer across formats that ended bowled by a ball from Dilshan ­Madushanka that swung away and nipped in, the left-hander was ­coming off a fluent 67 in Leeds and 141 against the might of India at Lord’s mid-season.

Buttler remains a lock in the side, fundamentally, although Cox has seen his stock rise significantly this season. Arriving at 218 for three in the 35th over – Brook having ­mis‑timed his latest attempt to clear deep ­midwicket – he initially took a look, going at a run a ball to reach 30 before accelerating at the death. His half-century was also his first in List A cricket, this his 10th match in the format.

Changing UK benefits for young people a ‘moral crusade’, says minister

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:33:17 GMT

Pat McFadden urges Labour MPs to back overhauls, amid signs party looking to cut payments for some 16- to 24-year-olds

UK politics live – latest updates

Labour MPs have a moral responsibility to accept significant changes to the welfare system to help get more young people into work, the work and pensions secretary has said.

In a sign he is looking to overhaul the welfare state, Pat McFadden said it was time for Labour to “renew” the system first created by the Clement Attlee government and given a new deal by New Labour.

The cabinet minister said there would be “decisions to make and responsibilities to take” after two reviews of the system are published this autumn – on young people by Alan Milburn, and on a key disability benefit by the Timms panel.

He said Labour must decide “how we have a new system focused on opportunity, how we move from asking what are you entitled to, to asking how do we change your life … It falls to us, the party which did so much to create it, the party that holds it dear, to embrace the change needed.”

His speech is a sign that the government is preparing the ground again for changes to the welfare system after Keir Starmer’s government was forced to U-turn last year on a £5bn-a-year programme of disability benefit cuts in the face of a Labour backbench rebellion. The revolt was fuelled by outrage that the plans would push hundreds of thousands of disabled people into poverty.

Andy Burnham, Starmer’s replacement as prime minister, has said he will not shy away from changing the system in a “Labour way” that helps people back into work, rather than putting a figure on trying to save money on the overall bill.

However, many charities supporting disabled people are nervous about the prospect of an overhauled system, after so many cuts in the past.

After the Timms and Milburn reviews conclude, the government is expected to design a new system and assessment process for disability benefits that is likely to require new legislation. It will also focus particularly on how to support younger people into jobs and training, building on the current “jobs guarantee” that funds employment placements for under-25s for six months, with disabled young people given fast-track access.

Officials have been looking to see whether elements of other countries’ benefit systems can be borrowed, such as the Netherlands, where youth hubs tackle unemployment, and Denmark, which restricts access to the country’s “disability pension” for the under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they permanently have no ability to work.

A million young people are now out of work, employment and training in the UK, and there has been a sharp rise in numbers of young people claiming disability benefits, particularly since the pandemic. This has prompted a political debate about the sustainability of working-age disability benefits spending, which is forecast to rise from £14bn in 2019 to £34bn in 2030.

Some types of claim have particularly surged among young people. About 205,000 16- to 24-year-olds received the personal independence payment (Pip) for disabilities linked to ADHD or autism in April this year, a more than threefold increase since 2019, at a cost in 2025-26 of £1.36bn. The average Pip claim for this cohort was £8,800 a year.

McFadden said both the financial cost and the human cost of the system were “too high”.

The interim findings of the Timms review found that Pip was unfit for purpose and too often left vulnerable claimants feeling dehumanised and degraded.

The benefit, which helps with the extra costs of disability, is non-means tested and not related to employment status. A panel is consulting on measures to overhaul the system, with input from disability organisations.

Milburn’s interim report, published in May, made it clear young people diagnosed with lifelong complex needs who are never able to work must be protected by the benefit system. But it also hinted that young people with less severe conditions, who could be supported to work, may see reductions in benefits.

In his speech, McFadden said it was a “moral crusade” to stop so many young people being trapped on disability benefits instead of being helped into work, saying: “A young person who signs on for sickness benefits when they are 20 is now more likely to reach the age of 30 and still be on them than to have held down a steady job in a single year in between.”

He added: “And a young person left out of work is far more likely to die before their time than the friends they sat beside in school … this is shameful. We should not accept it. We have to change it.”

Elliott returned to the field after half-time – Earl shifting to the pack with Barbeary making way – and it was down his wing that Leicester had their third try, and Hamer-Webb his second, after good work from Wainwright.

The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:30:09 GMT

Bill payers should not fund another rescue for financiers of the water industry. Public ownership can end the cycle of extraction and failure

This month, a cross-party parliamentary committee said Thames Water should be placed in temporary state control and that any takeover by its creditors should be halted. The MPs were right. The “special administration” regime keeps the taps running while shareholders are wiped out, creditors take a haircut and the firm’s £19bn of debt is restructured. But it must not then be handed back to private hands. After Thames Water has failed its 16 million customers, polluted rivers, paid out billions to shareholders and repeatedly demanded higher bills, a City-friendly reprieve would only reward the outrageous behaviour that the regulatory system is meant to deter. Ministers ought to seize the opportunity to nationalise Thames Water.

In July, Andy Burnham agreed. On the campaign trail in Makerfield, he told reporters that “there’s a very strong case for public ownership [for Thames Water] to sort out its problems”. Having entered parliament and become prime minister, Mr Burnham is instead looking at letting elected mayors “oversee” private water companies. There is nothing wrong with more democratic scrutiny. However, oversight without ownership and proper control seems like a sleight of hand. Voices from different wings of the party recognise this. Mr Burnham can’t kick the decision down the road for ever.

In less than two weeks, water privatisation will be on the ballot in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when voters elect an MP to succeed Sir Keir Starmer. A campaign to boycott Thames Water bills has sprung up in the London constituency after repeated flooding caused by broken pipes. When asked by the Camden New Journal when the mains were last inspected, maintained or replaced, Thames Water gave “no answers”. If Labour cannot take a failing private monopoly that ruins lives into public ownership, voters may ask themselves who will?

Polls suggest comfortable majorities of Britons believe water companies should be run in the public sector. Under Sir Keir, Labour’s review of the water sector ruled out nationalisation. Some claim that new models of corporate governance could “subordinate” profits to the common good. But it’s hard to see how a failed regulatory regime will be fixed by more regulation. History has been turned on its head when British Rail is cited as proof that nationalisation is wrong. The state-owned rail firm had productive staff working in an ageing railway starved of investment. By 2011, privatised rail cost 20%-30% more. Sound familiar? Mr Burnham called water “an industry where the shareholders never lose and the bill payers never win”. Deeds, not just words, are needed.

England and Wales are outliers: 90% of the globe keeps water in public hands because others understand that a natural monopoly in water offers no competition to raise standards and leaves households as captive customers for financiers eyeing easy profits. Nationalisation comes with a price tag. But, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies acknowledges, assessing the true cost to the state requires valuing the whole deal and future cashflows, not just looking at metrics that exclude most of what is being acquired. An efficient nationalised water industry should mean cheaper bills. Currently, Ofwat allows industry’s backers to recoup £22bn over five years. A Greenwich University study calculates that nationalisation could save households up to £160 a year by accessing low-cost state financing. The upshot of public ownership is that it puts an asset on the nation’s books, whereas privatisation puts the cost on customers’ bills.

The Guardian view on Manchester City: a strange kind of glory

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:25:09 GMT

If a guilty verdict on multiple counts of financial misreporting is upheld against the club, its achievements in the modern era will be forever tainted

In surveys ranking the Premier League’s greatest moments, football supporters regularly give pride of place to Sergio Agüero’s championship-winning goal for Manchester City in 2012. Scored in injury time on the last day of the season, Agüero’s strike against Queens Park Rangers delivered the first league title for City since the 1960s. Knocking their historic rivals Manchester United into second place, it also signalled a new era in which the club replaced United as the dominant force in the English game.

“Aguerooooooo!” – the incredulous single-word response from the match commentator Martin Tyler – has entered football folklore. But an asterisk may now be needed at the end of all those Os. Reports that an independent panel has found Manchester City guilty of breaking Premier League rules between 2009 and 2023 cast a dark shadow over that day, and much else besides. During that period, the club won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Uefa Champions League, all while under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi ruling family. The inescapable implication of the apparent ruling is that those trophies were won unfairly.

The guilty verdict on more than one hundred separate charges against City has yet to be officially confirmed. It may be assumed that the club – which has consistently denied wrongdoing – will launch an appeal. But rivals are already taking advice over compensation claims and the Premier League, which began its investigation in 2018 after whistleblower leaks, must contemplate how tough it wants to be on the most successful English football club of the current era.

If the verdict is upheld, the punishment should be exemplary and severe, given the threat to the integrity and credibility of the world’s most popular domestic football league. In essence, Sheikh Mansour and his board stand accused of illicitly bankrolling the City men’s team’s ascent from Premier League also-rans to repeat champions, using inflated sponsorship deals and off the books payments to fuel the rise. The club hierarchy’s aggressive response to scrutiny conveyed a sense that it seemingly thought extreme wealth – and the political heft of Abu Dhabi’s soft-power project – could confer a kind of impunity.

The Premier League’s investigators should be congratulated for staying the course, and this extraordinarily long-running saga should now be brought to as swift a conclusion as possible. It is hard not to feel some sympathy for Manchester City supporters, confronted with the likelihood that the greatest period in their club’s history will be forever tainted. On the pitch, City’s football during the Abu Dhabi era has at times been of a sublime quality, overseen by an inspired coach in Pep Guardiola. But off it, the biggest financial scandal in English football history is a reminder that the volume of money now washing about at the top of the game has been bad for its sporting soul.

During the Premier League boom years, great footballing institutions have lost their spiritual bearings as dubious billionaires, debt-leveraging carpetbaggers and petrostates have muscled in for a piece of the action. In the case of Manchester City, the Sheikh Mansour takeover delivered undreamt of success and that Agüero moment. But if it took persistent cheating to get there, it was a worthless kind of glory.

Most of UK’s essential food supply grown in drought-risk areas, report warns

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:24:27 GMT

Keys crops such as cereals, potatoes, sugar and oils grown in areas with moderate to very high risk

The vast majority of the UK’s essential foods, including cereals, potatoes, sugar and oil, are grown in areas of England rated as having a moderate to very high risk of drought.

A very high proportion – 81% – of England’s fresh produce is concentrated in parts of the country that are already experiencing water stress, according to the analysis by the nature-focused investment fund Rebalance Earth.

Three-quarters of England’s wheat (77%), barley (75%) and oilseed rape (74%) grow in parts of the country rated as being at a moderate to very high drought risk, along with 70% of sugar beet and 67% of potatoes, it found.

It said about a quarter of the country’s staple crops were grown in areas facing an acute risk of drought, including 30% of wheat and barley, 28% of oilseed rape, 27% of fresh produce and 21% of potatoes.

“Drought builds slowly and quietly, and rarely gets the same attention as flooding, but its impact runs right through the economy: lower yields, strained supply chains and higher prices in all of our shopping baskets,” said Kirsty Wilman, the fund’s chief operating and financial officer.

Some of England’s traditionally most productive agricultural areas – such as East Anglia, long known as the country’s breadbasket, and Kent, often described as the garden of England – are among those facing the greatest pressure from drought and have seen prolonged periods of dry weather in recent years.

The yield from this year’s cereals harvest in England and Wales was described as disappointing in the final 2026 harvest report from the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), with volumes of wheat, spring barley and oats below historical averages across the UK.

Crop yields are also significantly lower than normal on the Elveden estate in Suffolk, which is owned by the Guinness family and includes 9,000 hectares (22,000 acres) of farmed land.

There was significant coastal flooding, rough surf, powerful winds, rain and dangerous rip currents from North Carolina through New England. Boston and the New York City tri-state area were among the regions affected.

Power was slowly being restored by Sunday afternoon , with about 110,500 households still without electricity, according to the website Poweroutage. US. In New York, more than 21,000 customers remained without electricity, while the power was out for about 11,940 customers in New Jersey.

The National Weather Service said the nor’easter was expected to weaken on Sunday night, with heavy rainfall persisting into Monday in several regions of the mMid-Atlantic and New England. Coastal flood warnings were canceled several regions of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) advised travelers to check with their airlines for updated flight information. FlightAware reported more than 5,000 US delays and nearly 550 cancellations. In Massachusetts, a temporary ground delay was issued at the Boston Logan international airport amid the weather.

As a result of the storm, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency covering the Bronx, Kings, Nassau, New York, Queens, Richmond, Suffolk and Westchester counties.

A fallen tree in the east New York City borough of Brooklyn resulted in a death on Saturday during the nor’easter. A 56-year-old New York City housing authority employee was killed when a tree came down on him in a parking lot.

Police said he was pronounced dead at Brookdale University hospital. Authorities had not immediately determined whether wind caused the tree to fall.

In Queens, high winds caused widespread disruption after a tree fell at about 5.40pm in the Glendale area, with downed power lines forcing authorities to close the roadway. As a precaution, the New York City fire department evacuated a nearby building. No injuries were reported in that incident.

Along the Jersey Shore, residents spent Saturday removing debris and cleaning up between periods of high tide after the nor’easter forced flood water into streets and homes near the New Jersey coast. Eight counties in New Jersey remain under a state of emergency issued before the coastal storm arrived.

The storm struck the mid-Atlantic and New England over the weekend and was forecast to continue into the early part of this week. As the week continues, flooding was expected to rise and recede along with the tides.

The National Weather Service (NWS) expected coastal flooding to bring significant flooding from the Jersey Shore south to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, with more moderate flooding forecast along the Massachusetts coast.

Does GLP-1 use result in significant hair loss?

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:00:08 GMT

Experts share what you need to know about GLP-1-related hair loss as the side-effect gets more attention from researchers

About 20 million people across the US, UK, and EU are taking GLP-1 receptor agonists like tirzepatide and semaglutide (Ozempic or Mounjaro are common brands) for weight loss and type 2 diabetes. As their use has surged, we’re learning more about their side-effects. One that’s been getting a lot of attention from researchers lately: hair loss.

In one survey of people who take these medications, 20% of respondents experienced hair shedding, although the lack of high-quality data from a randomized, controlled trial to assess this side-effect makes it difficult to know exactly how common it is.

While GLP-1-related hair loss is often temporary and reversible, it’s significant enough that some patients hesitate to take drugs they would otherwise benefit from using. Here’s what you need to know.

Most people who take GLP-1 drugs don’t have hair loss. However, those who do often notice it within the first year, usually peaking a little before the 12th month.

They’re usually experiencing one of two types of hair loss, says Lynn Petukhova, a geneticist at New York University who studies hair loss disorders. The most common type is a stress-related condition that dermatologists call telogen effluvium, where a stressor pushes an unusually large share of hair follicles into their resting phase. During this stage, the affected hair ceases to grow – and after two to three months, it falls out. This kind of hair loss is temporary; the growth interruption and shedding stops once the stressor does, and hair typically goes back to growing normally.

A much smaller proportion of people taking GLP-1s experience new or increased pattern baldness, says Petukhova. That’s the genetically influenced, usually permanent hair loss that causes a receding hairline or thinning at the crown in men, and widening of the center part in women.

In a recent study Petukhova led, men taking GLP-1 drugs were 7% more likely to experience this type of hair loss than men not taking the drugs. (The study was unable to assess the risk in women because their genes for the condition aren’t as well understood.)

Hair loss may also manifest differently depending on hair type. In one study, white patients were more likely to report hair shedding and thinning, while Black patients more commonly reported hair dryness and breakage.

Telogen effluvium has two possible causes in the setting of rapid weight loss: the shock of sudden and severe calorie restriction, and micronutrient deficiencies that result from dramatically reduced food intake.

The type of drug and dosage is also relevant; people taking tirzepatide and semaglutide, especially at higher doses, had the highest rates of temporary hair loss.

Women make up nearly 90% of people who report telogen effluvium when taking GLP-1 drugs. Women also commonly experience it after giving birth, as a result of abrupt hormonal changes. It frequently follows weight loss surgery too; as many as 60% of patients have hair loss after the procedure.

after newsletter promotion

Pattern baldness on GLP-1s is less well understood but likely occurs because of some biological connection between the genes that make someone respond to GLP-1 drugs and those that cause this type of hair loss, says Petukhova. “Some people have a higher genetic risk” for pattern baldness, she says, “and the drug will unmask it.”

If you’re considering starting a GLP-1 drug, it’s worth discussing the possibility of hair loss with your doctor.

Because hair follicles are extremely sensitive to certain nutritional deficiencies, eating enough protein and ensuring you’re consuming sufficient iron, zinc and biotin are sound strategies. However, these precautions are not guaranteed to prevent hair loss, especially if you’re losing weight rapidly. A lower dose and slower weight loss may also reduce your risk.

If you are experiencing hair loss, consult your regular doctor or a dermatologist who can help you determine whether it is temporary or permanent, and thus how to treat it. As mentioned above, temporary hair loss is reversible with nutrition, time and patience. For pattern hair loss, medications like minoxidil and finasteride may be useful.

If you have been prescribed a GLP-1 drug for health reasons and are concerned about side effects like hair loss, it’s important to talk to your doctor. The prospect of cosmetic changes alone shouldn’t discourage people from doing what’s best for the rest of their body, says Petukhova. “It’s more important for most people to get your metabolic health under control than to ensure that you have all the hairs on your head,” she says.

Tense standoff over loyalist march in Portadown as protesters block route
