Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow Garvaghy Road parade for first time since 1998

Portadown march: latest updates

Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking the route of a hugely contentious parade in Northern Ireland after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on a historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years.

The loyalist Drumcree parade along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness”.

It led to a weekend of intense legal wrangling which concluded at 2.15am on Sunday when the court of appeal said it could not interfere with the commission’s decision.

In driving rain on a cold Sunday morning, hundreds of nationalist protesters gathered to block the route. Many linked arms and sang songs as announcements were made over loudspeaker that they were liable to arrest and prosecution.

The Orangemen spent the day ensconced a mile away in a church, the proposed start of the march, and said they would wait until police told them the road was clear.

Among the protesters was the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, who said the decision to allow the parade was “madness” and “primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.”

She added: “The mood here has been peaceful. It has been united and orderly. This is a dignified and united community and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”

Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin vice-president and Northern Ireland first minister, was also there and said reigniting the dispute brought “into question how this whole peace process works”.

She told reporters: “We’re meeting families who feel collectively traumatised, who feel individually traumatised. Does anybody think that this is a good idea?

“No right-minded person would make this decision. I still do not know the answer to this question – why, after 28 years of a determination to block a march down this road, the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community.”

The local Democratic Unionist party (DUP) MP, Carla Lockhart, accused O’Neill of “whipping up hysteria” at an “unlawful” protest.

“It is unreal that we have a first minister behaving the way she is behaving,” she said. “If I did it, or if any of my colleagues did it, I would be in the back of a Land Rover.”

Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said: “We now have lawmakers acting as law breakers,” and he accused O’Neill of “giving two fingers to the courts, the police, the rule of law”.

The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, cut short his attendance at the Labour party conference in Liverpool to travel to Belfast, but said he did not have the powers to call the march off unless police formally requested him to do so. He said the nationalist protest was unlawful and called on politicians to “calm things down”.

Bryant said: “It is incumbent on everybody in political office to take this moment very, very seriously and to take the temperature down, to think twice before … inflating any argument and to think about what somebody else who doesn’t share your opinion might think about the way you’ve put your case.”

The tense standoff also drew in the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who appealed for “calm on all sides”.

The Irish taoiseach, Mícheál Martin, echoed that but described the Parades Commission decision as “incomprehensible and wrong”.

He called for the situation to be mediated sensibly in a way “that protects the gains that have been made and the peace and harmony that has prevailed for so long”.

The Drumcree parade on the Garvaghy Road – a Catholic enclave in a largely Protestant town – sparked some of the most serious and violent disorder in Northern Ireland’s history.

On Friday, the Parades Commission granted permission subject to restrictions, including a limit of 35 participants, an 8am start time instead of 1pm, and that it should be held in silence.

The decision was challenged and blocked on Saturday by a judge, Justice Patricia Smyth, who said the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland.

That decision was then challenged by the Orange Order, leading to two further hearings on Saturday night and Sunday morning.

The final, time-limited sitting, which began at 20 minutes past midnight on Sunday, was heard before Mr Justice Humphreys, who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances … with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”.

Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect the commission’s judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.

Burnham refreshes the parts others can’t reach on the Andy and Laura show

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 15:17:23 GMT

The PM oozes confidence and easy-going charm as he tells Laura Kuenssberg the hill he’ll die on is fixing social care

UK politics live – latest updates

In recent weeks there has been much speculation in some parts of the media that Andy Burnham would call an early general election. Speculation that existed largely in the heads of those writing the stories, as even the most favourable polls suggest Labour would lose its huge majority and become the largest party in a coalition government. But to stop the chatter dominating his party conference, Burnham made it clear there would be no early election. His reward? Headlines in the rightwing press that he had bottled it. By not calling an election he had never planned to call. Sometimes you just can’t win.

There again, you might call this a first-world problem for the prime minister. This time last year, Burnham had been hanging around the fringes of the conference as he and his allies attempted one of the most half-arsed coups in living memory. One that fizzled out almost before it had started and became the butt of many jokes among Keir Starmer’s inner circle. Andy looked to have blown himself up on the runway, leaving Keir safe for the duration of the parliament.

Fast forward a year and Burnham is in No 10, Reform UK’s lead in the polls has disappeared, and Labour is looking a lot more competitive than even the most rose-tinted party members could have reasonably expected in such a short period of time. Andy must be pinching himself. Unable to believe his luck. All that’s changed has been him. Energy prices are still sky high as a result of the war in Iran. The cost of living is still way too high. Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch might have been a problem for Keir but they aren’t for Andy. You might even call them assets.

No wonder then that Burnham was looking relatively chipper as he kicked off conference with the traditional lengthy interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg. Only relatively chipper, because you’d need to be a halfwit not to be a little wary. These interviews can go hideously wrong – Liz Truss’s at the Tory conference in 2022 is a collector’s item – and prime ministers generally regard them as exercises in damage limitation. To survive without generating the wrong kind of headlines is the dream.

“You look like you’re loving the job,” observed Laura. Somehow biting her lip and refraining from adding that it is early days and we’ll see how much you’ve aged by this time next year. Andy smiled. He was, he said. Not because he had the job he had always coveted. But because now he had a chance to make a difference. To end the drift and division of the decade since Brexit – he could have gone back another five years and included austerity. To do politics differently. To bring back hope. You’re going to hear a lot of the H-word in the next four days. It’s plastered over every wall of the conference centre.

And Burnham speaks as if he genuinely means it. He has the easy-going charm and self-confidence of a man who is comfortable in his own skin. He reaches parts that other politicians don’t get near. Nige has the same quality. Only, where he speaks to people’s fears and grievance, Andy has a way of making you feel better about yourself. You may still struggle to pay your bills, you may still fight to get a hospital appointment, but somehow you can believe in better days ahead. The triumph of hope over experience.

All of which is a much in demand – if not essential – skill for a politician. One that gives you a fighting chance of success. People feel both heard and seen by him. It’s almost uncanny. Burnham talks of being a different sort of politician, when the reality he is the archetypal career politician. You’d imagine he had spent years doing what he calls a real job as a hospital porter, but he’s been a politician almost all his adult life. Few understand the Westminster system better than him, he also suggests. You can’t escape the irony. Keir Starmer actually had a long and successful career outside politics, but he is the one who always sounded like the career politician. Speaking in soundbites and half truths. You’ve either got it or you haven’t.

The message Burnham really wanted to get across on Sunday morning was that social care was the hill he would die on. Other politicians had said they would tackle the issue but had recoiled when they realised how difficult it was. “I will grasp the nettle,” he said, opening his eyes still wider, hoping that viewers would fall into them. He would create a national care system that incorporated the NHS and social care. Old people were either paying through the nose for their own care, falling through the cracks or ending up bed blocking in hospitals. It was unsustainable and undignified.

How this would be paid for would be laid out in due course. It would be what Labour would campaign on in 2029. But make no mistake, people were already paying for it. Here he was preaching to the converted. My sisters and I had to sell my mother’s house to pay for her care during the last seven years of her life as she suffered from Alzheimer’s. We didn’t mind so much, but my mother would have been gutted had she been aware. It had mattered to her that she could leave her house to the three of us. Paying a little extra in tax to make sure that other people – possibly even you – don’t have to burn through their assets seems the kind of thing any fair-minded society would do.

Burnham ended by saying he very much hoped to work cross-party on all this. It was too important not to. This aspiration lasted all of five minutes. Because that’s how long it took the ever ridiculous Chris Philp – Kuenssberg’s next guest – to start going on about a “death and dementia tax”. Like clockwork. The Philpster becomes more and more a parody of himself. The Tory party’s very own Alan B’Stard. Venal, self-serving and not very bright. A man whose answer to everything is to cut the welfare bill still further, seemingly unaware his leader has already spent the cuts her party has proposed.

It’s as if Philp regards getting dementia as a personal failing, just as he sees being on benefits as morally deficient. If you get dementia then you deserve to pay for your own care. Now is not a good time to be one of Chris’s relatives. If you find yourself in need of care then you’re very much on your own. There’s no way the Philpster is missing out on his inheritance.

With turbulence all around, Armani plays it safe and easy in Milan

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 15:08:45 GMT

The late designer’s niece echoes his sense of relaxation, as the house seeks to prove itself to potential buyers

A year after the death of Giorgio Armani, the Italian fashion house he founded in 1975 is facing increasing uncertainty about its future ownership.

In his will, Armani, who ruled over the business for 50 years, instructed his heirs to sell an initial 15% stake of the company within 18 months of his death. If a private sale does not materialise, an IPO is mandated to take place. Now there are reports the group is readying itself for formal talks with the French conglomerate LVMH, the beauty giant L’Oréal and the eyewear group EssilorLuxottica – three of Armani’s preferred acquirers – over the possible sale of a minority stake.

Against this backdrop, pressure is mounting for the company to prove to potential buyers the continued allure of Armani. In 2025, its revenue fell for a second consecutive year, dropping 2.8% to €2.19bn.

In a turbulent luxury market, the question now is if Armani can remain a powerhouse without its founder – who turned it into an empire – at the helm.

So far during this era of upheaval, Armani’s niece Silvana Armani, who took over as creative director of womenswear after his death, has chosen to play it safe by leaning into continuity rather than any dramatic design shake-up.

Her latest show on Sunday – which closed out Milan fashion week – reflected this with a collection that further cemented her uncle’s legacy.

Relaxed suiting echoed Armani’s approach to tailoring. He famously did away with heavy shoulder padding and stiff linings. This sense of ease was boosted further by whisper-thin silk shirting and cardigan-like delicate cashmere jackets. In a recent interview, Silvana, who only wears trousers, jackets and shirts, said: “My woman inevitably ends up looking a bit like me.” The biggest changes she has implemented have been ditching her uncle’s beloved hats, adding more pockets to pieces including dresses, and using cotton, a material Armani disliked.

A double-breasted, black tailored suit styled with white gloves was inspired by a photo Silvana found of a young Armani at his communion. Another look included a sparkling printed bomber jacket featuring a printed portrait of the late designer.

Key to Armani’s success was his dominance of the Hollywood red carpet. From Diane Keaton in a greige menswear jacket at the 1978 Oscars to Julia Roberts in an oversized suit at the 1990 Golden Globes, Armani spearheaded the fusion of fashion and Hollywood.

More recently, a younger cohort of A-listers has been delving into the Armani archive, including Zendaya who wore a webbed dress from a 90s collection to the recent premiere of Spiderman in Italy. A series of liquid black slinky gowns and shimmering champagne tasselled looks showed the sustained capability the brand has when it comes to creating red-carpet drama.

However, there are hints greater change may be afoot at the company. Last week, it appointed Dario Vitale as creative director of Emporio Armani, making him the first external designer to lead an Armani line. The Italian designer has been tasked with revitalising the diffusion line launched by Armani in 1981. Aimed at a younger customer, it accounts for almost a third of the group’s revenue.

Vitale will also oversee the accessories offering at Giorgio Armani. He previously worked at Miu Miu, where he has been crediting with shaping its viral success, before landing the top job at Versace after Donatella’s departure. Despite widespread acclaim, his tenure ended abruptly last year. It is widely expected that Vitale will eventually take over the creative role at Giorgio Armani too, which for prospective buyers could add further enticement.

Elsewhere, on Saturday night, Sunderland-born Louise Trotter showed her third collection for Bottega Veneta. The brand famously created Intrecciato, a distinct handwoven leather technique in 1966, which Trotter has now reimagined across everything from giant bags to trench coats. Chunky crochet and handmade lace further added to the homespun mood. Trotter also secured one of the starriest moments of Milan fashion week.

The model Kendall Jenner closed the show, while her boyfriend, the Wuthering Heights actor Jacob Elordi, who has been an ambassador for the brand since 2024, snapped a photo from the front row. He sat alongside the musicians Tyler, the Creator, Solange and the actors Lauren Hutton and Julianne Moore.

The kindness of strangers: Two helicopter pilots flew down low to wave to my three-year-old son – he was beside himself with joy

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 15:00:08 GMT

My son adores helicopters, so we waved as hard as possible as it flew past. Then it suddenly looped and came back around

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

My sister lives in Ukraine; I live in Australia. We had gone five long years without seeing each other when we finally reunited during a trip to Los Angeles. One day we took my three-year-old son to the beach and spent the afternoon catching up.

We had a lot of conversations about people and kindness that day. I told her how I had noticed a softer side to men since having a son. As a woman, you’re often wary of construction workers, for example – what might they say to me when I walk past? But now when I pass a building site with my son, the workers often let him play with their radio, or beep a tractor to make him laugh. It was very heartwarming and gave me a whole new perspective on the other sex.

As I shared this observation with my sister, a coastguard helicopter flew overhead. My son adores helicopters and is always fascinated to see one, so we all waved as hard as possible as it flew past.

But instead of carrying on up the coast, the helicopter suddenly looped and came back around. It began flying super low and circled around us twice, with both pilots – two men – waving at my son and mouthing “Hi!” from the cockpit. It was so close it felt like it almost landed right in front of us.

We were shocked, as was everyone else at the beach – many people began filming. My sister burst into tears. My son was beside himself with joy. It was, simply, the coolest thing ever.

It felt like an embodiment of what I had just been telling my sister – that having a little boy of my own had shown me how good men can be.

After the helicopter flew away, we were left with the memory of those two pilots who saw a little kid and decided to do something to delight him, just because they could.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.

When a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships?

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 15:00:08 GMT

These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress

The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work

“It came as such a shock. I just can’t believe he’s gone.”

Psychologists are accustomed to seeing bereaved individuals. But working with Jodie* presented a unique challenge – she’d never met the person she was grieving. Jodie was reeling after the recent death of a well known singer. Despite not knowing the singer personally, Jodie’s grief and loss seemed as palpable as other patients speaking about the deaths of family members or loved ones. Jodie reported that weeks after the singer’s death, she was struggling to attend work and was sleeping poorly, describing herself as consumed with thoughts of the singer.

Jodie was experiencing grief related to a parasocial relationship. This is a social phenomenon in which a person experiences a one-sided psychological connection with a public figure or famous person. While an intimate and intense sense of friendship or connection is felt, the object of attention is oblivious to their admirer’s existence.

Parasocial relationships are a normal part of modern life. Many of us are engaged in some sort of parasocial relationship – perhaps with a famous actor, sportsperson, musician or even a fictional character from a novel or television show. We feel we know these people and become invested in their lives. It’s an uncomfortable truth for some that the people we are focused on are, in fact, strangers. They have no reciprocal care for us, nor investment in our lives the way a friend or family members might have.

At best, parasocial relationships allow us to tap into a brief fantasy of a life beyond our own, usually one of wealth and privilege. This daydreaming provides a break from the mundane and opens up space for creativity and lateral thinking for some people. But for others, such as Jodie, parasocial relationships can lead to emotional over-involvement and boundary-crossing behaviour. This can fuel psychological distress, especially when a celebrity dies or experiences a controversial or adverse life event.

Despite my own general indifference about the singer’s death, I was mindful to not dismiss Jodie’s feelings. The loss was significant to Jodie; pointing out the crude fact that they were strangers would likely damage our therapeutic rapport and may have led to Jodie becoming further entrenched in the parasocial relationship.

I attempted to relate to Jodie’s grief by tapping into my own experiences and observations of parasocial relationships: the anguish of many of my peers after Kurt Cobain’s death, the shock at Michael Jackson’s passing (and the complicated grief that followed), and the unprecedented public outpouring of sorrow following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. More recent examples of parasocial relationships also came to mind: fans’ unashamed obsession with Taylor Swift’s wedding, and, on a different note, fierce debate about Ariana Grande’s health and wellbeing.

It was important to manage Jodie’s acute distress before we sought to understand why the singer’s death had been so impactful. We devised a plan to reduce exposure to information about the singer and his death, using a blocking app to taper social media scrolling and news consumption to 20 minutes per day. Together with encouraging a walk twice a day, limiting time online went some way to reducing Jodie’s rumination and improving her sleeping patterns.

Jodie felt a strong connection to the singer. She listened to his music heavily during a difficult time in her own life, crediting the lyrics as “saving her”. She came to rely on his songs to lift her mood, providing a sense of company and comfort in an otherwise desolate period. These feelings had resurfaced upon hearing of his death. Allowing Jodie time and space to talk about her experience – of both her connection to the singer and the difficult time she had endured – helped alleviate her grief.

While our therapeutic work was prompted by the singer’s death, Jodie also detailed other parasocial relationships. She spoke about famous people as if they were in her own social circle, and expressed genuine delight at their personal and professional achievements.

It seemed apparent that Jodie was lacking vitality in her own life and had attempted to fill this gap by investing in parasocial relationships. But her focus on other people’s lives had been to the detriment of her own. We set about bolstering Jodie’s real-life relationships and enriching social interactions, included reconnecting with old friends, trying a range of hobbies where she might meet like-minded people, and making new connections through meet-up groups and local community events.

For Jodie, parasocial relationships felt safe. There’s little chance of rejection from someone viewed only from afar, and no need to navigate the usual difficulties and disagreements typical of real-life relationships. While parasocial relationships went some way to meeting Jodie’s fundamental need for affiliation and human connection, establishing genuine friendships brought reciprocity that parasocial relationships never could – people who Jodie cared about, who also cared about her.

*All clients are fictional amalgams

In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978. In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline. org.

Dr Bianca Denny is a clinical psychologist based in Melbourne. She is the author of Talk to Me: Lessons from Patients and Their Therapist

Britain knew about the Holocaust as it happened. A new exhibition reckons with that truth

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 14:00:06 GMT

Research draws upon reporting and witness testimony, while a permanent memorial is planned for London

The “complex and unsettling” story of what Britain knew during the Holocaust is being explored amid plans to create a new permanent national memorial.

An exhibition highlighting how news of the atrocity reached Britain much earlier than is commonly understood will tour the country after being viewed privately by MPs at Portcullis House on the parliamentary estate at Westminster in September.

The research draws upon newspaper reporting, broadcasts, academic scholarship, witness testimony and government archives. The exhibition is a sample of a more extensive, permanent exhibition for the national Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which is planned for a site in London.

Martin Winstone, the senior historical adviser to the Holocaust Educational Trust, said: “There’s a feeling today that Britain really only found out about the Holocaust at the end of the war. But in 1942, the year in which most victims of the Holocaust were murdered, you couldn’t really escape this information in Britain. It was in every newspaper. It was on the BBC.

“The Manchester Guardian was the newspaper that reported most extensively on the Holocaust, taking a crusading position that there was more the British government and allied governments could be doing.”

For years, the Manchester Guardian, which was banned from Germany in 1933 for highlighting Adolf Hitler’s antisemitism, called for immigration restrictions to be lifted for Jews, lobbied for pressure to be applied to neutral nations to open their borders to refugees and for special rescue measures, realising that “the Nazis were aiming at the complete elimination of an entire group of people”.

Much of the information about the Holocaust, including the locations of death camps, was smuggled out of Poland – where the murders were “happening in plain sight” – by couriers to the London-based Polish government-in-exile.

Winstone said: “It was a challenging situation. There were lots of things the government had to deal with. And for much of that war, Britain was on the defensive.

“On one level, the government’s response was always, ‘we’ll win the war, that’s how we stop this’; while critics said, ‘there’ll be nobody left to save, if that’s what you’re waiting for’.”

During the second world war, the government commissioned reports on antisemitism in Britain, with agents opening people’s mail and recording conversations overheard in air raid shelters to gauge public opinion.

In what Winstone described as a “complex and unsettling story”, Ministry of Information bulletins revealed that while there was mass public sympathy for Jews in occupied Europe, it contended with anti-migration and antisemitic sentiment.

Winstone added: “Nearly everybody in Britain was disgusted about these mass murders, but at the same time you start getting more antisemitic discourse about Jews in Britain – that Jews were running the black market, avoiding military service and spreading panic.

“Even before the mass murder began, during the 1930s, there was a significant body of opinion which felt Britain should not be admitting refugees.”

after newsletter promotion

Winstone said UK immigration laws in the 1930s were highly restrictive, in part because of antisemitism earlier in the 20th century. But after the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938, Britain relaxed restrictions to some extent, allowing Jewish children to come from Europe without visas. The Manchester Guardian reported how Jewish communities and Quakers in the city set up organisations to support refugees.

British women – from MP Eleanor Rathbone, to grassroots fundraisers and those who found themselves interned alongside Jews in France – were at the forefront of humanitarian efforts, Winstone said.

A 2021 survey by Claims Conference found 21% of the British public knew the UK government was aware of the mass murder of Jews as early as 1941.

UK Holocaust Memorial Foundation is co-chaired by the broadcaster and former Labour politician Ed Balls and the Tory peer Eric Pickles, who said the exhibition would give an early insight into the work being developed for the forthcoming memorial.

The exhibition will be at the Northern Ireland assembly from 30 October until 13 November; the Scottish parliament from 7 to 10 December; before travelling to Cardiff from 16 January to 4 February 2027, coinciding with Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January. It is also expected to visit Manchester, with a date and venue yet to be confirmed.

The UK Holocaust Memorial and Learning Centre, which would be at Victoria Tower Gardens, Westminster, does not have a confirmed opening date yet, as a planning application is being redetermined by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The Holocaust Memorial Act 2026 received royal assent this year, granting legal clearance and government funding for the project.

What’s funny, what’s offensive? And are Mitchell and Webb comedy villains now?

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 14:00:06 GMT

The deletion of 11 old sketches from BBC’s iPlayer has angered culture warriors and raises questions about how society has changed

“Are we the baddies?”, asked the comedy double act Mitchell and Webb in their most famous sketch, in which two uniformed SS officers look one another up and down and arrive at that inescapable conclusion. And lo, it turns out they are, if this week’s news about the supposed offensiveness of the duo’s back catalogue is to be believed.

Their newfound unpalatability made headlines last Monday, when 11 of the pair’s sketches were pulled from the rerelease of That Mitchell and Webb Look on iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary – a move that led to loud condemnation from the keyboard cavalry in Britain’s never-ending, and never much fun, culture war.

Was the BBC right to expunge the skits? There’s an argument that in this instance, a warning or disclaimer might have been sufficient. The sketches in question variously involve jokes about Jimmy Savile, Robert Webb playing a rude Gandhi (seemingly wearing skin-darkening makeup) and two further scenes in which the comedians wear blackface. In neither sketch are they doing so to depict people of colour, but instead to depict white people (in one scene, re-enactors of historic battles having a go at an African skirmish) who themselves wear blackface. In both, they are alert to their own indelicacy: “Are you sure,” asks Webb repeatedly throughout one, “that this isn’t racist?”

Some have argued that sketches such as these – satires on chauvinism, not examples of it – should therefore be spared the editor’s scissors. But that’s missing the point, which is that blackface (and indeed the N-word, which caused the standup comic Alfie Brown so much trouble recently when he used it in his own anti-racist routine) is considered beyond the pale, irreducibly hurtful to a portion of the BBC’s audience, regardless of context.

Is it right that it is so considered? There’s no question these terms and behaviours are associated with very real harms. Perhaps the corporation focus-grouped that question – or perhaps it is pre-empting criticism, erring on the side of caution and care. Is it so outrageous that they should do so? The BBC is, as the comedy producer Jimmy Mulville stated this week in the most sensible comment yet made on the controversy, “in an impossible position”.

For my part, I can’t get too exercised by the removal of a handful of sketches – one of them, which jokes about the recently deceased Bill Oddie, for reasons of common decency, and others on the same basis that 70s sitcom It Ain’t Half Hot Mum has long been withheld, without great controversy, from our screens. It feels important, mind you, that the episodes in question should be prominently marked as abridged, much as those Roald Dahl books adjusted for modern sensitivities were marketed as “updated texts”, in a move even more contested than this one. (Interestingly, David Mitchell responded very cynically to Dahl’s “updating”.)

That act of bowdlerism felt more extreme because it affected (some would say diluted) the entire text, leaving readers uncertain what was Dahl and what was edited Dahl. (On the other hand, unlike in the case of Mitchell and Webb, the unexpurgated versions remained freely available.) In sketch comedy, by contrast, individual sketches can be removed wholesale, leaving the others unmolested. And yet in both cases, there’s a risk the public will be misled into thinking the past was just like the present, and a chance missed to consider that values – and the boundaries of the acceptable – are perpetually shifting and up for grabs.

Do measures such as these give comedians the collywobbles? Mitchell and Webb themselves have apparently sanctioned the sketches’ withdrawal. In 2017, Matt Lucas disavowed his sketch series Little Britain (“I wouldn’t make that show now. It would upset people”) and didn’t sound as if he were doing so just to stay employable; three years later, the show was removed from iPlayer and Netflix for its egregious use of blackface. In my experience, comics don’t tend to consider anything sacrosanct, least of all old episodes of comedy shows. No one is more aware than a comedian of the shifting of social attitudes over time.

But equally, comics are – or should be – constitutionally averse to piety. None would wish to see abridgements to vintage comedy become commonplace, nor for what is sayable to be any more strictly policed. All would defend the space for comedy to be uncomfortable, to tease at cultural faultlines, probing what we think and feel about ourselves, one another and the world.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

I doubt many comics will expend outrage on this isolated instance of pruning that renders a well-loved series palatable on a mainstream, licence fee-funded platform in 2026. What they will, and what we should, care more about is that the BBC invests in new comedy. And empower it to explore and address the issues that define and discomfit our times as irreverently as Mitchell and Webb did theirs.

Brian Logan is the Guardian’s comedy critic, and the artistic director of A Play, a Pie and a Pint

Monty Don says he may have to let go of his gardeners after leaving BBC

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 13:06:15 GMT

Presenter reveals corporation has been paying part of their salaries to keep his Herefordshire garden camera-ready

For 15 years, viewers have looked in amazement at Monty Don’s beautiful Herefordshire garden, known as Longmeadow, as he hosted the show Gardeners’ World from his own back yard.

But now the BBC presenter, who announced earlier this month that he was leaving the show, has said he may have to let go of the gardeners who have kept the space beautiful and broadcast-ready.

Speaking for the first time since announcing his departure, Don revealed that the BBC had paid part of the salaries of two full-time gardeners to tend to Longmeadow ever since he began hosting the show from his garden in 2011.

“I have had two full-time gardeners, and have had them since I have been on Gardeners’ World, and from day one it’s been in my BBC contract that I have to have two full-time gardeners,” the 71-year-old said during an event at the RHS Malvern autumn flower show.

Answering questions from the audience during a session hosted at Three Counties Showground, he said this was because the garden had to look camera-ready at all times. “If I’m off filming in the Rhine or India or somewhere like that, somebody has got to be getting it ready,” he said.

“The BBC pays a contribution towards their wages. Not enough, but they do pay something, which is great. Obviously, that contribution is going to go.”

His current team of two gardeners, a propagation expert and a landscaper have been with him for 10 years, he said. “They are a great team and we all work together really well. I will have to think of ways – I can’t afford it unless we earn money from it, so I am going to think of ways of earning something from the garden, but I can’t do that until the middle of next year at the earliest.”

The presenter has said he would not open the garden to the public as it was a private space, and organising parking in the area would be too difficult.

Don and his wife, Sarah, created the 2-acre garden in the village of Ivington in 1991, at which time it was a neglected field with one hazel tree.

It is now split into four gardens: the cottage garden which is filled with shrub roses, the jewel garden with its bright, multicoloured flowers, the Islamic-inspired paradise garden, and the vegetable garden, which provides produce almost year-round.

Don said he was leaving the show, which he has hosted along with his dogs, after 23 years because it was “the right time for a change”. He will continue working with the BBC on other programmes, as well as pursuing his own projects, such as writing books.

The final series hosted by Don will continue to be broadcast from Longmeadow until later this year. It is understood he will shortly begin filming a travel programme for the BBC, named Island Gardens.

Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 12:00:04 GMT

President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office

With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing.

“All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language.

“Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.”

Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language.

Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second.

He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally.

A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn.

Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025, when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.)

Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April.

“President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.”

Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies.

In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”.

Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”.

A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard.

These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through.

Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem.

“The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians.

“Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.”

In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics.

Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”.

Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.”

Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity.

Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January.

Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.”

While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care.

“The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.”

Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language.

“There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them.

“It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.”

Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”.

The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses.

“I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.”

But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.”

In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics.

“We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands.

“Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”

Labour is nostalgic for two-party politics. That cosy, simple time is over – let it go

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:57:37 GMT

Our fragmented political model will endure for the foreseeable future – and Reform will benefit from it until Burnham learns that cooperation is key

As I wrote last week, whatever its current troubles, Reform UK has hardly disappeared. Meanwhile, those black-clad quasi-paramilitaries may well be another augury of a frightening immediate future. One more English settlement – the town of Barnham, in Norfolk – is seemingly poised to stage a pretend independence referendum in protest at plans to locally accommodate asylum seekers. Oh, and our new Labour prime minister has just held cordial talks with a US president who has not only brought a modern de facto fascism to his homeland, but wants to export it to Europe.

But hold all those cheerful thoughts for a moment, and let us have a look at the Labour party as it gathers in Liverpool. The slogan plastered all over its conference is “Hope Again” – which, unlike last year’s dreadful “Renew Britain”, suggests that a few people at the top might have belatedly learned the basics of pithy political storytelling.

The influence of the two slogans that are accepted modern classics – “Take back control” and “Make America Great Again” – is obvious. In Labour’s case, “again” not only implies how badly Starmer’s reign went, but looks back to a better past and implies that something comparable is eminently possible. You might take it as a reference to the best aspects of the New Labour period, Harold Wilson in his pomp or the magical glories of the Attlee years.

The slogan also echoes some of the pronouncements made by Andy Burnham when he became leader, about the positive response of the voters of Makerfield to “the promised return of the Labour they once knew”. And it has to be said: those words and the conference tagline tap into his party’s ingrained nostalgia, and the idea that with enough effort, Labour might return to winning a commanding share of the vote, as it did back in the days when footballers chain-smoked and bowler hats were still a common sight (in 1951, although it lost to the Tories, Labour won a record 48.8%, and Wilson came very close to the same figure in 1966).

Numbers aside, Labour still largely believes that by rights it should monopolise the progressive half of politics. The Tories have the same idea about the right of the spectrum, which has recently fed into a seductive notion held by both “main” parties and many pundits: that with Zack Polanski’s PR slip-ups and the trouble that has engulfed Nigel Farage, we may be witnessing the rebirth of comfy, cosy, simple two-party politics.

What utter rot that is. The UK’s passage into a multiparty system is deeply rooted in a society and economy whose complexity can no longer be smothered by our ludicrous voting system. Look at what has happened where the electoral machinery is different. Labour recently lost control of Wales to Plaid Cymru, attracting a mere 11% of the vote. The SNP’s dominance in Scotland may have weakened, but it is more than intact. Meanwhile, even with first past the post still creakingly in place, whole swathes of what used to be considered middle England – particularly in the home counties – have switched from the Tories to the Lib Dems.

At the time of writing, the latest YouGov poll puts Labour on 23% (if that’s accurate, the “Burnham bounce” looks more like a modest bunny-hop), the Tories level with Reform at 21%, and the Greens and Lib Dems on 14% and 12% respectively. The same polling group has also done a multi-level regression and post-stratification – or MRP – that offers a picture of the House of Commons that would be elected if a contest were held today. It forecasts a hung parliament, with Labour dropping to 241 seats, and facing the inevitability of cross-party cooperation. Here, clearly, is further evidence of a fragmented model of politics that will endure for the foreseeable future. And in Liverpool, mostly at fringe meetings, it will be talked about, but not nearly enough.

Before he became leader, Burnham seemed to be the only senior Labour politician positively responding to these shifts. He has repeatedly backed proportional representation (which he insists he still supports), and said that embracing it would pave the way “for agreement with other parties on wider reforms”. With that, he said, would come “a more honest and collaborative way of doing politics”, a phrase that chimes with his promises of a lot less “finger-pointing” and “point-scoring”. Aside from his talks with the Tories and Lib Dems about social care, what this might look like is unclear; all we know is that Burnham’s drive for English devolution will definitely mean ceding power to other parties, and probably substantially change politics at a national level.

And so to the really important bit. Eleven days after the start of Labour conference comes the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Publicly at least, Labour seems to be running a content-lite campaign, though it has attacked the Greens’ alleged fiscal impossibilism and sent members a communique framing the contest as a chance to “get our revenge” for Green triumphs in May’s local elections. The Green leader and candidate, Polanski, is aggressively accusing Labour of a miserable lack of solidarity with Palestine, while an ally also charged Burnham’s party with choosing its contender – the former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali – on the basis of opportunistic “identity politics”. It all looks like politics as usual – and as the far right gains more and more traction here and abroad, what is happening in this corner of London should make us feel very nervous about the next UK general election.

The left-leaning cross-party pressure group Compass is about to convene the first meeting of a “council for the progressive majority”, which will bring together leading figures from each of the UK’s progressive parties – including Plaid and the SNP – to firm up how they might collectively defeat Reform. To quote from a recent Compass statement: “There is a progressive majority in this country … yet our outdated political system divides us … splitting the vote and clearing a path for extremist voices to win with little public backing.” This is the kind of urgent warning that will become very vivid in the buildup to the next election, amid campaigning – whatever the efforts of Burnham’s new National Centre For Information Defence – festooned with lies, deepfakes and worse.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

A lot of us remain unsure of the exact solutions to a split left taking on a confident, tech-savvy and possibly united right. Electoral pacts tend to look like stitch-ups; parties agreeing to limit their campaigning in certain marginal seats can work much better. Whatever, millions of us – including, it seems, the new PM – increasingly feel that a cultural change is overdue, not least to stop the most basic civilisational values buckling before our eyes.

Talking of which, it’s grimly ironic that the man still benefiting most from the fractured politics of the 21st century is Farage, a self-styled throwback permanently surrounded by a cloud of Rothmans smoke. Here, then, is a question for everyone gathered by the old Liverpudlian docks: how can he be comprehensively beaten, possibly when he may end up healing divisions on the right by striking a deal (pre- or post-election) with the Tories, and even Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain? By ludicrously insisting that people must vote Labour whatever their political circumstances? Or somehow cooperating with other parties to ensure his defeat? Those parties also need to change, of course. But the age of monopolistic Labour hegemony is over. Let it go. We need to fight today’s most important battles together, so the prospect of hope might actually start to feel real. Again.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Tony Blair would like Andy Burnham to take his advice on rejoining the EU. Should he?

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:05:08 GMT

The former PM has been consulted by many who came after him – but Burnham might want to shake his New Labour past once and for all

Tony Blair can, apparently, sound slightly wistful when he describes how he once had a cloak-and-dagger meeting with Andy Burnham, who wanted to talk to him about standing for the party leadership. Before anyone gets too excited, however, this wasn’t in the past few months, during which Burnham succeeded in landing the job. The story dates back to 2010. That was when he was a callow member of Gordon Brown’s cabinet and understandably wary of his boss discovering not only his ambition to take over if Labour lost the looming general election, but also from whom he wanted advice.

Much has changed since then, not least Burnham himself. His journey out of Westminster and back again – which in his telling has become an almost spiritual pilgrimage of personal redemption – enabled him to shed the New Labour baggage that proved so cumbersome during his previous, and unsuccessful, runs for the leadership. In common with Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer – all of whom tried with varying degrees of success to distance themselves from Blair – Labour’s latest leader now also wants to keep Blair at arm’s length, and certainly far away from his party conference in Liverpool this week.

Their secret meeting long ago nonetheless underlines how often, since he left Downing Street in 2007, Blair has had a residual and sometimes illicit allure for those aspiring to fill his shoes. Part of that is because – with the exception of Starmer – those who came after him failed to win a single general election, let alone three. But it is also that this leader from the past still has a possibly unmatched ability to raise our sights, away from whatever the media tells us is most urgent, towards the colossal compound crisis now casting its shadow across the world and over Britain’s future.

Blair does not, of course, always make it easy to agree with him. There was an awful lot to dislike about his 5,700 word essay earlier this year, which said Britain had no power to stop either the AI revolution or Donald Trump. It led some to question once more the motives of a former PM whose proximity both to big tech firms and successive US presidents has so tainted his reputation. Burnham swiftly responded to the essay by saying Blair just didn’t get “what’s going on” with the impact of “40 years of neoliberalism” on working-class communities. He later promised that the interests of voters in Makerfield, where he was standing in a byelection, would be his test of what made good policy.

It was, however, a bit disingenuous for him to claim that Blair agreed “our relentless focus now should be on domestic issues, and fixing our own underlying problems, rather than on re-running divisive arguments about rejoining the European Union”. Indeed, the bulk of the former PM’s essay was about the inability of this country’s politics to navigate an international landscape being churned at terrifying speed by forces far beyond Britain’s control.

Conflicts in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have since put further pressure on government borrowing costs and household fuel bills. It is increasingly difficult to see how the inward-looking vision Burnham has painted so far, largely consisting of new powers for mayors and more regulation of privatised utilities, will deliver his promised “good growth in every postcode” any time soon. This week, his determinedly domestic focus relented and he acknowledged the government must also offer “resilience” in the face of global storms, before delivering a speech to the United Nations in New York on Tuesday night. The speech veered wildly from No 10 North in Manchester to Ukraine, Israel, Iran and China, briefly taking in the climate crisis, before setting out the need to create international safety standards on frontier AI and protect democracy from all kinds of Russian threats, including disinformation on social media.

It didn’t go nearly far enough for Blair. On Thursday, his policy institute published a paper calling for Britain to set a course for re-entry into a “reformed European Union” over the next decade. Rather than re-run old arguments about Brexit, he would prefer to start a new one, saying the need for the UK and the EU to build capability in defence and capacity on AI is more pressing than it ever was in the past.

Although Blair can point to polls showing a majority of the public and an even bigger slice of Labour voters would support rejoining, there is plenty of evidence to suggest relations with Europe have gone backwards under Burnham’s government. The prospect of Britain drifting alone on the tide of history felt closer to becoming reality last week when the annual state of the union speech from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, made repeated references to Canada, a country about 3,500 miles away to which she offered an associate EU membership, while barely mentioning the UK at all.

An EU-UK summit, originally scheduled to have taken place under Starmer’s premiership in May, was delayed until July and then to a yet-to-be confirmed date at the end of the year. What had been talked up as a “done deal” for a youth mobility scheme – by which young people from the EU and the UK could live, work and study in each other’s countries – risks being unstitched by new objections from some of Burnham’s newly appointed minsters that it fails his “Makerfield test”. There are similar claims that the EU’s “made in Europe” policy on supply chains will disadvantage British industry and be a further obstacle to an agreement, while progress that began in February to resolve the issue is said to have stalled.

There are a lot of mixed messages on all this just now. Recent comments that it must be possible to get a deal agreed with Europe in “an amicable way that will add percentage points to our growth” perhaps made him sound too much like a regional mayor who had missed the past decade of Brexit mayhem in Westminster. But others believe Burnham is considering a big leap beyond the “red line” election pledges that prevented Starmer from rejoining a customs union, the single market or allowing freedom of movement. Over recent days some of those around him have dangled out questions about how, “purely hypothetically”, a case for re-entry could be included in his speech to conference this Tuesday, the 10-year plan later this year or, as Burnham himself notably failed to rule out this week, Labour’s manifesto at the next election (whenever that might be).

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Either way, the freshly minted new PM will not want to be seen taking inspiration from a sometimes toxic old one. There has been no contact between them since Burnham entered Downing Street and a meeting – clandestine or otherwise – is not scheduled. That seems a shame because, on the issue of Europe at least, Blair really isn’t the worst person from whom Burnham could take advice.

Tom Baldwin is a former assistant editor of the Times and a former senior adviser to the Labour party. He is the author of Keir Starmer: The Biography

Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:03:59 GMT

Surging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bind

As Labour heads to Liverpool this week, Andy Burnham has promised to deliver “stability” in the public finances; but the economic backdrop is anything but stable.

The longer the US-Israeli war on Iran persists, the more likely it is that UK consumers will have to swallow higher mortgage rates and energy bills – just as the government is wrestling with its own surging borrowing costs.

We are only a few weeks into the three-month period tracking energy price moves that the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will use as a basis to set the energy price cap in January – but it’s been a pretty bleak period so far, with the cost of a barrel of crude above $100 for much of that time.

Based on the pricing in energy futures markets, the Bank of England reckons Ofgem could increase the energy price cap, which sets the maximum energy rates paid by homes on standard tariffs, by an eye-watering 24% in January.

At the same time, the Bank’s policymakers – from the governor, Andrew Bailey, down – have repeatedly signalled that while they are reassured high energy prices have not yet fed through into wider inflation, they can’t hold off from raising rates for much longer.

“We’ve made it quite clear … that it’s going to be harder to maintain that stance, the longer we have high energy prices,” Andrew Bailey said on Friday.

Or as his deputy, Sarah Breeden, who like Bailey did not vote to raise rates in September, put it: “The more sparks we’re throwing in the tinderbox, the more likely we might ​have to turn the hose on it.”

Donald Trump made clear over the weekend that he has no intention of staunching the flames himself, by bringing the conflict to a close.

“I’m rejecting their deal,” he told reporters, after Iran made a fresh proposal. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly … we’re winning tremendously.”

With UK inflation already above 3% and likely to rise further, markets are expecting the Bank to raise rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.

Such a situation almost certainly won’t happen – the economy would probably be clobbered into submission long before they got there, and inflation with it. But Bailey and his colleagues are widely expected to make a start in November, the week after John Healey’s first budget.

Policymakers will also have to reckon with the impact on prices of what is expected to be the most powerful El Niño weather system in 1,000 years, which as well as being devastating to human life, is likely to drive up the cost of important foodstuffs.

Burnham has made offering the public a “breathing space” from higher costs a hallmark of his early weeks in power, with sensible but modest policies, such as the £2 bus fare cap. A new iteration of the Tories’ help-to-buy scheme for first-time homebuyers will follow at the budget, he announced this weekend.

But while these offerings show a government keen to help, they risk being overshadowed by the wider picture. With the threat of a surge in energy bills looming, the government is keen to avoid announcing a large new support package, conscious of the cumulative cost of Labour’s interventions over the last year.

“I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” Burnham said this weekend. These include the £2.3bn Rachel Reeves spent on lowering energy bills – including by shifting some green levies on to general taxation – and his own VAT cut on domestic electricity, which the Treasury has yet to explain how it will fund.

Yet if, as Trump has hinted, the conflict continues until after the midterm elections in early November, global oil and gas prices could remain high for many more weeks – locking in a sharp rise in bills for UK consumers in the new year.

after newsletter promotion

Economists are urging Healey to be bold on energy in the budget, rather than wait and hope. Experts at the research and innovation foundation Nesta are calling for a gas price stabiliser, for example, that would cushion the blow of higher prices now, at the Treasury’s expense – but bring in additional revenue as market prices dropped in future.

Any policy that cuts utility bills has the added bonus of bearing down on inflation, helping ease the pressure on the Bank to act.

Adding to Labour’s woes, though, the government’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as the global bond selloff has gathered pace.

It has been yet another harsh reminder of how exposed the government’s fiscal position is to the vagaries of global markets, with a knock-on effect for the budget forecasts.

There are growing warnings, too, about the risks of market instability caused by the interaction of febrile bond markets and the AI mega-bubble.

Labour was already in a tricky fiscal bind, given demands for higher defence spending – not least from Healey himself, who now has the job of finding the resources.

The difficult decisions about how to do so – let alone fund Burnham’s wider priorities – look likely to be delayed until a spending review some time in 2027. It is very hard to see how that won’t necessitate a fresh round of tax rises.

The plan had been for a relatively modest budget, focusing on plans for devolution, and filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced in the summer.

This caution looked out of step with Burnham’s promise of a radical political reset and may be untenable if energy bills are going to soar. He and Healey face a tough autumn.

The ‘elixir of long life’: how the elusive Chartreuse quietly became the trendiest drink around

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:00:04 GMT

With its garish ‘grellow’ colour, mythological origins, secret recipe and limited supplies, the herbal liqueur made by French monks is now the coolest thing to order at the bar

It’s just after 9pm in drizzly Belleville, Paris. Too late for cocktails, too early for bedtime, but up the steep hill that straddles the 19th and 20th arrondissements, digestif hour is in sight.

In the past few years, more and more Parisians have been reaching for a glass of Chartreuse, an intensely green/yellow herbal liqueur with a folkloric backstory involving Carthusian monks, cholera and a recipe of omertà-like secrecy.

There are several types, of varying strengths, colours and prices, but none are that easy to find. At La Commune, a cultish leftwing hangout in Belleville, where tequila shots cost less than €4, they finished the Chartreuse the night before. A few doors down at Les Triplettes de Belleville, I spot a third-full bottle of the cheaper yellow stuff sandwiched between the gins. Hugo Césard, the 19-year-old bartender, pours me a €7 shot, my third of the night. On first taste, it behaves like ouzo: sweet, fennelly, cloyingly thick. Then you hit the more complex notes, which are closer to an Alpine meadow. This one is a navy-strength 40% ABV, while the green version is about 55%. In theAlps, you’re more likely to drink it in hot chocolate. To down it at room temperature is sacrilege, unless “you want to get very drunk”, says Césard. For me, alas, that ship has already sailed.

Round the corner at Combat, an edgy-cool bar run by women and frequented by thoughtful students and dressed-up boomers, they mostly serve it cold in a crystal-cut sipping glass or a cocktail called The Last Word, mixed with gin, lime and a maraschino cherry. I try both. Combat bartender Marie-Paule Corby, 30, loves its “complicated flavour”, though outside, a customer called Nour (also 30) is not a fan. “I only ever drank it in the Alps. Too sweet for me,” she says, and sticks out her tongue in disgust.

You’ll find Chartreuse in most ambitiously stocked bars, but interest among younger drinkers shot up mostly after the pandemic, says Theo, who works in La Cave Pigalle, a small chic wine shop in Pigalle in the 9th arrondissement. The same thing happened in the US, where it became a “sleeper” ingredient during the giddy era of the craft cocktail movement of the early 00s. Then came lockdown, and a taste for the weirder, top-shelf stuff grew further still, particularly here.

At the award-winning, taxidermy-filled bar Satan’s Whiskers in east London, it appears in various cocktails. The Pig on the Beach on Dorset’s Jurassic coast sells five different types, one of which – the Eau de Vie from 1941 – costs £50 a measure. It’s always been pricey, though disaster hit in 2021 when the Carthusian monks suddenly announced plans to cap production in order to “protect their monastic life and devote their time to solitude and prayer”. In a letter in 2021, they said: “Making millions of cases does not make sense in today’s environmental context and will have a negative impact on the planet in the very short term”, though rumour has it the decree came from the Vatican, which pointedly reminded the monks “that they were monks, not businessmen”. Today, according to a spokesperson for Chartreuse, the brand is shifting its focus back toward herbalism.

Back in Paris, at the beloved bottle shop La Cave de Belleville, Chartreuse is scarce. “We have an allocation – 24 bottles of green and 24 bottles of yellow, but that’s for a year”, says Remy Pousse-Vaillant, 46, a knowledgable liquor expert with a Kandinsky tattoo. There are currently five on the shelf, but that’s it until the next order. Under French consumer law, any item displayed with a visible price is considered sellable, which is partly why some caves stash the good stuff in the basement. The brand won’t divulge the numbers, only to say that they keep half and export half to the US, Japan, Australia, and “countries surrounding the Alpine arc”. They only make what they need to sustain the order, though Pousse-Vaillant thinks it’s not much over 1m bottles worldwide. Like most wine shop staff, he will neither confirm nor deny if he’s got Chartreuse in the basement.

Still, if we’ve learned anything from Birkin economics, it’s that few things sharpen our appetite like the prospect of scarcity. Is that why Chartreuse is back on the map? “Yes, partly,” he says. The stuff that creeps on to cocktail menus – espresso martinis, negronis, cosmos – “used to come from TV shows like Mad Men or Sex and the City”. Now it’s aggressive advertising campaigns meticulously engineered by savvy publicists. Take Campari, which turned Aperol into a global aesthetic, and M&S’s Clemencello, which, according to the supermarket, will be the most in-demand drink this Christmas, despite the fact that most of us have never heard of it. Chartreuse has a much lower profile. I only know about it because Jay Gatsby kept it in his secret cocktail cabinet – and from Bruce Springsteen’s memoir, in which he reveals he got hooked on the stuff when he first started drinking. Tom Waits is also a fan.

The story of Chartreuse began in earnest in 1605 when the Carthusian monks – herbalists, scholars and expert alcohol distillers – were entrusted with the recipe by Duke François Annibal d’Estrées. His manuscript outlined a 130-ingredient “elixir of long life”, which contained plants, barks, spices and roots and took the monks over a century to decipher. Finally they landed on what they call the “élixir végétal”, which is the base of today’s Chartreuse. The monks continued to develop the elixir while also trying to create a liqueur that was easier to drink. The first version was created in 1838 and was white, but variations in green and yellow followed in 1840, the green being more herbal in taste and the yellow sweeter. The green “health elixir” version of the recipe was even given to cholera patients – while it clearly wouldn’t have treated the disease, it may have provided some pain relief.

Today, just three people in the world know the recipe, and they’re all monks. It’s thought that the original two monks only shared the recipe with the third because one of the two was considering retiring. They are helped in the distillery by five lay people, who are also anonymous.

It’s a fine story and, as social media weasels its way into everything we eat or drink, perhaps it was only a matter of time before it landed on Chartreuse. The majestic labels, the photogenic shade of “grellow”, the mythological origins – and now the sheer dearth of the stuff. It all feels perfectly suited to the trend-fatigued in 2026, says Pousse-Vaillant. “In this era of AI, of Meta and of constantly [being online] I think people want something real, something authentic, something unchanged.” And the brand agrees. “As the monks say: ‘the cross stands firm while the world turns,’” a Chartreuse spokesperson said. “It is a good motto because the world is difficult right now. So what else can we do?”

Dining across the divide: ‘Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa’

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:00:03 GMT

How did a solicitor who is the leader of the English Democrats and a Norwegian national fare on Brexit, surveillance and Ukraine?

Occupation Solicitor

Voting record As leader of the English Democrats – an anti-immigration party that wants an English parliament – Robin votes for himself. Never successfully

Amuse bouche Every year Robin and his wife do a cycle tour of the Netherlands. “There are separate cyclist lanes everywhere and it’s not hilly”

Occupation Software engineer and entrepreneur

Voting record He has lived in the UK since 2010 but, as a Norwegian national, hasn’t been able to vote here. He votes Labour in Norway

Amuse bouche Runs an art gallery that will shortly unveil a controversial work featuring a Norwegian royal

Robin I thought I’d be put with a full-on social justice warrior, but he wasn’t like that. I told him my father was in the army, I was born in Malaya, then sent off to boarding school when I was eight.

Aslak He was dressed nicely, shirt and blazer. Almost a stereotypically British chap. We talked a bit about the Vikings because everyone loves to talk about the Vikings when they meet a Scandinavian. He didn’t seem that interested in me or my opinions.

Robin I had a prawn starter, he had calamari, we shared a bottle of rioja. Apparently, they do karaoke there – not on this occasion, thankfully.

Aslak If there had been karaoke, I would have done Seven Nation Army. I’ve sung in several bands. For main we both had lamb chops, so that’s one thing we agreed on …

Robin We shouldn’t be involved in Ukraine. We need to focus on our own interests and not get involved in foreign adventures.

Aslak Whether we like it or not, we live in a globalised world, with international trade, migration, alliances. You can’t isolate yourself. If there’s a war somewhere in Europe, it affects everybody. My worry is if Russia takes Ukraine, or a part of it, they won’t stop. Then there’ll be much more to pay – in money and lives – than from giving some support now.

Robin When the Soviet Union was dissolved there were promises that Nato wouldn’t expand to the east, promises that have been completely ignored. Most of Ukraine has been part of Russia since Catherine the Great. So from a historical point of view, you can see Putin’s argument.

Aslak Even if that was true, it isn’t today. A lot has happened in the meantime. Robin was happy for us to arm Ukraine, provided we charge for it. But he also said we should be willing to arm Russia at the same time, like a win-win situation. That sounds more like a business model than foreign policy.

Robin We agreed people should be able to talk about things rationally. Once you think of another human being as an enemy, you’re not far off the next stage, which is that violence against them is acceptable.

Aslak We agreed a bit on surveillance. I’m against the government collecting information on citizens without any suspicions. It creates a scary power balance and causes people to self-censor, which is bad for democracy.

Robin The English Democrats campaigned for Brexit, and were obviously very pleased with the result. For a long time we have thought the British state, and its commitment to internationalist entities such as the EU, was against our interests. It hasn’t been a disaster economically; trade has continued to grow.

Aslak The biggest problem has been alienating your biggest trading partners. And students aren’t coming to Britain to study any more because they don’t know if they can stay. And it’s now no longer people from Europe coming, but from all over the world. I don’t see how this aligns with what a lot of Brexiters wanted.

Robin Aslak is a proper lefty, but he’s a proper lefty of the type I used to encounter years ago: rational about it, whereas one of the things we get with the culture wars is wild irrationality. We both said we’d enjoyed it.

Aslak We disagreed about most things, but it was friendly and respectful. Every rightwing person should have a woke friend and vice versa. Not that I’m woke … Well, maybe a bit.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

Aslak and Robin ate at Zebrano in Brentwood, Essex.
