I spent a full hour watching Trump TV. It’s a digital pathway to hell

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:00:03 GMT

The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull

Are you currently at an airport? Strapped to a hospital bed, with various tubes protruding from your body? Maybe you’re on a treadmill or visiting an elder care facility? Chained to a radiator in the basement from the Saw movies?

If you said yes to any of these questions, you might be watching cable news while reading this column. Or maybe you’re one of the hundreds of people currently watching Donald Trump’s answer to cable news, Trump TV – a YouTube streaming channel that airs nothing but White House-sanctioned content 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

Kudos to you for multitasking, and thank you for the click. I know Jacob Soboroff is hard to look away from, but at least finish this.

I don’t typically watch cable news. Or broadcast news. I feel like the best way to consume vital information is through the glorious written word, full of context and detail, rather than various “experts” yelling at each other about which one is the harbinger of the antichrist. Instead, I can yell all I want at a newspaper or an internet article and no one can tell me not to. Except the people in the dentist waiting room with me.

Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching. I gave myself the challenge of watching this neverending digital pathway to hell for one single hour, hoping I could capture whatever joy is being derived from this American horror story.

When I first logged onto the stream, I was “treated” to a 11 March 2016 speech Donald Trump gave in Hebron, Kentucky – which Trump on more than one occasion pronounced “Keentucky”, presumably to mimic local speech patterns. That Donald Trump is just a good ol’ country boy, after all.

I came in right smack-dab in the middle of the remarks, which very clearly were not prepared. As someone hyper-allergic to cable news, I don’t often witness the president’s speeches in full. I immediately felt as though I were succumbing to a form of intense psychosis, where reality had begun to melt before my eyes, like an ice cream cone that’s sat out in the sun too long.

Trump was describing the stairs at the event, stairs he had to walk up and down. Stairs that he traversed despite his own natural sense of self-preservation. “I might slip, it’s soaking wet,” he said of the stairs. “They’re steel stairs. Four sets of stairs.” I immediately begin to imagine him counting the stairs. Slowly.

From there, he played his greatest hits and mocked Joe Biden for falling down. But the big swerve was a backhanded compliment to Barack Obama for not falling down. “The only thing is how he bobbed down. He bobbed. I couldn’t believe that he made it without a major, noticeable fall.” The shock on his face that a healthy adult man would not trip on his descent from an airplane certainly made me wonder. You can tell this man has thought a lot about the best ways to not fall down stairs. Eventually, Dr Oz showed up, and I needed to mute my computer. My Uber Eats order had just arrived, and I didn’t want my neighbors getting the wrong idea when I opened the front door.

We got a brief respite from Trump up next, with a re-airing of Melania’s ad … excuse me, speech about how great artificial intelligence is, from 16 January. “The most powerful skill is knowing what to ask,” she declares. I realized the thing I should be asking right then was: “Why am I watching this?”

I hung in a little longer for one more event: the National Prayer Breakfast from 6 February. Paula White-Cain, senior adviser to the White House Faith Office, opened the proceedings by saying: “No president in modern history or perhaps all of history has done more to elevate and protect religious liberty” than Donald Trump has. Except maybe George Washington, who presided over the ratification of the first amendment to the US constitution. The first amendment enshrined freedom of religion into the country’s laws. Also, awkwardly, freedom of speech and freedom of the press. You know, the press Donald Trump kicked out of the White House.

Trump TV seems like the next escalation of the president’s obsession with and animosity toward cable news. I remain flabbergasted that someone could care about anything on television that much.

At last census count, 342 million people live in the United States. Of that population, between 2 and 3 million watch cable news in a given day. The vast majority of those people watch Fox News. And the majority of that majority is over the age of 54.

When I say “no one watches cable news,” I am only being mildly hyperbolic. To coin a term, I’m being “semibolic”. Just a “hint of bolic”.

Yes, there are people who can’t seem to just turn their TV off out there, but MSNOW, CNN, and Fox News aren’t capturing the same level of enthusiasm as the latest episode of HBO’s Lanterns or your local bird-watching club. That cable news retains any significance in our daily discourse is a testament to how fiercely committed our nation’s leaders are to using it as a battlefield for their ideological warfare. And as a retirement community for ex-politicians.

When Trump tried to ban CNN, MS Now and the website Politico for allegations of unfair, dishonest coverage of his administration, journalists had a reasonable fear for the state of freedom of the press in this country. Covering the goings-on at the White House is not, as Trump says, a “privilege”. It is a solemn duty. One that defines what’s left of our democracy. Maybe now, I’m being fully hyperbolic, but I’m a journalist. I should declare my own bias on this topic.

Trump’s media blackout gambit backfired, as Fox News joined with their cable cousins to abandon coverage of the president’s activities, thereby ending the press pool that provided audio and video for news outlets. Without the press pool, no one can hear what Trump says during his speeches. Thankfully for those who use Trump speeches to calm their nerves before a midday nap, they can count on Trump TV to help them off to slumberland.

Back to the Trump TV live stream. He was wearing the same purple tie at the prayer breakfast that he’d worn in Kentucky. If you were not an attentive viewer of Trump TV, you might think you were watching the same speech. I realized that just about everything on this stream is from this year, that we’ll probably never see anything from, say, 2020. But I couldn’t stick around long enough to find out, and Trump TV doesn’t seem to list its programming lineup anywhere.

I left the house during the National Prayer Breakfast, just as Trump was getting going, declaring “something is wrong” with the Republican congressman Thomas Massie from … Kentucky. You know, the state Trump loves so much. I started to wonder if today’s Trump TV schedule was merely a troll directed at Massie, who lost his re-election bid in the Republican primary, to the former Navy Seal Ed Gallrein, whomm Trump endorsed. The absurdity of using a 24/7 YouTube stream to subtly mock a political rival for an audience of 800 people seems far more possible when you remember the person behind this project is Donald Trump.

I took a 30-minute walk with my dog, and when I got back to my desk, I was shocked to learn that Trump was still talking at the National Prayer Breakfast. Specifically about the size of our military budget, which I believe was a direct quote from 1 Corinthians 13:4–8. As Trump droned on (pun intended), the view counter kept going down. Even the die-hards were getting bored.

The launch of Trump TV has been a fairly obvious disaster. Unlike cable news, YouTube has real-time data to tell you how many people are watching something. Multiple media outlets took a swipe at Trump for this folly, though in his defense, most YouTube streams get pitiful concurrent viewership unless it’s MrBeast or live footage of a police chase on an LA freeway. Trump TV was obviously never meant to be anything significant. No one in charge of this stream is trying, unless you count trolling Thomas Massie as “trying”. There are no graphics or lower thirds other than a number to text for “updates” from the White House. There’s no slick editing or editorial perspective outside of the purple tie/Massie element.

But is this any worse than the ideologically minded focus of cable news – with the three major channels pointing their rhetorical ICBMs at each other all day long? Maybe Trump TV is actually the best way to consume our sitting president. Nothing else presents him in all of his repugnant glory: vain, myopic and worst of all, deeply, deeply dull. This holiday season, turn on Trump TV for your conservative family members. There’s always a chance that the uncut, unfiltered lethal dose of nonsense will break the spell for good.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Tomi Adeyemi on the film of her hit novel Children of Blood and Bone: ‘I don’t plan to watch it’

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 11:00:02 GMT

Her debut earned a record-breaking YA book deal – then came her fallout with Hollywood. The author talks about the pressures of success and why she is pictured on the cover of her new novel

There is a photograph of Tomi Adeyemi staring out from the cover of her new novel, The Siren. It is an arresting image: her face fills the frame, unsoftened by a smile, her piercing gaze fixed directly on the viewer. “It’s terrifying – like the Mona Lisa, staring at you everywhere,” she says, laughing.

Using an author portrait on the cover of a novel is highly unusual, and a decision that Adeyemi says is a statement of ownership. After 12 years spent inside the world of Children of Blood and Bone – the first book in the YA trilogy that made her a literary star and its film adaptation which has become a source of profound distress – Adeyemi wanted this book to belong unmistakably to her.

“It was an intense choice, and I think it’s because I needed people to see me in this one,” she says. “I’ve had so much success, but it was also done in a way where so many people’s interpretations were put on to who I was.”

The recent public fallout from the forthcoming film adaptation may have drawn attention, but the 33-year-old Nigerian American author had already spent much of her adult life being watched. Children of Blood and Bone, her 2018 debut, became a publishing phenomenon, netting a major seven-figure deal and debuting at No 1 on the New York Times young adult bestseller list. Its story of Zélie, a young woman fighting to restore magic to the kingdom of Orïsha, was inspired by West African mythology and offered something Adeyemi had craved as a child: a dark-skinned Black girl at the centre of an epic fantasy.

The success brought its own mythology. Adeyemi was not merely a successful young writer; she became, she feels, a symbol of what the next generation of Black YA literature might be, something she felt the weight of acutely.

“I felt pressure to be the perfect dark-skinned Black girl, to be ‘Oprah good’,” she says. “This was the biggest YA book deal in history, not just for a female or Black author. And so few of us are given a shot at all, so for the last 12 years there’s been this sense of carrying everyone.”

Readers would tell her what the book had meant to their children. “You have no idea what this did for me,” they would say. Such responses were moving, but also difficult to know what to do with.

Now, with The Siren, Adeyemi has moved from epic fantasy to something more contemporary. The standalone novel follows Emery, a Black student arriving at Dartmouth College determined to leave her troubled past behind. She is drawn into a mysterious sorority of “Sirens” and desperate to fit in. In some ways, Adeyemi says, the book is deeply personal. “[Emery] is my inner teen,” Adeyemi says. “I just want to give her a hug.”

She may have found success, but in the beginning Adeyemi’s career never looked certain. She wrote her first story at five – a Parent Trap fan fiction because, she says, she “wanted a twin and a horse”. She then spent years trying not to become a writer. Her parents had moved to Chicago from Nigeria in their early 20s, and Adeyemi grew up with the ethos of relentless achievement that often comes with first-generation immigrants – one that does not take kindly to creative pursuits. She considered medicine, investment banking and consulting, but kept coming back to writing. “Being called to be an artist is terrifying,” she says. “It’s not a logical choice.”

After studying English at Harvard, Adeyemi won a fellowship to study West African mythology and culture in Salvador, Brazil, an experience that would later inspire Children of Blood and Bone. She moved to California and began working part time at a film production company in Los Angeles, alongside writing her first novel.

That first attempt took four and a half years to write and received 63 rejections. She decided to drop the manuscript and wrote Children of Blood and Bone instead. When it was finally published in 2018 it quickly became one of the most talked about YA novels of the year. For a writer who had spent years being turned down, the speed and scale of what followed were dizzying. “I never really adjusted, because there was so much work still to do,” she says. “It’s been 12 to 14 years of intense grinding.”

And then came the film. On paper, it was the stuff of a writer’s dreams: her novel was to be transformed into a major Hollywood production, with an impossibly starry cast including Viola Davis, Idris Elba, Regina King, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg and Cynthia Erivo, premiering in January 2027. Adeyemi co-wrote the screenplay, but as the adaptation progressed, she became increasingly unhappy with the process.

In July, Adeyemi posted a five-minute video on TikTok in which she described the adaptation process as “the worst thing I have ever had to live through”. She said she had left the set “hyperventilating and sobbing”, and that afterwards she experienced severe physical pain and panic attacks. “I never want to hear about this project again,” she said.

She says she had little hesitation about speaking publicly. “I understood that if I didn’t speak up, I couldn’t move forward,” she explains. “I can’t really worry about the response, because I don’t have to live with how people respond to me – I have to live with me, every day.”

When I ask what exactly happened on set, however, Adeyemi hesitates. “I won’t go into the specifics,” she says carefully. “[But] the whole journey of the trilogy and the adaptation felt biblical … It took all of me.”

There has, though, been public discussion around the film’s casting of Amandla Stenberg, who is mixed race, and questions around colourism: Stenberg’s character is described in the book as having “dark copper skin”. Adeyemi’s July TikTok also appeared to show messages she sent to Stenberg in February 2025, around the time Stenberg responded to the colourism backlash, telling the actor: “Do not ever use my name in an interview or video again. Do not text me. Do not call me.”

When I ask Adeyemi whether she wants to clarify anything about the casting, she demurs. “With a film, the director makes every decision,” she says. “With my book I can talk about every choice down to the commas, because that’s truly in my hands. So there’s nothing for me to add, other than the clarity that these aren’t my choices.”

She is clear, though, about one thing. When I ask her if she would ever adapt another one of her books for screen she responds simply: “Never.” She has no desire to watch the upcoming film either. “I still don’t plan to watch it, but it’s not really for me to watch,” she says.

Instead, she is trying to leave the world of Children of Blood and Bone behind, and focus on what she has achieved. “I’m proud of my strength, resilience, and grace,” she says.

She is also proud of what she believes her debut set in motion: the fact that she can now walk into a bookshop and see shelves of dark-skinned protagonists across fantasy, romance, thrillers and mysteries. “The girls who grew up after me will never have that experience,” she says. As her publisher told her: “You changed things.”

The Siren by Tomi Adeyemi is published by First Ink on Thursday. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘It’s like the Scottish Upper East Side’: shame and snobbery as American students blamed for St Andrews classism

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 07:00:59 GMT

Online comments reflect class tensions at Scottish university between those from lower-income families and wealthier US undergraduates

When Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return to St Andrews University this academic year because of her experiences of classism on campus, she did not expect much of a response. But in the two weeks since she published her story on LinkedIn, it has resonated with hundreds of others.

“Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” the former comparative literature and classical studies student wrote in a lengthy post. “Arriving at a university ranked first in the UK at the time from a background like mine, I thought I was doing everything right.

“I don’t mean for this to be a sob story but an explanation. I recognise the privilege of access to higher education, however I am also brutally aware of the hidden privilege of having unobstructed access to studying for a degree. There is a deep gap between the two, and it is never addressed.”

For many responding, her comments touched on a growing tension at St Andrews, driven by the funding model of Scotland’s cash-strapped universities. Places for Scottish students, who study for free, are capped by the Scottish government and account for about 30% of students at St Andrews. Maintenance loans and bursaries cover basic costs, but those from lower-income families are still often left with less disposable income than their contemporaries – including wealthy international students who pay much higher fees.

St Andrews, ranked second in the Guardian’s university league table for 2026, accepts one of the highest percentages in the UK of privately educated students. The British aristocracy has long adored the medieval town’s cobbled streets, wind-swept beach and grand stone buildings: Prince William and the Princess of Wales met there.

But the recent influx of wealthy US students has changed the dynamic on campus, students say. Americans account for around a fifth of undergraduates at St Andrews, the highest proportion in the UK, with each paying £33,250 for this academic year, more than three times what British students pay.

“My parents were worried about me coming here. They didn’t want me to be left out,” said one Scottish fresher who is on a scholarship to study classics. “Most of the people I have met are international students. I didn’t grow up with tons of money. Maybe they can be a bit ignorant to the cost of things.”

Another said: “There’s a Pret here. You have to ask yourself why that is in such a small town.”

Aspects of fraternity and sorority culture have started to blend with the upper-class experience of British university, some students say. Regular black-tie dinners and balls are now rivalled by fashion shows and exclusive societies. A short walk from the student union bar, an interior design shop advertises luxury bed linen for students, while a popular coffee shop sells designer clothes and candles alongside speciality matchas.

“I totally see her [Jenkins’s] perspective,” said one privately educated student from Edinburgh, who was returning from hockey practice with friends. “It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans. We knew lots of people from hockey already so it’s easy to feel left out if you’re not from that environment.

“The American culture is coming in and it massively influences everything at the moment. They compete with each other. If you look at how they dress, people arrive in lectures as if they are going on a night out.”

One student referenced a well-known student newspaper article published last year about how St Andrews had turned into the Scottish Upper East Side, which said: “Our beloved Scottish town is day by day turning into a microcosm of Manhattan’s elite world; complete with intrigue, privilege, and secrets that spread like wildfire.”

Underlining the point, an American student walks past the student union loudly explaining to a friend: “Everyone is going to think you’re rich if you have a Ralph Lauren bag. But that doesn’t make you rich.”

St Andrews said it had reached out to Jenkins to better understand her experience, but she had decided not to engage for now. It said it had a robust system for reporting complaints from students, and only a handful of complaints had been made in the last five years.

“Yes, some students do arrive here in St Andrews, and at every other university, with immature, offensive and classist views. But they tend not to leave with them,” said the vice-principal Niall Scott.

“This isn’t a St Andrews issue – it’s a societal issue. Classism begins in the home or at school, not at university. Universities like St Andrews have a crucial role to play in challenging these attitudes by bringing together people from different backgrounds, cultures and perspectives, encouraging understanding, respect and inclusion.”

The debate around classism at Scottish universities is not new. In 2024, Edinburgh University offered guidance on how students should treat one another after rising claims of discrimination and classism. “Don’t be a snob!” read the advice given out to students. At St Andrews, some students said the issue of classism was not only linked to the rise in American students.

“It is generally an attitude thing. There is an idea that working-class students can’t speak about issues that are going on elsewhere in the world because they are not as well travelled,” said one science student. “At St Andrews, even for moderately wealthy people, it feels like there is an old money level above that you don’t even get to speak to.”

Rasmus, a Danish student, said he was bemused by the social dynamics at the university.

“It took two weeks for me to meet a Scottish person. They are surrounded by people here who have the money for international tuition, which is quite narrow. I can imagine that being quite a difficult experience,” he said.

I have seen with pride how British overseas aid saves children’s lives. That is why I say cuts should be reversed

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 05:00:55 GMT

I understand the pressure on the public purse, but I have also seen the effect of our spending on the ground. Our choices can do so much good

David Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassador

As Labour party conference approaches, politicians will debate spending priorities, fiscal pressures and the UK’s place in the world. Before those discussions begin, I want ministers to picture a hospital ward I visited in Sierra Leone with Unicef (United Nations Children’s Fund).

Inside the special-care baby unit at Makeni regional hospital were rows of tiny premature babies, some no bigger than my hand. Around them stood dedicated nurses and anxious parents, all willing these newborns to survive.

Then I saw something that stopped me in my tracks. It was 2019, and I noticed a UK aid sticker fixed above a tiny incubator. Inside was a premature baby fighting for breath. Nearby stood oxygen equipment that staff explained had been funded through UK support. I learned that when power outages struck the hospital, as they often did, that equipment helped keep vulnerable newborns alive.

Being in the presence of these sometimes inconceivably small children, seeing the UK aid sticker labelled across the incubators that were keeping them alive, emotion completely overcame me. It was not only sadness. It was pride. Pride that people in Britain, most of whom would never meet that baby or their family, had helped make survival possible. Seven years later, that moment remains one of the most impactful of my life.

When you are standing beside a newborn fighting for every breath, politics feels very far away. But the truth is that babies live or die because of political choices.

Since 2017, Unicef has supported Sierra Leone’s government to establish special-care baby units, providing sick and premature newborns with specialised treatment that was previously unavailable to many in the country.

I met doctors and nurses doing extraordinary work despite limited resources. I saw community health workers connecting families with health facilities, and mothers receiving advice and support.

One of them was Josephine, whose one-month-old daughter, also called Josephine, had been born dangerously premature at seven months. She told me she believed that without the special-care baby unit, both she and her daughter might have died during or after labour.

That is what aid means. It is not charity, and it is not an abstract number on a government spreadsheet.

The results in Sierra Leone show what that investment can achieve. Since the expansion of the special-care baby units began, annual admissions have risen from around 1,000 to 14,000, while survival rates had improved from 78% to 90% by the end of 2025.

But those gains are now under threat. Since the start of 2025, global aid funding has fallen sharply as major donors have scaled back support. The UK has already reduced spending on overseas development from 0.7% of national income to 0.3%. Around the world, programmes that help keep children healthy, safe and in school are facing growing uncertainty. In Sierra Leone, those cuts are no longer a future concern. They are already being felt.

I learned last week that the UK funding for Sierra Leone’s newborn care programme is now expected to end this December, two years earlier than planned.

I’m already hearing about the consequences. International paediatric support and specialist neonatal nurse training has ended. Reductions affecting the free healthcare programmes have also damaged the availability of lifesaving medicines for newborns, children and pregnant women.

The danger is not just that units such as Makeni might suddenly close. It is that the foundations supporting them are gradually eroded. Medical equipment needs spare parts and trained technicians. Oxygen must remain available. Nurses need continuing training and clinical mentorship. Medicines must reach hospitals. Infection prevention, referrals, outreach and follow-up for small and sick babies all require sustained investment.

Without that support, the progress I witnessed will be lost.

Sierra Leone is building national capacity. But transferring skills and building resilient health systems takes time. Ending support prematurely risks pulling away the scaffolding before the structure is strong enough to stand alone.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The scale of the unmet need makes that risk even more alarming. About 45,000 newborns in Sierra Leone require specialised care each year, but existing services reach only about 31%. Approximately 31,000 small and sick babies are still left without access to the essential care they need.

This is not a programme that has finished its job. It is a programme that is working, but still reaches only a fraction of the children who need it. That is why I support Unicef UK’s No Choice But Childhood campaign.

The Guardian’s recent report suggests that ministers are looking for ways to make a smaller aid budget work harder. That is an important discussion. But the question should not only be how aid is spent: it should also be who it is spent for. If children bear the greatest consequences of poverty, conflict and climate shocks, they should be a clear priority in how aid is allocated.

The UK government should ringfence at least 25% of its overseas development spending for programmes that directly support children. The government must also set out a credible route back to spending 0.7% of national income on overseas development. Restoring that commitment will not happen overnight, but without a clear path, temporary reductions risk becoming a permanent retreat, with tragic consequences.

I understand the pressures on public finances: governments must make difficult choices. But we should be honest about what those choices mean.

In Makeni, they can mean whether oxygen is available when a premature baby cannot breathe. Whether a nurse has the training and equipment to act. Whether a mother goes home carrying her child.

The special-care baby unit I visited remains open, for now, but declining support is making it harder to sustain its quality, while extending the same care to thousands of newborns who are still not being reached.

No child chooses where they are born, and as Labour conference gets under way, I hope ministers think of children – like the tiny baby I saw in the incubator. That is what our choices can do.

David Harewood is a Unicef UK ambassador

‘I turbocharged my career then pressed eject’: why couples are getting divorced later

The Guardian Sun, 27 Sep 2026 05:00:55 GMT

Financial pressures, legal changes and shifting attitudes may help explain why couples are staying married for longer

“We don’t know anyone whose marriage hit the skids after just a few years,” Celia said, reflecting on her divorce. “Everyone seemed to cling on to their relationships for as long as they possibly could.”

It took Celia two years to initiate divorce after realising her 12-year marriage wasn’t going anywhere – and the latest figures show this experience is increasingly common, with marriages that end in divorce now lasting longer than at any point since records began.

“I approached it very methodically,” the AI analyst said. “I knew that women almost always end up financially worse off after divorce, especially where there are children concerned, so I took the time I needed to turbocharge my career before pressing ‘eject’.”

It helped, Celia said, that she and Martyn, her former husband, had been in their 40s when they got married.

“Because we were older and wiser, we took the time to try to mend our relationship instead of rushing off to start a new life,” she said. “When that didn’t work, Martyn was mature enough to know it was best for the children, me and us that he subtly left me alone to get to where I needed to be before we formally called time on the relationship.”

According to figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) released this week, the median length of a marriage before it ends in divorce reached 13 years in England and Wales in 2025. The figure for opposite-sex marriages has risen from 12.7 years in 2023 and a low of 8.9 years in 1985.

At the same time, the proportion of couples divorcing during their first decade of marriage has fallen sharply. Among couples who married in 2015, an estimated 16.3% had divorced by their 10th anniversary, compared with 24.7% of those who married in 1995.

The ONS research does not give any answers as to why marriages are ending later. But it does suggest several hypotheses, including that couples may delay the legal end of their relationships until they can afford what comes next.

Prof Emma Hitchings, the deputy head of the University of Bristol law school, who led the Fair Shares project, a nationally representative study in England and Wales examining how divorcing couples divide their money and property, said: “Divorce may have become legally easier, with the advent of no-fault divorces, but separating one household into two has not.”

She said that the longer a couple stayed together, the more tightly entwined – and harder to untangle – their finances became.

“Every financial aspect of divorce is harder,” she said. “From higher tax and mortgage rates, childcare and school fees – as well as the general cost of living. Then throw in the cuts to legal aid for almost all private family law proceedings in England and Wales, and you can see why couples need to spend more time trying to calculate how they can feasibly afford to separate – which may well account for why marriages are lasting longer before divorce.”

Celia said she and Martyn had a number of friends who also broke up after marriages of similar lengths. “It was the oddest thing. But we have three groups of friends, across Europe and in the US, who went through divorces after marriages of a decade or more.”

The research bears out Celia’s experience. In the US, the Pew Research Center found that the median length of marriages ending in divorce rose from 10 years in 2008 to 12 years in 2023.

Germany’s federal statistics office put the average length of marriages ending in divorce at 14.6 years in 2025. In the Netherlands, the figure was 14.7 years. Belgium’s statistics office recorded a median of 12.03 years in 2024.

The figures are not directly comparable as countries collect and present divorce statistics differently. But the broad pattern of marriages lasting longer before divorce is not solely a British phenomenon.

Anne Barlow, professor emeritus of family law and policy at the University of Exeter, said there was a curious feature of the British figures. “No-fault divorce, introduced in 2022, made the legal route out of marriage more straightforward – but there has been no corresponding rush into divorce,” she said.

One possibility was that knowing you could leave made it easier to wait, said Dr Alexander Maine, a senior lecturer at the City law school who leads a research project called: “Queer families and the law after ‘I do’.”

“Another is that no-fault divorce could allow couples to work through a separation without the acrimony that previously accompanied assigning blame,” he said. “If there is no need to prove fault, there may be less pressure to bring the marriage to an immediate legal end.”

Greg Ceely, the ONS’s head of population life events, emphasised that until more research was done, these all remained hypotheses. “The change can’t definitively be attributed to any one thing – or any number of things – because there are so many social and economic factors that could also affect the trend,” he said.

Certainly, experts find no problem in pointing to other possible reasons for marriages lasting longer before divorce, from disruption to the family courts affecting the timing of divorces in the years around Covid, as well as influencing the duration figures, to the 2022 changes introducing a minimum 20-week period between the start of proceedings and application for a final order.

Julia Carter, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of the West of England, Bristol, who is researching couples living together after divorce or separation, said wider global and environmental uncertainty was also having an impact.

“I hear people saying that even if their marriage isn’t great, they don’t want to introduce uncertainty into their homes as well, especially if there are children in the relationship who are having to negotiate this unstable world outside their family homes,” she said.

Carter pointed to the fact that women remain overwhelmingly the main instigators of divorce. “So if we’re saying that people are waiting later to get divorce, we’re actually saying that women are waiting longer in order to get divorced. So you’ve got to look at what’s changed for women,” she said.

In the 1990s and 2000s, she said, “society was all about female empowerment, girl power, Sex and the City, and ‘let’s go out and grab our opportunities’. But there’s been a rolling back from that kind of positioning, especially for women, because we’ve been through so many crises since then: economic, environmental, political, jobs.

“I think we can see the impact of that in intimate family lives where there’s an embedding of marriage as a kind of refuge, a place of long-term stability and security for couples – and especially for women,” she said. “That has reignited a reluctance to go through divorce.”

The ONS’s same-sex figures give a different set of questions. The median duration of same-sex marriages ending in divorce was 7.5 years for male couples and 6.6 years for female couples in 2025. The figures need to be treated cautiously because same-sex marriage was introduced in England and Wales only in 2014, meaning the pool of marriages that could have reached divorce is still relatively young.

But the ONS says the 6.6-year figure for female couples is nevertheless the highest recorded since the first same-sex divorces in 2015.

Maine suggested that same-sex couples might have particular reasons for taking marriage seriously. “Marriage equality was something many gay people spent so many years campaigning for very hard,” he said. “Because of that, divorce in the LGBT community sometimes carries an additional sense of having failed not just the relationship but the whole community.”

Brienna Perelli-Harris, a professor of demography at the University of Southampton and director of the UK Generations and Gender Survey, suggested a more fundamental change that might underpin the change: the rise of cohabitation.

More than 90% of people in Britain cohabited before marrying, said Perelli-Harris, whose research across 10 European countries found that an increasing proportion of first partnerships were ending before marriage.

“Marriage may therefore be becoming a more selective institution,” she said. “Couples who move in together and discover that the relationship does not work can separate without ever marrying. Those who stay together and eventually marry are, my research shows, the couples who are happiest.”

From Sense and Sensibility to Kill Jackie: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 05:00:29 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Daisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caper

Sense and SensibilityOut now Daisy Edgar-Jones has a big bonnet to fill in the role Emma Thompson made her own in Ang Lee’s Oscar-winning version of Jane Austen’s romance. But let’s not compare: Blue Jean director Georgia Oakley’s take sees a fresh cast place new emphasis on the bond between sisters Marianne and Elinor.

Her Private HellOut now Professional provocateur Nicolas Winding Refn returns with another slice of the outre, this time in a science fiction mode. It’s the tale of a young woman, Elle (Sophie Thatcher), who encounters a supernatural killer in diamond-encrusted gloves in a mist-shrouded city.

RemakeOut now Taking on the devastating subject of the death of his own son, revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee makes the film that no parent would want to make. Using his own home video and family archive, he creates a bereavement memoir that traces a life from infancy to adolescence to an adulthood marred by addiction.

Heart of the BeastOut now Training Day screenwriter David Ayer directs this thriller about one man and his dog attempting to survive in the wilderness after a plane crash. But not just any man and dog: he’s an ex-special forces officer and the dog is a retired combat dog. Curiously, it stars Brad Pitt where you might expect Jason Statham. Catherine Bray

Jill ScottLondon, 28 September; Birmingham, 29 September; Manchester, 1 October; London, 13 & 14 October; touring to 14 OctoberThe R&B and soul legend heads out on tour in support of To Whom This May Concern, her first album in 11 years. Cole also plays London’s Vortex on 29 & 30 September. John Fordham

Miriam Gillinson

Rhys James 30 September to 15 May; tour starts FolkestoneYet to achieve household-name status, 35-year-old James is widely considered one of UK standup’s master craftspeople. His new show Chop Logic combines a relentless stream of ingenious gags with the story of his circumcision. Rachel Aroesti

Subjects include the writer James Baldwin, lesbian seagulls and the dust in Quentin Crisp’s flat. Lyndsey Winship

Kill Jackie Prime Video, 2 OctoberCatherine Zeta-Jones goes full madcap camp – and even gets to keep her native Welsh accent – in this big, bonkers crime caper about an ex-con art dealer whose past catches up with her. Daniel Ings, Raff Law and Sidse Babett Knudsen also star.

WarSky Atlantic & Now, 2 October, 9pmIt’s Sienna Miller v Dominic West in this deluxe new thriller from George Kay (Lupin, The Long Shadow). A film star and tech titan face “the biggest divorce trial in British legal history”, meaning their respective teams of lawyers, including Nick Mohammed, will stop at nothing in order to come out on top.

East of Eden Netflix, 1 OctoberZoe Kazan follows in her grandfather Elia’s footsteps with this adaptation of Steinbeck’s 1952 opus. Florence Pugh gets her teeth stuck into one of fiction’s most notorious antiheroines in Cathy Ames, whose author described her as having a “malformed soul”. Christopher Abbott plays her abandoned husband.

Break ClauseChannel 4, 1 October, 10pm A former couple – promising young architect Lil (comedian Lara Ricote) and directionless graduate Ben (Samuel Bottomley) – are forced to cohabit in a London flat due to a watertight rental contract in this sweet and goofy will-they-won’t-they (get back together) comedy from Jess Bray. RA

Nivalis NightsPC; out 29 SeptemberA cyberpunk life-simulation where, instead of running around with a futuristic pistol and getting caught up in gang wars, you are just trying to make a living. Starting out with a food stand, you can eventually own the night through a network of bars, restaurants and clubs – and learn everything about the city from your loose-lipped patrons.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – RemasteredAll platforms; out 29 SeptemberOutcast monster hunter Geralt of Rivia gets caught up in the dark machinations of phantom huntsmen and warring kings in this updated and complete version of an all-time great role-player. If you have somehow yet to play this eastern European dark fantasy masterpiece, you really have run out of excuses. Keza MacDonald

Blondshell – ViolinsOut nowAfter Sabrina Teitelbaum’s first pop-leaning incarnation as BAUM imploded in 2020, the New Yorker morphed into alt-rocker Blondshell. While the musical backdrop is heavier and more guitar-based, that pop nous still runs through this third album, especially on the galloping Fur Elise.

Julia Jacklin – The GemOut nowNamed after her local pub, the fourth album – and her first for the much-loved label 4AD – by Melbourne-based songwriter Julia Jacklin is full of lovingly crumpled rock. Exploring reinvention, longing and excavation, songs such as The Hardest Thing and I Wish are full of unforgettable melodic nuggets.

Tinashe – PopstarOut nowAfter getting lost in the major-label system, US bop-maker Tinashe has thrived as an independent artist. On her eighth album she dabbles in hyperpop elasticity via the undulating Melatonin, while the low-slung Crash Out adds trap and R&B to the mix.

M83 – I Wrote You a LetterOut nowThe French synth-pop outfit, led by Anthony Gonzalez, return with their 10th album, and first in three years. Worked up from demos recorded in 2024 as a way of capturing the spirit of the band’s earlier work, it opens with the blown-out alt-pop of the cinematic Blister Sunrise. MC

90 Minutes or Less Film FestPodcast Host Sam Clements programmes his dream film festival lineup in this charming series celebrating the art of well-edited cinema. Picks include Godard’s Breathless, as chosen by director Richard Linklater, and Jackass, as selected by Steve-O.

DeconstructedYouTube Detailed 3D animations dissect some of history’s most complex machines and structures on this fascinating channel. Discover the inner workings of an ancient Greek water clock and the unusual design of the Eiffel Tower elevators.

Mapping India: The World’s Largest CountBBC World Service, 26 September, 12.06amIndia is undertaking one of the largest counting exercises in the world: a census of its 1.5 billion inhabitants. This astounding documentary follows the logistical challenges of the process, from Delhi streets to Himalayan mountains. Ammar Kalia

Five Great Reads: A week in Gaza, the queen of toddler TV, and bunkering down

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 22:05:30 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

This week, we could not look away from the series Gaza: a week in the life. In the story linked below, a Palestinian mother recounts how she is rebuilding her future in the ruins and fragments of the past she lost. Across the rest of the reads in this newsletter, there is hope, resistance and rebirth in the history that continues to define our present.

I hope you enjoy them all as much as we did.

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week the Guardian followed five ordinary Palestinians going about their daily lives. Each piece tells the story of their day, revealing the conflict’s terrible toll. On day one of the series, Alaa Hessi brought readers into her world. Hessi lives in a tent pitched on the ruins of her house, which was destroyed by an Israeli airstrike that killed all three of her children.

Life in the rubble: Gaza holds the memory of Alaai’s lost children, and she finds beauty in the ruins that surround the tent. In the late afternoon, Alaa scrolls through old photos and videos to hear their voices.

Notable quote: “I do not tell nurses at the clinic about my circumstances and my children who died, because even the healthcare workers are emotionally exhausted. They are unable to offer comfort or psychological support. My story is not unusual in Gaza. Many women here have lost their children.”

How long will it take to read: About three minutes.

Further reading: A week in Gaza day two, day three and day four.

You may not be familiar with the process of “cuckooing”. It’s where a drug dealing gang takes over the home of a vulnerable person, usually exploiting them to use their home as a base from which to operate. In the past couple of decades it has been increasingly used as a way for gangs to avoid detection. And just as it sounds, it’s grim and dangerous. But as the author and journalist Max Daly writes here, the reality is complex.

From misery to an unusual “friendship”: Daly’s friend Duncan, a musician, artist and father, ended up opening his doors to drug gangs – not once but twice – but his two experiences turned out to be completely different. The first brought him only misery; the second, in his telling at least, brought him a strange kind of friendship. Did it save him? The answer to that is perplexing.

How long will it take to read: 13 minutes.

Further reading: The history and the victims of cuckooing.

Rachel Accurso, better known as Ms Rachel, has become a global star in the world of children’s entertainment. Accurso has been labelled a “toddler whisperer” and racks up billions of views on YouTube with her catchy videos. Having signed a deal with Netflix, Ms Rachel dolls, rattles, talking toy phones, books and pyjamas are now all available. But statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have prompted criticism as well as support.

Why get involved in politics? In the beginning, Accurso was advised to keep quiet about political issues. She was told that if she avoided controversial topics, more viewers would follow, and she would eventually be able to help more kids. But after watching footage from Gaza and speaking to families on the ground, Accurso says, she doesn’t understand why anyone would not do all they can to stop the violence: “How could we not want to help everyone?”

Notable quote: “We’re the grownups of this world and we’re meant to keep children safe. And the fact that we are not is horrific.”

How long will it take to read: almost nine minutes.

Further reading: Matching Macklemore, and the TV event of the year.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Having made its debut on Broadway in 1935, the play Till the Day I Die found itself at the centre of controversy in Australia when it was banned by the federal government at the request of the Nazi party. Written by the US playwright Clifford Odets, the play is about a communist who was arrested by the Nazis for producing leftwing political pamphlets. But the ban created a groundswell of support, leading to a creative production being performed on the back of a truck in Melbourne. Ninety years on, it’s being staged again.

A symbol of rebellion and resistance: Theatre-makers Mark Wilson and Katie Sfetkidis were inspired by that surreptitious production, which took place in the bed of a pickup 90 years ago. Wilson and Sfetkidis view their modern-day production as “as an act of leftist solidarity with the past and a spur for future activism”.

Notable qoute: “The work is long and the work is ongoing, and fighting against the forces of fascism is going to be much larger than anybody’s lifetime.”

How long will it take to read: less than two minutes.

Further reading: When a theatre becomes a culture war.

Across the Nordic countries of Finland, Sweden and Norway, something is happening underground. Bunkers made during the cold war now have a new purpose as Russia’s war in Ukraine revives old fears of conflict across Europe. These once disused bunkers remain ready for a crisis.

“It was a debate before, but thanks to Putin, it no longer is”: For years, the legacy of underground shelters was viewed as a costly one. Jukka Lehtiranta, the head of Helsinki’s Civil Defence Association, who continues to train volunteers for wartime, says that has now changed. In addition to their renewed use as a civil-defence system, these spaces designed for conflict have become a part of Finnish everyday life. Across Helsinki, underground bunkers now contain a 300-metre karting track, a popular axe-throwing club, garages and a shooting range used by reservists.

Can you oppose a datacentre if it is underground? Sweden has found a different use for their neglected shelters. The cold war spaces beneath Stockholm have been transformed into datacentres. Deep beneath the earth, rows of servers stand beside granite walls lined with green vegetation.

How long will it take to read: about two minutes.

Further reading: The super-rich “preppers” planning to save themselves from the apocalypse.

England v Spain, Azerbaijan GP and county cricket finale – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:27:53 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The Premier League may be on a break but there is no slacking at our essential gateway to the weekend’s football action. Front and centre, we will have the latest news on Manchester City’s legal battle. Plus England’s mouthwatering confrontation at Wembley with the world champions, Spain, on Saturday evening, the hosts’ first match since that semi-final freeze against Argentina. At 2pm, a new era for Scotland commences as Sébastien Pocognoli’s side kickstart their Nations League campaign away to Slovenia. We will not be forgetting Leagues One and Two either, and if the National League is your passion and you are travelling to a match, we would love to hear from you. You will be a lot of things, but one thing you will not be is bored. Emillia Hawkins has all the breaking news and more.

As the campaign rushes to its conclusion, Tanya Aldred keeps those on tenterhooks updated with all the highs and lows, wickets and runs. Champagne corks are planned to pop at Warwickshire who are striding toward clinching the County Championship title against relegation-threatened Leicestershire at Edgbaston. A win would guarantee a first pennant since the Covid-shortened 2021 campaign, with second-placed Somerset faltering against Surrey. In Division Two promotion hopefuls Kent are battling rock-bottom Gloucestershire at Canterbury. Northamptonshire, just four points behind second-placed Kent, need to step up against Middlesex. Why not join the conversation?

Azerbaijan is marking 10 years since its first F1 race but this year’s event is a little different. The grand prix is taking place on a Saturday because Sunday is a national holiday, Remembrance Day. The Baku City Circuit hosting Saturday’s race is about 105 miles from the nearest point on Azerbaijan’s southern border with Iran, yet the turmoil of the regional conflict that has accounted for other motor sport events has not shunted this fixture off the F1 calendar. Two other world championships governed by the FIA have abandoned plans to race in the Middle East this year. The World Rally Championship last week scrapped its season-ending event in Saudi Arabia after travel concerns from teams. The World Endurance Championship cancelled races in Bahrain and Qatar in July and replaced them with European venues. Azerbaijan has been less directly affected by the Iran war than the Gulf nations, many of which host major US military bases and were targeted by Iranian strikes. So, F1 racing will go on, as Kimi Antonelli commands a vast 81-point lead over his Mercedes teammate George Russell. Baku is where Oscar Piastri’s title challenge started to crumble a year ago but Antonelli’s lead is more than double the biggest advantage the McLaren driver had last year and he is coming off back-to-back wins. Dominic Booth covers the race lap-by-lap. Giles Richards reports.

So to the first of Saturday’s two big games. In an extended international break, the Scots face the Slovenians twice, Switzerland and North Macedonia as they strive to get out of League B. Enter Sébastien Pocognoli, tasked with building on the groundwork laid by Steve Clarke, under whom Scotland qualified for three major tournaments, including this summer’s World Cup in North America. “We arrive in the timeline of the Scotland national team [where], in the natural way, you will have some changes. But I don’t see this as a bad challenge, I think it’s a needed challenge,” the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager said in the buildup. Those Scotland followers of a jaded nature might say t’was ever thus: a challenge. Maybe it will take a Belgian to take this generation of players to a higher level and provide some cheer for the longsuffering Tartan Army. Barry Glendenning live blogs the match, with Ewan Murray reporting from Ljubljana’s Stadion Stozice.

Spain’s visit to Wembley is a painful reminder to England of what might have been, and Thomas Tuchel needs a positive response to silence criticism of how the Three Lions’ World Cup fizzled out against a snarling, brutal Argentina. Had England held out for the final five minutes plus stoppage time in their semi-final two months ago, they would have met Spain in the final. Instead Tuchel’s players wilted, conceding twice after he had attempted to batten down the hatches with a series of defensive substitutions. The German coach admitted to being left “unfulfilled” by failing to achieve his target of a second star on the England jersey. Bukayo Saka went even further in midweek by revealing “there’s still a scar in us” over what happened in Atlanta. Time to start healing those wounds against the best international team on the planet. It is a tall order, particularly with a string of high-profile withdrawals. Rob Smyth will keep the blog updates flowing while our top team of David Hytner, Barney Ronay and Jacob Steinberg provide reports and analysis from the national stadium.

Matchday live returns with more buildup, breaking news, good vibes and reader comments, with Billy Munday, Will Unwin and Yara El-Shaboury keeping it all flowing. There will be the latest updates on Manchester City v the Premier League and wash-up from England and Scotland’s Nations League clashes, as well as looking forward to Sunday’s key clashes: Israel v Ireland, Denmark v Wales, Serbia v Netherlands, Germany v Greece and Norway v Portugal. There is no better place to start your footballing day. Join the conversation by emailing your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com

Rob Smyth and Tim de Lisle have over-by-over coverage of the third ODI after Sri Lanka levelled the series in thrilling last-over fashion at Headingley on Thursday. England were cruising to a target of 322 while Tom Banton (73) and Ben Duckett (67) shared a first-wicket stand of 143. Sri Lanka had been hammered 3-0 in a preceding T20 campaign but Dunith Wellalage dragged them back by removing both openers and captain Harry Brook to reduce England to 157 for three. The left-arm spinner finished with figures of three for 49 after captain Kusal Mendis hit a fine century. The teams now head to London for a series-decider at the Oval. In the aftermath Brook insisted this was just what England needed before next year’s 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. “We’ve got a great opportunity now to try to win this series, and a great opportunity for 12 months’ time,” he said. “In pressure situations, like the one that awaits us at the Oval, it will be great to see where we are as a team.” Our cricket correspondent Ali Martin reports.

The season’s final day – will it be Warks? Or will Somerset gatecrash the pennant party? Tanya Aldred is back to steer the live blog as the domestic campaign hurtles to the grandest of grandstand finishes. Join her for all the latest developments.

Renée Slegers’ unbeaten Arsenal face their derby rivals at Stamford Bridge after draws against Crystal Palace and Manchester United. However, only two goals and five points from three WSL matches is a telling indication of their season so far. Yet Tuesday’s 1-0 Champions League victory over HB Køge was achieved while several first-choice players were rested. They should be back in red and white for one of the campaign’s blockbusters as the two most successful clubs in the WSL era collide. Chelsea recorded their own Champions League success in midweek, with Wieke Kapteina’s strike securing 1-0 win over Austria Vienna, having struggled to impose themselves over Birmingham City last weekend. Will Unwin hosts the live blog, with Sophie Downey reporting.

Buckle up, NFL fans: Graham Searles’ rolling blog is the best way to follow all the unfurling action on a Sunday evening. He’ll be focusing on two of week three’s key games: Dolphins v Chiefs and Bills v Chargers. Miami lost to San Francisco 49ers last time out – unraveling in the second half of an eventual 35-13 defeat – and face another tough challenge when the three-time Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs visit. The Chiefs are off to a 2-0 flyer, thanks largely to a balanced offence bolstered by the former Seattle running back Kenneth Walker III. The reigning Super Bowl MVP began the season with consecutive games of more than 175 scrimmage yards, creating room for Mahomes to have more success through the air. The Chiefs are averaging an NFL-best 457.5 yards through two games, which is about 137 more than their per-game average last season. Likewise, Buffalo are rolling after two straight wins, while the Los Angeles Chargers are winless as they hit the road for Sunday’s game.

John Brewin has rolling coverage of Sunday evening’s big internationals, and he’ll be zeroing in on the Republic of Ireland’s troubled clash in Hungary. The Irish face Israel before a designated “home” game in Serbia on 4 October, amid protests and calls for a boycott over Israel’s war in Gaza. The country’s strong support for the Palestinian cause dictates there will be no Irish supporters in the stadium, no home match in Ireland, and no pundits or Irish commentary on television. The game is being staged in Debrecen because Israel cannot host international matches. Ireland’s manager, Heimir Hallgrimsson, raised tension levels last week by saying that many of his squad were uncomfortable about taking part, adding: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide.” Those comments drew a furious response from the Israel Football Association, which accused Hallgrimsson of “hypocrisy and stupidity”.

In a wide-ranging interview, Prime Minister Mark Carney described a tense, evolving relationship with President Trump.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada during an interview with The New York Times on Wednesday. Credit... Daniel Berehulak/The New York Times

Supported by

By Matina Stevis-GridneffDavid E. SangerTyler Pager and Colby Smith

Matina Stevis-Gridneff is Canada bureau chief. David E. Sanger and Tyler Pager cover the White House. Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve. They were among Times journalists who interviewed Mr. Carney in New York.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said that he had prepared over the past year for the “extreme tail risk” that President Trump might order military action against Canada, but disclosed that the two men have spoken “frequently,” even since trade talks collapsed last month, describing a tense, evolving relationship.

In a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times at its headquarters in Midtown Manhattan on Wednesday, Mr. Carney described in meticulous detail how he was systematically reducing Canada’s reliance on the United States for key technology — from space satellites to fighter jets — in an effort to make his country far less vulnerable to American threats. He outlined a plan to diversify Canada’s relationships and suppliers, and said that even with a different future president “we will be a better partner for the U. S. because of what we are doing.”

He talked about reducing reliance on Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite systems; considering alternatives to buying F-35 fighter jets; and a focus on deepening economic — though not defense — relationships with China. Mr. Trump’s exploitation of Canadian dependency on American products had taught the country a bitter lesson: “There’s certain things, once you’ve seen them, you can’t unsee them.”

When pressed on whether he took Mr. Trump’s threats to make Canada a 51st state seriously, Mr. Carney suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of U. S.-led military action, but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” said Mr. Carney, a former central banker for Britain and Canada who approaches the world by meticulously assessing worst-case scenarios and drafting responses. He added: “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare.

Mr. Carney spoke for an hour on a variety of challenges, including artificial intelligence, trade, and Canada’s role as a “middle power.”

Over the past year, he has emerged as the most prominent global leader to take on Mr. Trump. Along the way, he has also begun to define a path toward reducing dependence on a superpower neighbor that he has come to regard as predatory. Around the world, other leaders have looked to him as a model for dealing with an erratic, unreliable ally — one that remains, in Canada’s case, critical to national defense and economic survival.

But few of those leaders have articulated their interests as clearly as Mr. Carney, who used a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year to describe a strategy for dealing with the rupture. “Either you retreat wholly into yourself or you diversify,” he said then, making the choice he faces stark.

Still, Mr. Carney said he speaks “frequently” to Mr. Trump and that they had spoken “a number of times” since trade talks broke down last month.

“From my perspective, we have a good relationship in the sense of we can pick up the phone and talk to each other about issues,” he said on Wednesday. “He’s direct. I’m direct in terms of where positions are. It’s much more efficient that way, and so you know that exists and that will continue to exist.”

The Canadian leader made the case, too, that in many ways, what’s good for Canada is also good for the United States because of their decades-long integration that has created stability and prosperity. Mr. Carney gave the example of the automobile industry, which is highly integrated across the U. S.-Canada border but has been at the center of the Trump administration’s tariff policy against Canada.

“My entire life, and I’m 61, we’ve had an integrated auto sector,” Mr. Carney said, adding that breaking that deep connection to repatriate all auto production to the United States is not good policy. “We think it doesn’t make sense,” he said.

Mr. Carney said that a path remains to resuming negotiations with the United States that would revive the trade agreement that fell apart in late August. Since then, the two countries have imposed rounds of tariffs on each other, and rhetoric has been menacing, particularly from Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly called Canada’s leadership “nasty.” But Mr. Carney brushed that off.

“Is there a mutually beneficial trade deal between Canada and the U. S.? Absolutely, absolutely there is one,” Mr. Carney said. He said that he was interested, for example, in adding potash to the talks. Canada provides almost 90 percent of all potash, the key ingredient for fertilizer, imported into the United States. Earlier this week, Mr. Trump said that he wanted to replace Canada’s supply with potash from Belarus — an authoritarian state aligned with Russia that is under U. S. sanctions for its role in the war in Ukraine.

Mr. Carney said that Canada, the United States and potentially also Mexico could become “fertilizer independent” by securing special access to Canada’s potash, the world’s largest reserve. He added that the Canadian option was clearly better than buying potash elsewhere that would then need to be transported through the Black Sea or the Strait of Hormuz.

“I think this is a doable component of the deal, and there are other examples that exist, and we’re ready to work toward,” he added.

At home, Mr. Carney has come under pressure to use Canada’s most sensitive and important export to the United States — energy — as leverage in the trade war. Some 60 percent of all oil imports into the United States come from Canada, while the country is also a major source of electricity for American households and industry.

Mr. Carney said he was very reluctant to limit, tariff or otherwise curb those exports to the United States.

“If you’re a reliable partner and you supply energy or food to somebody it keeps running, it’s a very, very, very high threshold to change that,” he said. “Never say never, but it starts from a position of, we need to be a reliable supplier in all cases.”

Although optimistic that efforts to strike a trade deal could be revived, Mr. Carney said he was cleareyed about areas where Canada needs to reduce its dependence on the United States.

“Starlink, we will diversify away from, no question,” Mr. Carney said, referring to the American-based cluster of communication satellites, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, that have revolutionized the industry. He alluded to past disruptions and to Mr. Musk’s reluctance to provide Ukraine with data that would enable it to target parts of Crimea and Russia.

He acknowledged that other satellite network options are still less capable and resilient, but added that “from a defense perspective, and certainly pooled with other partners, Europeans, Koreans potentially, you get to scale and you cut that dependency.”

The Canadian government is reviewing a planned order of 88 Lockheed Martin F-35 jets and is also considering a counterproposal to acquire Swedish Saab Gripen fighters. Mr. Carney did not specify where he was on that decision, but he did say that he wanted to use Canada’s newly bolstered defense budget to order aircraft that perform well in the Arctic.

“It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies, and because of the economic return,” he said.

Mr. Carney on Wednesday also reiterated his long-held view that a global financial system wholly dependent on the U. S. dollar was unsustainable. A move to a multipolar system in which there are several reserve currencies would “provide more flexibility,” he said.

He acknowledged that there was a “directional shift” underway in which countries were re-evaluating their exposure to the U. S. dollar, but he conceded that any pivot would be limited until there was “proper liberalization” of China’s currency and financial system. Still, Mr. Carney said he expected the demand for U. S. dollar alternatives to grow, in part because of the Trump administration’s decision to rewire trading relations and use integration as “leverage.”

“It’s the ‘fool me once, fool me twice’ point,” Mr. Carney said. “Once you see that, then you start to think, how do I diversify away?”

Matina Stevis-Gridneff is the Canada bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the country.

David E. Sanger covers the Trump administration and a range of national security issues. He has been a Times journalist for more than four decades and has written four books on foreign policy and national security challenges.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

The New York Times September 27, 2026

Trump Administration

Dario Amodei, who is also the company’s chief executive, will join the president at the White House for a private dinner. Mr. Trump has dismissed his cautions.

By Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Reporting from Washington

President Trump will have dinner on Sunday night with Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, who sparked the ire of the president earlier this month when he called for a slowdown of the rapidly developing technology.

Mr. Trump will host Dr. Amodei at the White House, according to a U. S. official and a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to confirm the private dinner.

The dinner comes as the Trump administration appears increasingly focused on meeting with A. I. and technology executives amid concerns about the potential risks of artificial intelligence.

Mr. Trump on Thursday dined with other A. I. executives during a state dinner for President Xi Jinping of China. He is also scheduled to hold a summit on Tuesday with technology executives to discuss A. I. and to unveil a new government website designed to help Americans navigate federal information, according to a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity to preview the event.

Dr. Amodei co-founded Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, and has warned about the safety risks of A. I. for years. Earlier this month he urged global cooperation in creating rules around A. I. development. Mr. Trump has rejected such concerns.

“The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel,’” Mr. Trump said in a social media post earlier this month. “And we will continue to do so!”

While Mr. Trump has dismissed potential serious threats around A. I. as a “hoax,” some in the Trump administration have pushed for a more cautious approach to the technology. Mr. Trump’s dinner with Dr. Amodei may suggest an openness to hear out those warnings.

The White House and Anthropic declined to comment. Axios earlier reported on the dinner with Mr. Trump and Dr. Amodei.

The Trump administration and Anthropic also clashed earlier this year when the company was effectively cut off from working with the federal government after battling with the Pentagon. The two sides disagreed in negotiations over a $200 million contract about the use of A. I. in warfare, with the Pentagon later designating Anthropic a “supply chain risk to national security.”

The administration scored a legal victory on Friday when a federal appeals court in Washington ruled that it had acted legally and constitutionally when it said Anthropic was a national security risk and barred the company from working with the government.

The ruling left the San Francisco company in an awkward position, one that Dr. Amodei may have an opportunity to address with Mr. Trump on Sunday night.

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.
