Saturday Night at the Massachusetts Lesbian Bar Everyone Is Talking About

The New York Times September 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Last Ditch, a bar and art space, ended its Covid mask requirement as a way to attract more people. What it got instead was outsized attention.

By Mark Arsenault

Reporting from outside a suddenly famous lesbian bar in Greenfield, Mass.

A few locals stopped by the Last Ditch lesbian bar early Saturday evening, intending to drop a few bucks to support a struggling business that had become something of a celebrity.

But the bar’s purple door was closed. Opening time was not until 10 p. m.

“I have a lot of friends in the queer community and I’d hate to see this place go under,” said Melinda McCreven, of Greenfield, who had never visited the Last Ditch, but came by to try to spend a little money.

Last Ditch, a basement bar down a set of concrete steps, beneath a Mexican restaurant, drew news coverage in Europe and the United States this week after a Boston Globe story about the bar’s plan to lift its Covid mask requirement on Saturday nights went viral.

The article came after a podcast had covered a vitriolic, hourslong meeting, when Last Ditch patrons and its owner argued over whether the bar was abandoning its mission to be welcoming to all.

Early Saturday evening, a sign on the closed door said another meeting was taking place inside.

Greenfield, a Western Massachusetts town of about 17,000, is not accustomed to the national spotlight.

As darkness fell on Saturday evening, downtown went quiet. One man with a long stringy beard sat alone on a bench, eyes cast downward. Another man in some distress yelled obscure questions at passers-by, such as “How do you build a skyscraper?” and “What kind of music is jazz?” Someone called the police on him.

A group turned away by the closed purple door at Last Ditch made their way a half-block to throw darts at the Victoria bar, a locals pub with a tiny pride flag in the window.

“Friends from all over the country have been sending me the articles about it,” said Hallie Abelman, 34, of the Last Ditch controversy. “It’s the talk of the town.” While she was being interviewed outside the Victoria bar, a man tried to bum a cigarette from her group.

“There are many different Greenfields,” said Phoebe Glick, 35, who also tried to get into Last Ditch. There are crunchy lefties, conservative MAGA fans, people of all incomes, and an L. G. B. T. Q. community migrating from places like Northampton in search of cheaper housing, she said.

Around 6:30 p. m., four people in masks came out of the Last Ditch and confronted a small group of journalists hanging around outside. When one photographer snapped a flash photo of them, they demanded he delete the picture, and threatened to call the police if other journalists didn’t leave.

Three housemates, Asa Rosario, Jackie Matellian and Sage Territo, opened the bar in 2025 as a fun place for “Dykes, Transexuals, Gender Freaks, Workers, and their friends.” Two queer bars in the region had closed in recent years, and they hoped to fill the need.

Western Massachusetts would appear to be a customer-rich environment for a such a business: Nearby Hampshire County has the largest percentage of lesbian couple households in the country, according to the 2020 census.

The bar’s sudden fame comes from the fact that it had never really left the pandemic era, even though it opened just last year.

Patrons were required to wear KN95 or better masks, the face coverings ubiquitous during the heights of Covid-19, and which most of the country had left long ago to dental hygienists and people who don’t want anyone to sit next to them on the train.

Looking back, explosive feelings over the bar’s Covid safety policy were lurking from the day the owners announced the rule on social media, shortly before opening.

One respondent posted gratitude, saying they had felt “locked out of queer spaces as an immunocompromised disabled queer.”

“With respect,” another poster wrote, unknowingly foretelling the international controversy to come, “would you consider one night per week as a mask optional evening?”

A third poster shot the argument straight to 11: “aka one night a week where disabled/high risk people aren’t welcome. where’s the respect you mentioned?”

The new bar maintained a busy event schedule after opening, with dance and karaoke parties, drag shows, watch parties for WNBA games, and a variety show billed as “Not your grandmother’s burlesque.” Promotions for Last Ditch events on social media often contained the reminder to mask up.

But in time, business fell off and the bar felt a financial squeeze. Looking to attract more customers, ownership announced on social media on Aug. 31 that the Last Ditch would go mask optional on Saturday nights.

Hundreds of comments poured in, many accusing ownership of being ableist and risking the lives of immunocompromised customers.

The anguish was catnip for online trolls. In the days after the Globe story went viral, an anti-backlash backlash emerged, with people mocking the bar’s patrons with cruel social media quips and long think pieces.

As the evening approached 10 p. m., several dozen people — couples and people in small groups — walked through light rain to Last Ditch.

Patricia Sonaike, 24, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst student, said she had become interested in visiting Last Ditch after the bar had announced its relaxed mask policy, and before the controversy had made the news. The new policy, she said, is a bid to broaden the bar’s customer base.

“People are forgetting that this is a business that needs revenue,” she said.

While she was speaking to reporters, a man approached and asked if anyone could give him exactly 55 cents. He accepted a dollar, and offered to give back change.

Two visiting professors at Smith College, LeiAnna Hamel and Gianna Albaum, said they tried to get into Last Ditch but were turned away because they didn’t already know anyone who was inside. They were told the event was a “private party.”

Come back on another day, they were advised, once the hubbub has died down.

The infighting over the Last Ditch’s masking policy made headlines across the country and throughout Europe. But I wanted to look at the rest of Greenfield, a small town not far from where I grew up in rural Massachusetts. How does a community actually process a viral news story in their own town, involving its own friends and neighbors?

Mark Arsenault covers higher education for The Times.

Connections Coach

Ms. Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, has complicated politics: She is pro-gun, pro-oil and pro-gas — but also pro-environment and especially pro-fish.

Credit... Ash Adams for The New York Times

Supported by

By Michael Kruse

Michael Kruse chartered a boat and took seven flights in Alaska for this profile of Mary Peltola, reporting from Fairbanks, Anchorage, Bethel, Kwethluk and Kodiak.

Hard by the murky brown water of the Kuskokwim River, in a region reachable only by plane or boat, past weather-stunted willows and crude seasonal fish camps, dogs roamed muddy, rutted roads under low, dreary skies.

Here in the small village of Kwethluk in the vast tundra of southwestern Alaska, in the window of a house with unpainted sides and rotting wood steps, was a campaign placard for Mary Peltola.

“We are related,” said the man inside.

James Nicori, 77, sat in his chair and unspooled his Alaska Native connection to Ms. Peltola, the Democrat running for the Senate.

“Mary’s great-grandma and my grandpa were half sister, half brother,” Mr. Nicori said. Her mother was a girl here, Mr. Nicori said. She was a girl here.

“She understands how we struggle,” he said. “She is one of us.”

Ms. Peltola, a former congresswoman, is an uncommonly capable candidate. In Alaska, where Republicans far outnumber Democrats and independents far outnumber both, she is the rare member of her party who has proved she can win statewide. This year, she has campaigned on four-wheelers and floatplanes, in Xtratuf boots and traditional kuspuk shirts worn by the Indigenous Yup’ik people of Alaska. She has made stops in locales as isolated as an island 30-some miles from Russia, curating social media snippets while playing hard-to-get with most of the mainstream press four time zones away. The approach has been largely effective. Ms. Peltola beat the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, in the nonpartisan primary in August, and polling and fund-raising suggest she could do it again in November.

But in ways that have not been aired until now, Ms. Peltola, 53, is also an uncommonly complicated candidate. Genial and unassuming in public, she can be crass and apoplectic in private. Her campaign has been marred by accounts of her outbursts that left some aides unnerved. When she served in the House, she had one of the highest staff turnover rates on Capitol Hill.

The daughter of a Yup’ik woman from Alaska and a white man from Nebraska, Ms. Peltola grew up in three villages and the port city of Bethel, population 6,000, some 70 miles upcountry from the Bering Sea. She went to three different high schools and four different colleges. She has had three husbands — two children from her first, two more from her second, three stepchildren from her third — and moved from Bethel to Juneau to Anchorage and back.

Her politics are complicated, too, reflecting the idiosyncrasies of her state: She is pro-gun, pro-oil and pro-gas — but also pro-environment and especially pro-fish.

And she is, at root, a person whose people’s way of life is dying after decades of disruption to salmon fishing, the cascading consequences of climate change, corporate excess and government restrictions. There are fewer fish and more limits on fishing. People smile, but grievance stews.

In the Kwethluk Native Store, next to the sparse shelves with $6 canned chili and $7 jars of jelly, a sign warned that it was illegal to sell food stamps. In the Kwethluk Sport Store, a hand-drawn notice urged shoppers to stop huffing gas to get high.

Along another dirt road, in the house of another one of Ms. Peltola’s many relatives in Kwethluk, almost 1,000 miles from the state capital of Juneau and almost 4,000 from Washington, D. C., a wood stove burned.

“It’s getting to be hard to live,” said Alexie Nicolai, 73.

A single bulb lit the room, and a cross hung on the wall.

“My uncle, he used to tell us, ‘All the animals will go toward the ocean to die,’” Mr. Nicolai said. “He would tell us, ‘When starvation comes, it will come not just overnight, but slowly.’”

On her first political campaign, she was in the womb.

In early 1973, in the special election that kick-started the congressional career of Don Young, Alaska’s longtime Republican representative, two of his most ardent aides were the expectant parents of Ms. Peltola.

Ward Sattler, a teacher and small-plane pilot from the Great Plains, was Mr. Young’s district chairman. Liz Ann Andrew, “an Eskimo interpreter,” in the phrasing of a local newspaper, was an indefatigable canvasser, snowmobiling from village to village in subzero conditions.

Ms. Peltola was born five and a half months after Mr. Young won.

She grew up in Bethel, Kwethluk (with a population of roughly 500 at the time), Tuntutuliak (300), Platinum (50) and Bethel again, as her parents split up. She ate moose and seal and spent her summers on the Kuskokwim, captaining tender boats and cleaning, drying and smoking salmon.

“She was doing the things that I would traditionally put in the male category,” one of her best friends, Ana Hoffman, said this month in Bethel. “She didn’t wait for a guy to come back up the boat. She would back up the boat.”

Ms. Peltola spent her sophomore year in high school at a boarding school in Bethlehem, Pa.; her junior year at Bethel Regional; and her senior year in Fort Collins, Colo., where her grandmother lived.

She went to the University of Northern Colorado, the University of Alaska Fairbanks, the University of Alaska Southeast and the University of Alaska Anchorage — but never graduated.

As a college student, she was the runner-up for the Miss World Eskimo-Indian Olympics in 1993 and then crowned Miss National Congress of American Indians in 1995, performing two Yup’ik dances and wearing a wolf-hair headdress when she won.

In an article about her achievement, she said she wanted to get into politics. “I just have this fire inside me,” she told The Juneau Empire, “when I start reading these cases about Indian rights.”

She was an intern in the State Legislature in 1996. That year, at the age of 23, she ran to be a representative herself and barely lost. In 1998, the year she married for the first time, she ran again.

Then known as Mary Sattler, she campaigned for the State House as a Democrat, prioritizing would-be voters in villages. “Villagers say Sattler is a kass’amirteq, meaning someone who acts like a white person,” a reporter from The Anchorage Daily News wrote that August. Her campaign manager, who spoke better Yup’ik than she did, doubled as her interpreter.

She gave birth to a son in October, posing with him and her husband in an ad in the local newspaper, The Tundra Drums. “I will work hard to make sure our rural way of life is protected,” she wrote. “Our people need protection from outside interests determining how we hunt and live.”

She was elected that November.

“I’d explain that my mom is from Kwethluk, my dad was a schoolteacher in these villages,” Ms. Peltola said this month in Fairbanks in an interview with The New York Times.

“I think it’s important for people to know who you are,” she said, “so they understand your back story.”

In the 10 years she spent at the Capitol in Juneau, Ms. Peltola was chair of the “bush caucus,” the bipartisan group representing Alaska’s most remote regions. She worked to reduce teen alcohol abuse, stressed the importance of teaching the Yup’ik language and appealed for more state aid for rural areas. “We’re sitting,” she told a local reporter, “on a powder keg of poverty and resentment.”

She started meetings in her office, where she served her colleagues salmon. She befriended Lisa Murkowski, then a fellow state representative, now Alaska’s other Republican senator.

“She was very sure of herself,” said Ethan Berkowitz, a former state representative and the minority leader at the time. “She’s incredibly proud of her Yup’ik heritage, but she was able to walk in both worlds.”

Along the way, too, she had another son, divorced, remarried and had a third son and a daughter. Managing an increasingly topsy-turvy personal life, she also missed votes nearly 20 percent of the time, according to records — in part a result of having and caring for her kids.

She did not run for re-election in 2008. She separated from her second husband in 2009 — the same year she got together with her third.

In 2010, she helped Ms. Murkowski with her Senate campaign, and she was on the Bethel City Council from 2011 to 2013. She helped the community get a public indoor pool but missed more than a third of the votes.

Away from public office, she worked for a gold-mining project and as a lobbyist.

And the fish crisis mostly kept getting worse. The Yup’iks of the Kuskokwim couldn’t fish the way their people had fished for thousands of years. In an attempt at conservation, state and federal restrictions now determined when, how and how much they could fish, a scenario utterly counter to their culture of subsistence, severing the rhythms of generations and upending their relationship with the river and the salmon.

In 2017, in an interview with The Associated Press, Ms. Peltola likened the state of affairs to “a family member being sick.”

That year, she became the executive director of the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission, an intermediary between Alaska Natives and the outside agencies establishing and enforcing the rules and regulations.

“Like nearly everyone raised on the Kuskokwim, I am made of fish,” she wrote in 2020 in the commission’s annual report. “Not only do I crave eating fish year-round, but by May and June, I physically feel the need to catch and process fish.”

But things were different now.

“I have had to adjust my mind-set,” she wrote, “because there are fewer fish.”

And then, in 2022, the death of Representative Don Young led to a wide-open scramble of a special election.

The day of Mr. Young’s memorial service on Capitol Hill, Ms. Murkowski got a text from Ms. Peltola, according to the book Ms. Murkowski published last year. She wanted advice. She was thinking about getting into the race, calling it “the most crowded clown car ever.”

Ms. Peltola jumped in.

“One thing led to another,” she told The Times, “and of all the unlikely circumstances. …”

She won.

Ms. Murkowski worried for her.

Ms. Peltola, she thought, according to her book, was “a warm, positive, smart and authentic Yup’ik woman.” Now she was in Washington. “I thought of her mostly as a friend and mom suddenly in the middle of the complex, high-pressure world of the House with no time to prepare,” wrote Ms. Murkowski, who declined a request to comment for this story. “I offered her my son’s room to stay in and tried to make sure she got fed.”

Ms. Peltola wore Native mukluk boots to her swearing-in, alongside her third husband, Eugene Peltola Jr., her children and his. “I am humbled and deeply honored to be the first Alaska Native elected to this body, the first woman to hold Alaska’s House seat,” she said in her first floor speech.

She won again in the regular election in November, earning a full two-year term. She joined the moderate Blue Dog caucus as well as the Western caucus — “106 Republicans,” as she said, “and me.” She was one of the most bipartisan Democrats, bucking her party on guns, border security and oil and gas extraction.

She also missed more than 17 percent of the votes — significantly more than most of her peers. And her uneven temperament was an all but open secret.

“Everybody who knows anything about her, she has two things: a terrible work ethic and a terrible temper,” Art Hackney, a longtime Alaska-based Republican strategist who supports Mr. Sullivan, said in an interview this month in Anchorage.

In May of her first full year in Congress, her mother died. Four months later, she lost her husband. Mr. Peltola, 57, piloting a small plane, was hauling the antlers and meat of a moose that a group of hunters had killed. He labored to take off from their tundra site, according to the National Transportation Safety Board report, and crashed on the side of a hill in low-lying bushes and shrubs. The closest hospital was 400 miles away. One of the hunters unbuckled his lap belt and covered him in blankets. Mr. Peltola died in less than two hours.

Amid her grief, Ms. Peltola lost her 2024 re-election bid, to Nick Begich, a Republican — albeit by less than three points in a year when President Trump won Alaska by 14. She moved to Anchorage and was hired by a lobbying firm, making more than $340,000, according to a financial disclosure. Last fall, she was, briefly, a fellow at the Institute of Politics at the University of Chicago, teaching a seminar she titled “Blood Lines: What Does Being Native Even Mean?”

All the while, Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, worked to persuade her to run for the Senate. He considered her one of his top recruits.

“She is special,” said Lauren French, a Senate Majority PAC spokeswoman. “She has everything that it takes to be really successful there.”

Ms. Peltola thought so, too.

“I know that there’s a tendency to say people are half something, half another,” Ms. Peltola told The Times. “But I always thought of it as double. I really had, you know, double the language, double the perspectives, really different perspectives, really different values, really different worldviews — but double. And I thought that was a huge advantage.”

All summer long, she was all over — in Alakanuk and Savoonga and Nome, in Gambell and Galena and Unalakleet, in Dutch Harbor and Fort Yukon and Tok — listening to voters in school gyms, union halls and community theaters, hugging, waving and smiling on Facebook, Instagram and X.

In August, though, her campaign was on its way to a primary win and simultaneously in disarray. She fired a top adviser. She fired a deputy campaign manager. She changed her campaign manager. She made headlines for distancing herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris, who had issued a fund-raising appeal on her behalf.

Behind the scenes, as The Times reported last week, she could be a mercurial boss, with some former aides describing her as sometimes angry and profane. A spokesman for the campaign denied any pattern of abusive behavior. “Like any person who has gone through multiple personal tragedies in the span of a few months, Mary sometimes struggled to deal with her grief,” a campaign spokesman said.

Through it all, Ms. Peltola was dealing with the legal fallout from her husband’s death. She was worried about her children.

Her staff made her scarce to the mainstream press, providing scant details about where she would be campaigning. She was running what she called an “Alaska first” campaign, her staff insisted, focused on talking to Alaskans, not reporters from Washington or New York.

But on the ground, the arm’s-length strategy made more sense. During recent events in Fairbanks, Ms. Peltola didn’t sound simply off script. At times, she sounded as if she had no script.

“I’ll admit to you, every single place I go, I don’t go to the grocery store, I don’t go to the gas station, I don’t go to community events unless I have my passport,” she told a crowd that had packed a community center. She wore a blue flannel shirt and glasses with white rims. “Because early in this administration there was talk about ICE deporting Natives back to wherever it is they came from,” she said. “My mom’s family walked across the land bridge from Mongolia. …”

People laughed.

“We laugh,” she said, “at the things we’re most scared of.”

The next afternoon, at a different community center in Fairbanks, she said she had forgotten to help her 18-year-old daughter register to vote in the primary in August — but promised she would be registered for November.

She said that when she grew up in Alaska, it was “a state of abundance,” and that now “we are being starved out and nobody even cares.”

She said she wasn’t even feeling “aspirational” anymore — and just wanted to “get back to where we were in 1999.”

A few days later, at Alaska’s Senate Fisheries Debate in Kodiak, on the third anniversary of the death of her third husband, she wore salmon-shaped earrings made from the tusk of a walrus and asked moderators to repeat questions.

“Can you restate it please?”

“Say it again?”

To succeed statewide here, said John-Henry Heckendorn, an Anchorage-based Democratic strategist, a Democrat must assemble a convoluted coalition almost at odds with itself — Natives and not, rural and not, commercial fishermen and subsistence fishermen, on and on.

“Mary’s political talent,” he said, “has been her ability to inhabit those tensions.”

She inhabits those tensions because she is born of those tensions. Ms. Peltola is Alaska and Nebraska, the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and the Lower 48, Yup’ik collectivism and American individualism. Being “double” can be an advantage, she says, and she is not wrong. It also, though, can be a source of some untenable tug.

She is leading by a bit in polling and by a lot in fund-raising, but voters in Alaska are characteristically contrarian and unpredictable. This race, say independent analysts, could go either way.

On a recent rainy, windy evening in Anchorage, at a canvassing kickoff at an Alaska Democratic Party field office, Ms. Peltola was introduced by the former president of the Alaska A. F. L.-C. I. O. Ms. Peltola was wearing black Adidas and a kuspuk. She touched her face and smiled, looked out at her supporters and began her speech.

“Where do you even start?” she said.

Kitty Bennett, Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

Mary Peltola is one of the most important candidates in November's midterm elections. She's also one of the most complicated characters. It's why I flew 10,000 miles and chartered a boat to report this profile, traveling to courthouses, campaign events and the remote village of Kwethluk in the tundra of the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta.

In many ways, she embodies the frictions and idiosyncrasies of her one-of-a-kind, out-of-the-way state. How the voters of Alaska think about Ms. Peltola might very well determine the partisan balance of power in the country heading into next year.

Michael Kruse is a politics correspondent for The Times.

Some Republicans Issue a New Call on Trump’s War With Iran: End It Now

The New York Times September 27, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

As their midterm picture darkens, and gas and diesel prices soar, some Republicans who backed the war for months are now changing their tune.

By Tim Balk

As President Trump warned in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly in recent days that he might “annihilate” Iran, a growing number of Republicans were scrambling to find distance from a costly war that has swelled into a midterm crisis for the party.

The split screen showed how Mr. Trump and his party’s battleground candidates are increasingly at odds as the November elections approach. With no clear resolution in sight, the war has sent the prices of gasoline, diesel and heating oil upward, and cost increases have spilled across the economy. Mortgage rates have also climbed to seven percent, squeezing prospective homeowners already struggling with inflation.

While Mr. Trump is talking about escalating the war if he cannot strike a deal with Iran, Republicans in competitive races are losing patience with the fighting.

Representative Ashley Hinson, the party’s Senate nominee in Iowa, called at a news conference Friday for an “immediate” end to the war, saying she was “incredibly frustrated” by rising costs. Former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee in the Senate race in Michigan and an early cheerleader for the war, released an advertisement on Monday in which he declared that it “needs to end.”

Brinker Harding, a Republican trying to win a swing Nebraska congressional district that has been in his party’s hands for nearly a decade, said in an interview Friday that “we need to bring the war in Iran to a close as quickly as possible.” And Senator Jon Husted, who is working to fend off the Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, told reporters on Friday that “we got to bring the war to a close” — even as he added that any resolution should be on “acceptable” terms.

Still, many Republicans have been cautious about crossing Mr. Trump, fearing a backlash that could alienate Republican voters they need in November. Despite Ms. Hinson’s and Mr. Husted’s calls for an end to the war, they recently voted against resolutions to rein in Mr. Trump’s ability to carry on the conflict.

On Saturday, Mr. Trump said he rejected Iran’s latest cease-fire proposal, another signal that Republicans’ calls for an end to the war would not be swiftly answered. The proposal would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz — a vital oil-shipping corridor before the war — and restarted negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program.

Much of the conflict has played out as Mr. Trump conducted a primary season retribution campaign against Republicans he deemed disloyal.

“A lot of Republicans didn’t want to have a fight with him during the primaries,” said Carter Wrenn, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, referring to Mr. Trump. “But now that they’re over, it looks to me like some of them are now starting to separate.”

For Republicans in key races, Mr. Wrenn added, the war is a “big problem.”

Nationwide, the cost of a gallon of gasoline has climbed by 40 cents this month to roughly $4.50, according to the AAA motor club, with the Strait of Hormuz now stuck in a lethal monthslong stalemate. Mortgage rates are high and rising, and the cost of a gallon of diesel has climbed to about $6.50, threatening to further lift grocery prices by increasing transportation costs. The Trump administration is rushing to tamp down surging yields on some government bonds.

Republicans have worried about the conflict for months, as the president’s early promise of a military campaign lasting “four to five weeks” faded to months of on-and-off fighting and deepening public frustration.

Mr. Trump says his chief objective is to block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. “I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Mr. Trump said Tuesday in his speech to the U. N. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

And he has maintained that the coming election is not a factor in his decision-making on the war, going so far as to claim at times that he does not care about the midterms and does not think about Americans’ financial situations. “I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran,” Mr. Trump told the U. N. “It doesn’t even enter my mind.”

Not every battleground Republican has called for the war’s end, or offered even glancing criticism. In North Carolina, for example, the Republican nominee for Senate, Michael Whatley, has stood by the war. In Texas, the Republican Senate nominee, Ken Paxton, has avoided any daylight with Mr. Trump.

But Republicans have grown anxious that Mr. Whatley, a Trump ally, may face a narrowing path to victory. The party is also worried about Texas, a state where a Democrat has not won a Senate seat in decades.

“This war in Iran is a disaster,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, said at a news conference at a Dallas-area gas station on Saturday, warning that rising diesel costs would affect the price of a wide range of goods. “It must end.” (Mr. Paxton issued a statement saying, “Standing next to a gas pump doesn’t make Talarico the authority of affordability.”)

Some of the Republicans seen as having the best chances to defy a difficult political environment have been most vocally critical of the war.

Mr. Rogers’s reversal in Michigan was among the most striking. A longtime foreign-policy hawk and once a chair of the House Intelligence Committee, Mr. Rogers was an early supporter of the war. In May, Mr. Rogers told WDIV-TV that he viewed the war as a “win-win-win” for Americans.

But in his new ad, set at a supermarket, he acknowledged groceries cost “too much.” He also said that ending the war would swiftly bring down energy costs — a view that is generally not shared by economists.

In Iowa, a conservative-leaning state whose agricultural economy has been hit hard by rising fertilizer and diesel prices, Ms. Hinson was not alone in splitting with the president over the war. Two House Republicans in tough races, Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted this month to end the war or require explicit congressional authorization for it to move forward.

They were joined by five other Republicans, including two in competitive races: Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Tom Barrett of Michigan. Republicans still overwhelmingly voted to support the conflict, despite polling that suggests less than a third of likely voters in the midterms think Mr. Trump made the right decision in going to war. Ms. Hinson, a congresswoman, did not back the measure, but spoke out against the war in the days that followed.

A similar measure failed in the Senate last week, though Senator Susan Collins of Maine supported it. Ms. Collins, a centrist, has long opposed the war. She is seeking a sixth term in a Democratic-leaning state, and some polls show her in the lead or running roughly even with Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee.

Many Republicans are simply trying to avoid the issue, hoping to navigate past the economic headwinds by looking for other “positive things” they have done for constituents, said Matt Rexroad, a Republican strategist. But Mr. Rexroad expressed skepticism that either tiptoeing around the war or criticizing it forcefully would work.

“Republicans have a huge storm coming,” he said, “and it’s going to be pretty brutal for them all the way around.”

Emily Davies and Jesus Jiménez contributed reporting.

The Mean Girls Presidency

The New York Times September 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Molly Jong-Fast

Ms. Jong-Fast is a contributing Opinion writer.

I was once a teenage girl, but not a very cool one. I never had the right vintage jeans. I never wore the right high-heeled Free Lance boots, the ones that all the cool girls had.

I think about this a lot while watching how Donald Trump runs the White House and the world alongside a high school clique of dumb jocks (Pete Hegseth!) and hot cheerleaders (Natalie Harp!) and nerdy suck-ups (Mike Johnson!). My Queen Bee — my Regina George from “Mean Girls,” my Cher Horowitz from “Clueless” — wasn’t the president of the United States, but at the time she felt arbitrarily powerful, profoundly charismatic and definitely wealthier than I was. She bullied me about my weight and lack of style. She had her friends shun me, too.

My peers were rewarded with the social relevance that comes from pleasing the top of the food chain. Now, looking at the White House, I almost feel sympathy for Marco Rubio, wearing uncomfortable shoes in the hopes of fitting in.

Mr. Trump’s cabinet of curiosities wears matching $145 Florsheim Oxfords, gifted by the president himself. They’re reportedly eating the same “living diet,” which consists almost entirely of hunks of meat and globs of sauerkraut. (Adherents are said to include: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Vice President JD Vance, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. himself). Mr. Trump’s favorite aide, Ms. Harp, passes the president positive news coverage and good polls like she’s the “Mean Girls” gossip Gretchen Wieners. Other White House staffers and cabinet members have begun to emulate the president’s leggy blond echo chamber cultivator, so much so that the White House has been overtaken by a kind of sycophancy Olympics; members of Trump’s inner circle never miss the chance to praise him in televised cabinet meetings.

In short, our government is being run by a clique of middle-aged men. Marco and Pete don’t drink identical Iced Banana Bread Matchas or wear pink on Wednesdays, but the social-emotional engine behind our government is the same as the one that runs the popular girls’ clique at Spence. This dynamic — more than another unnecessary war or even a cost of living crisis — will be the key to Mr. Trump’s undoing.

Historically, White Houses have been Byzantine power structures with wildly elaborate interpersonal dynamics. Even George Washington’s cabinet was legendary for the fierce tension between Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. Centuries later, Joe Biden’s White House was a story of competing fiefs, from Anita Dunn’s to Antony Blinken’s to Jeff Zients’s. In a structure like this, ideas and proposals needed to be well developed, allies needed to be gathered, and, in general, bad decisions can often be slowed or stalled by the normal workings of bureaucracy.

Mr. Trump’s cabinet was picked like something out of Bama rush, and, boy, does the government run like it. The president reportedly considered sizzle reels of candidates’ cable news hits; the focus was not on who was most qualified to do the job, but who managed to best dazzle dear leader. Once a cabinet member was installed in office, it seemed like the only thing that mattered was continuing to tell the president what he wanted to hear — or saying the right thing on TV — as opposed to giving sound advice in service of the nation.

Those who didn’t do that could be dropped over the slightest misstep, and plenty of people who have spent much of the past few years dressing up just right and sucking up to the man in charge have already been kicked off the popular kids’ table — Pam Bondi, Kristi Noem, even Marjorie Taylor Greene. Axios recently reported that Mr. Trump’s people no longer try to stop him from doing things; as a longtime adviser and admirer told Axios: “Why bother? He’s the boss.”

Mr. Trump doesn’t want to hear it. And it shows.

He’s regularly saying things like “affordability is a con job” and “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody.” He’s obsessed with building a ballroom even if it ignores the fire code (“I am the code,” he reportedly declared), a triumphal arch with snipers on top, and slapping his name on the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts — or else. Our unpopular president thinks he’s actually popular (he denounced polls, which he often calls “fake,” at least nine times in August alone), so popular that he seems to believe that people are going to carve his face into Mount Rushmore. He doesn’t see the problem with A. I. or crypto or his family’s self-enrichment. Last week, he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists from the White House, simply because he didn’t like their apparently negative coverage.

Maybe because everybody around him was too scared to tell him.

Last week, Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit an all-time low, Hispanic voters are bailing on Republicans in droves, and the economy — the single most important issue to many Americans — is only working for the very wealthy. Does Mr. Trump have any idea?

This president, for much of his two terms in office, seemed to have a preternatural understanding of how to twist the press and the public to believe his narratives about the world; now he’s living in such a fantasy world that his greatest power has been effectively neutralized. It’s the same overconfidence that seems to have led to the failures of many Trump-branded products — steaks, mortgages, casinos, vodka, a for-profit university and an airline. It now seems likely that MAGA Republicans in the midterms could be his next project to fail.

In “Mean Girls,” that great parable of clique-dom, Regina falls from grace only after she loses what makes her powerful — her hot boyfriend, her hot body and her coterie of followers. She’s supplanted by one of them, Cady Heron, who eventually learns that teenage girl cliques are bad and gives up her spring fling crown.

I don’t think such a lesson is in store for Mr. Trump. What would learning not to be a bully even look like for him? Ending the trade war with Canada and getting mani-pedis with Mark Carney? Inviting Chuck Schumer for an Oval Office tea and glow-up? Promotions for the female and Black military officers who have been sidelined or fired? Checks from World Liberty Financial sent out in restitution for those rounded up in brutal ICE raids?

Eventually I learned to stand up to my bully. If the midterms go their way, the Democrats will, I hope, have the means to be able to as well. As he becomes even more self-destructive, the Republicans could — in a late-breaking fit of attempted self-preservation — do so too. Teenage girls can’t invoke the 25th Amendment on their bullies, but this cabinet theoretically could.

Molly Jong-Fast is the host of the “Fast Politics” podcast and the author of “How to Lose Your Mother: A Daughter’s Memoir.”

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The gap between technology and policymaking has gotten wider than ever with artificial intelligence, leaving a global policy vacuum as A. I. models rapidly advance.

Credit... Emmanuel Polanco

Supported by

By Adam Satariano and Cecilia Kang

Adam Satariano reported from London and Cecilia Kang from Washington and New York.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, gathered senior officials for an exclusive meeting at a 19th-century palace outside Brussels this month.

The goal was to prepare for a speech outlining the 27-nation bloc’s priorities for the coming year, with artificial intelligence dominating the agenda. The region’s new A. I. czar, Jim Hagemann Snabe, the chairman of German industrial giant Siemens, outlined ways that Europe could use the technology for economic gain. Others raised concerns about A. I. safety and growing risks, two people briefed on the gathering said.

Since the Sept. 4 meeting, Ms. von der Leyen and her commissioners have been left asking what they can do to address the fast-changing technology, one of the people said. Should they ramp up regulation to address A. I.’s emerging dangers? Or would doing so carry economic and geopolitical costs if other countries did not clamp down as well?

They have not landed on any final conclusions, with more discussions among European leaders planned this year.

“A. I. comes with a balance of possibilities and risks,” Ms. von der Leyen said at her State of the Union speech on Sept. 16. “Without addressing these risks, we will never be able to unlock A. I.’s potential.”

Versions of the Belgium meeting are playing out nearly everywhere as many governments struggle to get a handle on a technology that has rapidly outpaced their ability to respond. A. I. is evolving so quickly that laws passed two years ago are having limited effect, proposed bills to regulate the technology are stalling without a vote and international summits to discuss what to do are being swiftly forgotten.

A. I. has made the gap between policymaking and technology one of the widest ever, according to more than 20 interviews with lawmakers, technologists and policy experts. Many governments are torn between wanting to harness A. I. and fearing its risks. And they are further mired by national politics, limited technological know-how, geopolitical divisions and reluctance to fall behind in a race that could shape economic power and national security for decades to come.

Many countries are waiting for the two leading A. I. nations — the United States and China — to take a cue from their A. I. policies. Yet in the United States, the Trump administration has been divided over A. I. safety, with President Trump saying regulation would hurt innovation and cede ground to China. China itself has imposed some rules on A. I., especially to censor chatbot content, but also raced ahead with development.

“There’s this assumption that there are adults in the room on this issue, but there are no adults in this room,” said Sean Ó Heigeartaigh, director of the AI: Futures and Responsibility Program at the University of Cambridge, who is a member of a European Union advisory board on A. I. “That is what makes all of this so completely terrifying.”

What’s left is a policy vacuum, with A. I. companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI largely left to police themselves. While the European Union passed a law regulating A. I. in 2024, it has taken years to carry out, and some say it already needs to be updated to account for advances. India, Japan, Australia, Canada and Kenya have taken a lighter touch or a wait-and-see approach, while Brazil is debating more comprehensive rules.

Pressure to act is growing, especially after the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind recently called for slowing development of the most advanced A. I. models and for strengthening government oversight. Researchers have described scenarios in which self-improving A. I. could escape human control and cause catastrophic damage. Public opinion in the United States has turned against A. I., with a recent New York Times poll finding that 61 percent of likely voters opposed the construction of data centers that power A. I.

The policy challenges were on display last week. In Washington on Thursday, President Trump and President Xi Jinping of China stressed the importance of A. I. to their nations but did not agree on safety protocols. The United States and China are the world’s leading A. I. developers, making cooperation between them essential for international safety standards, but are also competitors wary of giving the other a technology advantage.

At the annual General Assembly of the United Nations in New York last week, many world leaders agreed on the need to address A. I.’s dangers, while Mr. Trump said the United States would reject “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” the technology.

Safety experts have warned that crucial time is disappearing before oversight becomes harder to impose because A. I. will have spread so widely.

“Governments consider things in time scales of years, not weeks or months,” said Darren Jones, a member of Britain’s Parliament who worked on A. I. and technology policy under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer. “Institutionally, we’re not set up to keep up with the pace of development.”

(The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

In 2024, Europe adopted the world’s first comprehensive law for artificial intelligence. The A. I. Act, which was designed to impose safeguards on the technology’s riskiest uses, was hailed by European leaders as a blueprint for regulation.

Two years later, it has become a cautionary tale.

Implementation has been slowed by shifts in priorities and fears that regulation could weaken Europe’s competitiveness against the United States and China. Some of the law’s most consequential rules governing high-risk A. I. uses have been delayed. Staffing and budget constraints have further complicated enforcement.

The A. I. Act was proposed in early 2021, 18 months before OpenAI released ChatGPT. Intended to grapple with issues like facial recognition software, the rules were revised to address powerful new general-purpose A. I. systems like OpenAI’s GPT.

But the technology has only accelerated since the law’s passage in 2024. Now the bleeding edge of A. I. comes in the form of so-called agents that can act with little human oversight. Companies are planning for a day when A. I. can create the next versions of itself.

“When we adopted it, we couldn’t even conceive of what A. I. is now able to do,” Valérie Hayer, a member of the European Parliament, said of the A. I. Act at a recent news conference. The law was ahead of its time, she said, but “we have to adapt.”

Europe’s challenge is made worse because it trails the United States and China in A. I. Last year, just six months after the law passed, Emmanuel Macron, the president of France, said Europe risked trying to police a technology it had no role in shaping.

“If we let the Americans and the Chinese have all the champions to themselves, one thing is certain: We may have the best regulations in the world, but we won’t be regulating anything,” he said.

The law’s limits are becoming clear. In July, OpenAI models broke out of a restricted testing environment and hacked the A. I. start-up Hugging Face. But because the breach happened during a testing period, it fell within a murky area for enforcement. The A. I. Act generally exempts research and tests done before a model is released in Europe.

Supporters of the A. I. Act argue it was designed to evolve with the technology. It includes transparency and test requirements that A. I. safety experts said were needed to ensure the technology was deployed responsibly. Regulators have powers to demand information, appoint outside experts to evaluate models and order fixes. Authorities can ultimately block an A. I. model across Europe and impose fines of up to 7 percent of a company’s annual revenue.

“Europe has always been clear that A. I. must be developed safely and transparently, and remain under human control,” said Thomas Regnier, a European Commission spokesman. “This is why we have the A. I. Act.”

Yet enforcement requires technical know-how that is still being built. A 60-member scientific panel established under the A. I. Act to offer expertise on frontier models and risks was appointed only in June. A new office in the European Commission meant to carry out many of the rules has only about 40 people working in an A. I. safety unit, prompting an amendment to the law to provide more resources.

Gabriele Mazzini, a European Commission official who was a lead author of the A. I. Act and resigned in 2024, said the law’s implementation and enforcement was disappointing.

“Their goal was to pass the law and think about implementation later,” he said. “There is a disconnect between the law and the reality of what is being regulated.”

Another disconnect was with the United States.

Representative Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts, said her jaw dropped when she read in April that Anthropic was warning that its latest A. I. model, Mythos, was too dangerous for the public. Anthropic said the model’s extraordinary ability to find software vulnerabilities could cause a cybersecurity “reckoning.”

During votes that day in the House of Representatives, Ms. Trahan crossed the floor to share her alarm with Representative Jay Obernolte, a California Republican who has a master’s degree in A. I. The two quickly drafted a bill to require safety testing of A. I. models.

Few lawmakers shared their urgency, she said. Some members wanted to wait until after November’s midterm elections to focus on a technically complicated issue. Others were reluctant to put guardrails on an industry that Mr. Trump wanted to keep free of regulations. Amid intense corporate lobbying, members squabbled over details, and the bill was revised multiple times.

Five months later, the bill and dozens of other proposals related to A. I. safety and security are on ice. Even after reports that models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic autonomously hacked other organizations, there are no votes in sight.

“It’s hugely disappointing,” Ms. Trahan said. “If Congress doesn’t keep pace with A. I., the dangers are even worse than with any other technology waves we’ve experienced.”

Representative Ted Lieu, Democrat of California, has spent years trying to make the same case. Soon after ChatGPT’s release in 2022, he wrote an opinion piece for The Times with the headline “A. I. Freaks Me Out.”

Mr. Lieu, who has a degree in computer science, later joined Mr. Obernolte to lead a congressional task force to educate lawmakers on A. I., inviting industry leaders like Sam Altman of OpenAI to give technology demonstrations.

But after an initial burst of interest, attendance at the events fizzled.

When OpenAI revealed the Hugging Face breach this summer, Mr. Lieu introduced a bill that would require a kill switch for A. I. models if they became too dangerous. He told colleagues that the moment was a five-alarm fire. Still, he couldn’t get enough interest.

“I’m more scared than I was in 2023,” Mr. Lieu said.

Representative Brett Guthrie of Kentucky, the influential Republican chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said Congress probably would not bring a vote on any A. I. legislation until next year.

At a recent conference, Mr. Guthrie said that he did not understand how the models worked and that he did not use A. I. frequently.

“We wouldn’t want to do something in a lame-duck session to do it quickly and not get it right,” he said.

The recent A. I. hacks have led to a burst of activity, with A. I. leaders calling for more government cooperation and collaborating on safety and monitoring techniques to prevent accidents.

In the United States, lawmakers introduced bills to create a federal agency to police A. I. models, kill switch requirements and a ban on the most powerful models that exceed human capabilities. Votes could be held after the midterms, particularly with A. I. becoming a key campaign topic.

Mr. Trump separately proposed an “A. I. Force” and a new “A. I. czar” for the White House, without providing details.

At the U. N. General Assembly, leaders from more than 20 countries — including Ms. von der Leyen and Mr. Macron — signed a letter calling for collective actions on A. I. safety. Members of the Security Council spoke in rare harmony on the need for global A. I. safeguards.

“Industry, governments and society must act now,” the letter read.

In Washington, Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi did not strike a deal on A. I., but the two sides established new paths for communication about managing the greatest risks related to the technology.

While Mr. Trump has called A. I. safety risks a “hoax,” Mr. Xi’s views remain less clear. At the White House, the Chinese leader said, “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage A. I. for good and ensure the development of A. I. is always under human control.”

The two countries said they would keep talking about the issue.

My colleague, Adam Satariano, and I began this story with a question: Why has regulation of artificial intelligence been so challenging for governments around the world. Adam, who is based in London, and I talked to government leaders, technologists and policy experts for Europe, China and the United States. We also talked to leaders on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York earlier this month. We wanted to take readers inside the rooms of decision-makers to show how across the globe, they were getting tripping up with the fast development of A. I.

Adam Satariano is a technology correspondent for The Times, based in London.

Cecilia Kang reports on technology and regulatory policy for The Times from Washington. She has written about technology for over two decades.

Kyle MacLachlan: David Lynch’s Singular Weirdo Is Secretly a Normie

The New York Times September 27, 2026

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Credit...

Supported by

By Melena Ryzik

Visuals by Sinna Nasseri

To hear him tell it, Kyle MacLachlan is not as eccentric as you might think. He plays a lot of golf. He likes to garden — or to stand, surveying his garden, with a cup of black coffee. To putter around his Manhattan apartment, where he welcomed me one recent sunny afternoon for a conversation that was notable for its genial mildness.

“I feel pretty regular — kind of boring, actually,” he told me, without actorly gloss. “Not that interesting, to be honest.”

But to know MacLachlan’s more than 40 years onscreen is to witness him as a series of weirdos — or normies in increasingly bizarre scenarios — basically from the jump. His very first role was the lead of David Lynch’s epic version of “Dune” in 1984, the beginning of a career-defining relationship with the avant-garde filmmaker that continues to disarm and enthrall fans, and MacLachlan himself.

“I put my faith in David,” MacLachlan, 67, writes in his new memoir, “Fictional Selves,” describing the audition for “Dune” and really, everything that followed. “In his simple, albeit mystical way, he gives me the confidence to get through it.”

Before the eerie oddballs of Lynch’s “Twin Peaks” and the sexually macabre “Blue Velvet,” before he portrayed a long line of what he called “doctors with issues” — including the emasculated Trey MacDougal on “Sex and the City” — MacLachlan was battle-tested by the surreal sci-fi of “Dune” when he was in his early 20s.

Constantly sprayed with smoke and sand during the seven-month shoot in Mexico, he spat up red grit at the end of each day; already lean, he lost 15 pounds during filming. The production was “insane, truly,” he said. But with no other movie experience, he thought, “This must be how it goes.”

“I can still remember the smell of the suit,” he said of his suffocating, otherworldly get-up. “It just felt like play.”

He digs into this in “Fictional Selves,” out Sept. 29 and written with Jon Sternfeld. It charts MacLachlan’s kinship with Lynch, who died last year; his roles, both earned and lost (he passed on “sex, lies and videotape”); and his romantic relationships, including with Laura Dern, his “Blue Velvet” co-star, and the actress he cheated on her with.

Going into the book project, he recalled saying: “If I’m going to do this, then it’s not all, ‘Look at me, look at all the great successes.’ You’ve got to see the other side. That was important to me.”

In the book, MacLachlan calls Hollywood “an industrial-size insecurity machine,” but he has navigated it handily, popping up in some of the most boundary-pushing TV shows and films. If it sometimes seemed as if he were being towed along in an off-kilter wake, like some dementedly gung-ho water skier — well, he knew when to keep bobbing up.

“You could call Kyle a postmodern matinee idol that was suddenly David’s to subvert,” said Graham Wagner, a creator of the dystopic Amazon hit show “Fallout,” on which MacLachlan stars as a darkly secretive father. They’ve known each other for more than a decade, having met when Wagner was a writer on the comedy series “Portlandia,” and MacLachlan played its doofy mayor.

“Kyle’s thing is to say yes,” Wagner said, whether that’s to singing the “Portland anthem” with no script or direction, or to starring in camp like “Desperate Housewives” and “Showgirls.” Wagner added, “He’s almost like a British actor — it’s full commitment with no cost to it.”

Wagner recalled when they were shooting a tricky “Fallout” scene on a specialized stage with limited takes. “It’s pressure, pressure, pressure, and then as soon as our director called ‘Cut!’ Kyle will turn to me and start doing a Popeye voice,” Wagner said. “Regardless of how heavy the work was, Kyle stayed bright and light.”

In his memoir, MacLachlan has another term for this trait; he calls himself the Great Compartmentalizer. That quality may be what intrigued Lynch, a wild visionary who also presented as an aw-shucks Boy Scout.

In “Twin Peaks,” too, as the F. B. I. agent Dale Cooper — the pinnacle role of MacLachlan’s career — he is both a Lynchian stand-in and a guide. “I feel I’m kind of walking the audience through the Lynch realm,” he said. “Like, you’re going to go to a very scary place now, you’re going to see some crazy stuff. But come with me and you’re going to be OK; we’re going to navigate this together.”

Losing the filmmaker is not something MacLachlan has come to terms with; in our conversation, he referred to Lynch in the present tense. “He is just such a big part of who I am,” MacLachlan said. They were neighbors in Los Angeles, and the actor would visit his director regularly. “He had a beautiful complex with a couple houses, these labyrinth sort of pathways,” MacLachlan recalled. “I’d see him from a distance, and he’s like” — MacLachlan dropped into an impression of Lynch’s barking voice, which in the book is represented in all caps — “‘Kale! Get out here.’” (Kale was Lynch’s nickname for him.)

Over coffee (of course) and croissants, or in Lynch’s wood shop, they reminisced or talked about film ideas — MacLachlan as an old Elvis, living in a trailer park. MacLachlan recorded some of these conversations, but Lynch asked him not to share them.

Creatively, “he was doing something every day, which was pretty inspirational,” MacLachlan said. “He was my anchor.”

Their relationship was almost legendary in artistic circles. It was symbiotic, authentic, “a staggering accomplishment,” said Ethan Hawke, a friend of MacLachlan’s. “There are a lot of other actors who would peacock around sets flaunting that, but Kyle does the opposite.”

He’s “extremely easy to be around, unpretentious, and disarming in his humility,” Hawke added.

Hawke, a co-star with MacLachlan in a cinematic “Hamlet” from 2000, said that his pal excels at playing the outer edges not because of his own quirks, “but because he’s a brilliant actor who had early exposure to great directors,” including Oliver Stone (“The Doors”) and Bruce Beresford (“Rich in Love”), in the ’90s. “And he’s carried that knowledge with him for his entire career.”

The original “Twin Peaks” discombobulated television and obsessed audiences when it aired in 1990, arguably paving the way for daring, prestige shows a generation later (in part because future creators, like Wagner, were watching). But it was in “Twin Peaks: The Return” from 2017 that MacLachlan thought he did his finest work, playing Cooper, his dastardly doppelgänger and Dougie, a blank simulacra who is primed for comedy. Lynch directed all 18 episodes himself, and when MacLachlan sees clips of it float through his social-media feed, it’s like Lynch is “alive again, and I’m feeling the energy and the joy,” he said.

His own goofy side is lately on display in his online persona. He posts skits and dances like a car lot windsock, and hosts a podcast, “What Are We Even Doing?,” on which he interviews Gen Z musicians and comedians. It’s a project he cooked up with his wife of 24 years, the producer Desiree Gruber. After dating the supermodel Linda Evangelista, he encountered Gruber at his chiropractor’s office. They have a son, Callum, a college freshman. (Callum has lent his wardrobe to his dad’s intergenerational TikToks.)

MacLachlan can still telegraph a boyish energy, though he now has a robust silver mane. In clear-framed glasses and a dark polo, slim khakis and sock sneakers, he showed me around his Manhattan space, one of two adjoining apartments in Chelsea that he and Gruber have (they mostly live in Los Angeles). The piano, the art supplies — they were all for his wife and child. He wrote his memoir in part, he said, for his son to read: One day, “he might want to take a trip down memory lane and learn a little bit more about who his dad was.”

MacLachlan grew up in Yakima, Wash., the eldest of three boys in a socially conservative family. His father was a lawyer turned stockbroker, an avid golfer who loved a routine, and his mother was a creative doer, who got her son interested in theater. His parents divorced when he was a teenager, and by doing plays and studying acting at college in Seattle, he found his niche: “I gave birth to myself,” he wrote in his book.

His mother, who died of ovarian cancer when he was in his 20s, remained a sounding board for him in his early career; he even showed her the “Blue Velvet” script (she had qualms). Gruber, a former Manhattan publicist, also helped steer him; it was at her insistence that he did “Sex and the City.”

He was nervous about being conflated with the character, whose marriage to Kristin Davis’s Charlotte implodes, in part because of his impotence. But the actors had chemistry. “I don’t think we had much time together before we were kissing all over Manhattan for the montage at the beginning of the Trey story line,” Davis recalled. After Agent Cooper, it’s the role MacLachlan is most often recognized for, he said.

Davis gets it, too. “People do still talk to me about Trey,” she said. “And online, there is often debate about whether Charlotte should have tried harder to make it work with Trey. Which is very sweet, and I really attribute that to Kyle’s talent.”

At this stage in his life, MacLachlan is a known entity. Wagner envisioned him for “Fallout” because MacLachlan once told him he wanted to do “a great big sci-fi.” But he also still sends in tapes for roles. “I think as an actor, you never are quite comfortable somehow,” MacLachlan said. “I don’t think you should ever be quite comfortable. You should just always be a little hungry.”

“I still love working,” he added. He might like to do a musical, or just showcase how he’s at ease “being me, warts and all.”

As this deceptively regular guy put it, “I like to be outside, running around, being an idiot.”

Melena Ryzik is a roving culture reporter at The Times, covering the personalities, projects and ideas that drive the creative world.

Washington Taxed Its Millionaires. Now the Rich Want It Repealed.

The New York Times September 27, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Washington State voters will get a chance to accept or reject the 9.9 percent income tax on millionaires approved by the Legislature, which broke the state’s taboo against levying income taxes.

By Anna Griffin

Voters in Washington State will soon be asked to decide which they resent more: rich people or new taxes.

At issue is the state’s new “millionaires tax,” a 9.9 percent tax on income over $1 million a year that is expected to bring in more than $3 billion annually and, in the process, ease if not solve the state’s ongoing fiscal problems.

Critics want voters to repeal it and bar state leaders from imposing income taxes in the future, arguing the millionaires tax will drive out wealthy entrepreneurs and eventually lead to income taxes on everyone else.

“The goal is to put an income tax on every Washingtonian,” former United States Representative Jaime Herrera Beutler, a Republican, said at a recent news conference organized by one of the campaigns working to repeal the tax. “Don’t let them fool you.”

The November election will test how voters feel about taxing the rich up and down the West Coast. In California, voters are considering both a “millionaire tax” and a “billionaire tax.” The less debated proposal asks voters to make permanent a temporary income tax hike on couples who earn at least $743,000 a year.

Voters will also decide whether to approve a new wealth tax on people with at least $1 billion in assets, a proposal that has generated enormous blowback from wealthy residents as well as teachers and health care interests who fear it will damage the state budget.

But Washington is unique on the so-called Left Coast, one of just nine states that do not tax personal income, and voters have rejected income taxes 10 times over nearly a century. It is also at a crossroads. The state’s fiscal system, which relies on property taxes, sales taxes and other fees that hit lower-income residents harder, has not kept up with expansions in government programs and the rising cost of basic services.

“People who don’t know much about Washington politics would assume we have a highly progressive tax code,” said Rian Watt, executive director of the nonprofit Economic Opportunity Institute, a progressive research and advocacy group in Seattle. “The reality is, we have a tax code written in the course of a couple of months in the 1930s.”

This spring, the Democrat-dominated State Legislature approved the income tax for wealthy residents along with a slate of tax cuts for lower-income households, such as eliminating the state sales tax on diapers, soap and over-the-counter drugs.

Repeal proponents say Washington’s tax system is a major reason the state has served as an incubator for companies like Microsoft, Amazon and Starbucks. The millionaires tax, along with the election of progressive and socialist candidates, including Mayor Katie Wilson of Seattle, sends a signal to businesses that they are no longer valued, they say.

“This has gone from one of the most attractive places to start a business to the least attractive,” said Brian Heywood, a hedge fund millionaire whose political action committee collected more than 500,000 signatures to place the tax repeal on the ballot.

Washington has suffered high-profile departures in recent years as the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Starbucks co-founder Howard Schultz moved to Florida. The Valve co-founder Gabe Newell recently bought an estate there.

But just 25,000 households make enough to pay the new tax. A Cornell University researcher named Cristobal Young studied the impact of taxes on higher earners in New Jersey and California and found minimal out-migration in their wake. Washington also hasn’t yet seen significant out-of-state movement after lawmakers created a capital-gains tax in 2021.

“Overwhelmingly, millionaires stay,” Mr. Young said. “They pay the new tax rate. They figure out ways around it. More likely there will be some people who were thinking of moving to Washington who change their minds, but it all amounts to migration at the margins.”

The other big argument against the millionaires tax involves the camel’s nose under the tent: Once an income tax is established, state lawmakers may look beyond millionaires. Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, has pledged to veto any attempt to expand who pays or to raise the rate, but he won’t be in office forever.

“Who do you trust?” Mr. Heywood said.

Until recently, Mr. Heywood, who is also responsible for Washington ballot measures this fall that would expand parental rights over school records and ban transgender girls from playing scholastic sports, was the chief public face of the anti-tax effort.

But allies recently turned to Ms. Herrera Beutler to replace Mr. Heywood, whose conservative politics have become one of the arguments for keeping the tax.

Progressives have described the repeal initiative as “a tax break for Brian Heywood and his friends.” They’ve also recruited their own pro-tax millionaires, including the travel writer and TV host Rick Steves, who lives in Edmonds, Wash., and the “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings, who commutes to California from Seattle to tape the quiz show.

“I like the idea that we could bring back an America where it’s embarrassing for wealthy people to say, ‘Even though I could afford this, and it will improve public services in our state, I’d rather fight it,’” Mr. Jennings said.

If the repeal passes, state leaders would lose billions of dollars in revenue that they are counting on for future budgets, forcing them to cut spending, reverse some of the accompanying tax relief or find other revenue.

Opponents of the millionaires tax have also sued to stop its implementation. They argue that it is illegal under a 1933 Washington Supreme Court ruling that income counts as property. That decision effectively blocked a graduated income tax in the state, because the Washington Constitution requires property taxes to be “uniform.”

The constitutional lawsuit is expected to reach the Washington Supreme Court before the tax takes effect in 2028.

Laurel Rosenhall contributed reporting from Sacramento.

Anna Griffin is the Pacific Northwest bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of Washington, Idaho, Alaska, Montana and Oregon.
